Alice praises Dinah's skill at catching mice and birds, and the remaining creatures depart.

knowledge.learns: The animals dry off by running; her account of Dinah frightens away the birds.

timeline.title: Chapter 4: The Rabbit Sends in a Little Bill
timeline.summary: Mistaken for a housemaid, Alice grows trapped inside the Rabbit's house, escapes by eating a cake, and meets a Caterpillar.
events: The Rabbit mistakes Alice for Mary Ann and sends her home for gloves and a fan.
In his upstairs room she drinks from an unlabelled bottle and grows until an arm is out the window and a foot up the chimney.
She frightens the Rabbit and Pat with her hand, then kicks Bill up the chimney.
The crowd throws pebbles through the window; they turn into cakes, and Alice eats one and shrinks.
She escapes the pursuing crowd, plays defensively with an enormous puppy, and runs away.
Beside a mushroom she looks up and sees a blue Caterpillar smoking a hookah.

knowledge.learns: The unlabelled bottle enlarges her, and a cake made from a thrown pebble shrinks her.
An enormous arm occupies his window; his attempted entry and Bill's descent fail.

timeline.title: Chapter 5: Advice from a Caterpillar
timeline.summary: The Caterpillar questions Alice and tells her the mushroom changes height; she experiments until she regains her usual size.
events: The Caterpillar asks who Alice is, tells her to keep her temper, and has her recite the altered Father William verse.
Offended by her complaint about being three inches high, it nevertheless tells her opposite sides of the mushroom change height.
Alice takes two pieces; the right-hand piece shrinks her sharply and the left-hand piece sends her neck above the trees.
A Pigeon attacks and calls her a serpent; Alice admits she eats eggs but denies seeking the Pigeon's.
Alternating mushroom pieces, Alice regains her usual height, then shrinks to nine inches before approaching a little house.

knowledge.learns: Opposite mushroom pieces shrink and enlarge her; careful alternation can restore her usual height.

timeline.title: Chapter 6: Pig and Pepper
timeline.summary: Alice enters the Duchess's peppery kitchen, carries away a baby that becomes a pig, and asks the Cheshire Cat for directions.
events: A fish-faced footman delivers the Queen's croquet invitation; Alice gets past the frog-faced footman by opening the door herself.
In the smoky kitchen the cook throws dishes while the Duchess nurses and shakes her sneezing baby.
The Duchess flings the baby to Alice and leaves; Alice carries it outside to save it.
The baby becomes a pig, which Alice sets down to trot into the wood.
The Cheshire Cat describes the Hatter and March Hare as mad, vanishes and reappears, and asks about the baby.
Alice chooses the March Hare's direction, sees the Cat vanish slowly to its grin, and enlarges herself before approaching the Hare's house.

knowledge.learns: The baby has become a pig; the Cat says both the Hatter and March Hare are mad and will see her at croquet.
Alice tells it that the baby turned into a pig.

timeline.title: Chapter 7: A Mad Tea-Party
timeline.summary: Alice endures an ill-mannered tea-party, leaves, and finally enters the garden by remembering the key before shrinking.
events: Alice sits at the March Hare's table despite cries of 'No room' and is offered wine that is not there.
The Hatter asks an unanswerable riddle and explains that his quarrel with Time has left the party at six o'clock.
The Dormouse tells an interrupted story of three sisters in a treacle-well; the party moves places for a clean cup.
Insulted by the Hatter, Alice leaves while the hosts try to put the Dormouse into the teapot.
A door in a tree returns her to the hall; she takes the key, unlocks the garden door, shrinks with mushroom, and enters.

knowledge.learns: The Hatter says Time stopped cooperating after the Queen's concert, so the party remains at tea-time.

timeline.title: Chapter 8: The Queen’s Croquet-Ground
timeline.summary: Alice protects three gardeners from the Queen, joins a chaotic croquet game, and helps the Cheshire Cat evade a beheading dispute.
events: Alice finds three card gardeners painting white roses red to conceal their mistake.
The royal procession arrives; Alice stands, answers the Queen, and calls her order to behead Alice nonsense.
The Queen orders the gardeners executed, but Alice hides them in a flower-pot and the soldiers report their heads gone.
Alice joins croquet with live flamingoes, hedgehogs, and card-soldier arches; the Rabbit says the Duchess is sentenced for boxing the Queen's ears.
The Cheshire Cat's head appears; Alice introduces it to the King, who asks the Queen to remove it.
The Queen orders its head off; while executioner, King, and Queen dispute the head without a body, Alice suggests asking the Duchess.
The executioner fetches the Duchess, but the Cat's head vanishes before they return.

knowledge.learns: The gardeners planted the wrong rose-tree; the Duchess is under sentence for boxing the Queen's ears.
The soldiers report that the gardeners' heads are gone.
Alice identifies the Cheshire Cat as her friend and says it belongs to the Duchess.

timeline.title: Chapter 9: The Mock Turtle’s Story
timeline.summary: The Duchess moralises at Alice until the Queen drives her away; Alice is then sent with the Gryphon to hear the Mock Turtle.
events: The affectionate Duchess walks with Alice, digging her sharp chin into her shoulder and finding morals in everything.
The Queen threatens the Duchess, who immediately leaves; croquet resumes until all other players are in custody.
The King quietly pardons the sentenced company as the Queen takes Alice to a sleeping Gryphon.
The Queen orders the Gryphon to escort Alice to the Mock Turtle and leaves to attend to executions.
The Gryphon says the executions and the Turtle's sorrow are fancy, then introduces Alice to the tearful creature.
The Mock Turtle describes his sea-school, punning subjects, and lessons that lessen each day.

knowledge.learns: The King has pardoned the croquet players; the Gryphon claims nobody is ever executed and the Turtle's sorrow is fancy.
The Mock Turtle says he was once a real Turtle and describes his lessons under the sea.

timeline.title: Chapter 10: The Lobster Quadrille
timeline.summary: The Gryphon and Mock Turtle demonstrate their dance, hear Alice's adventures, and interrupt a song to take her toward the trial.
events: The Gryphon and Mock Turtle describe the Lobster Quadrille and dance its first figure around Alice while the Turtle sings.
They explain whiting, shoes, and a fish's 'porpoise' through a succession of puns.
Alice recounts her adventures from the White Rabbit onward, including her altered Father William recitation.
At the Gryphon's command she recites altered verses, which the Mock Turtle finds confusing.
Alice asks for a song; the Turtle sings of beautiful Soup until a cry announces the trial.
The Gryphon takes Alice by the hand and runs off with her, leaving the song behind.

knowledge.learns: Alice recounts her adventures since seeing the White Rabbit, including the changed Father William verse.
Alice recounts her adventures and demonstrates that her recitation comes out differently.
A trial is beginning, though the Gryphon does not tell her whose trial it is.

timeline.title: Chapter 11: Who Stole the Tarts?
timeline.summary: At the Knave's trial Alice watches two unhelpful witnesses and begins growing before the Rabbit calls her name.
events: Alice sees the chained Knave, the tarts, and jurors writing their names; she takes Bill's squeaking pencil.
The Rabbit reads the accusation in verse; the King prematurely asks for a verdict.
The Hatter gives confused evidence while the Queen inspects a list of concert singers.
Alice begins growing and decides to stay while there is room; the Dormouse moves away from her.
The Hatter is dismissed and escapes before an officer can carry out the Queen's order to behead him.
The cook refuses to cooperate, says tarts are mostly pepper, and disappears during the commotion over the Dormouse.
The Rabbit calls Alice as the next witness.

knowledge.learns: The Knave is accused of stealing the Queen's tarts; she realises she is growing again.
She is called as the next witness despite the little useful evidence heard so far.

timeline.title: Chapter 12: Alice’s Evidence
timeline.summary: Alice challenges the court's evidence and the Queen's sentence, wakes on the bank, and tells her sister the dream.
events: Alice rises and overturns the jury-box; she replaces the jurors and rights Bill, whom she had put in headfirst.
She says she knows nothing of the business and refuses the King's newly asserted rule excluding people more than a mile high.
The Rabbit produces unsigned verses not in the Knave's handwriting; the King and Queen treat them as proof while Alice objects.
The King forces meanings onto the verses; the Queen demands sentence before verdict.
Alice refuses to hold her tongue and calls the court a pack of cards; the pack flies at her.
Alice wakes on her sister's lap, recounts the dream, and runs in to tea.
Her sister dreams over the creatures and imagines Alice grown up, preserving a loving childhood heart.

knowledge.learns: The newly produced verses are unsigned and not in the Knave's handwriting; she believes they prove nothing.
Alice tells her the strange adventures she has dreamed.
On waking, she recognises the adventures as a curious dream.

divergencePoints.label: After the White Rabbit
divergencePoints.moment: Alice sees the watch-carrying Rabbit disappear down the hole and follows without considering how she will get out.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: She drops into a deep well and reaches the hall of locked doors.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Alice stopped at the edge of the rabbit-hole and called after the White Rabbit instead of following him down?
divergencePoints.stakes: Her curiosity might bring Wonderland to the bank or leave its garden undiscovered.

divergencePoints.label: The Mouse Stays
divergencePoints.moment: The Mouse accuses Alice of not attending to its tale after she asks about the fifth bend.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Alice mistakes 'not' for 'knot'; the offended Mouse walks away without finishing.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Alice realised the Mouse meant a tale, not its tail, and persuaded it to finish its history?
divergencePoints.stakes: Alice could gain the Mouse's confidence instead of losing a companion.

divergencePoints.label: Burn Down the House
divergencePoints.moment: The Rabbit proposes burning his house down while Alice is trapped inside it.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Alice threatens to set Dinah on the crowd; they fall silent and later throw pebbles that become cakes.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if the Rabbit's threat to burn the house down were acted on before Alice could frighten the crowd with Dinah?
divergencePoints.stakes: Alice's escape and the Rabbit's home would both be in immediate danger.

divergencePoints.label: Keep the Baby
divergencePoints.moment: Alice carries the Duchess's baby outside, then discovers that it has become a pig.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: She sets the pig down, and it trots quietly into the wood.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Alice kept carrying the baby after it turned into a pig?
divergencePoints.stakes: Her attempt to save the creature could continue in a form she finds absurd.

divergencePoints.label: Stay for Tea
divergencePoints.moment: The Hatter tells Alice she should not talk if she does not think, and she rises in disgust.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Alice leaves the tea-party and discovers a door in a tree leading back to the hall.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Alice answered the Hatter's insult and stayed at the tea-table?
divergencePoints.stakes: Her route to the garden could be delayed by another encounter with the party.

divergencePoints.label: The Rose Gardeners
divergencePoints.moment: The Queen orders the three gardeners executed for the rose-tree, and they run to Alice for protection.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Alice hides them in a flower-pot, and the soldiers report that their heads are gone.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Alice openly defended the gardeners to the Queen instead of hiding them in the flower-pot?
divergencePoints.stakes: The gardeners' lives and Alice's standing with the Queen would be at risk.

divergencePoints.label: No Royal Pardon
divergencePoints.moment: As the Queen leads Alice away from croquet, the King quietly pardons the sentenced company.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Alice hears the pardon and is relieved for the many condemned players.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if the King kept silent instead of pardoning the croquet players?
divergencePoints.stakes: The assembled players would remain in custody under the Queen's sentences.

divergencePoints.label: Outgrowing the Court
divergencePoints.moment: Alice starts to grow during the Hatter's evidence and considers leaving the courtroom.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: She decides to remain as long as there is room for her.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Alice left the court as soon as she began to grow?
divergencePoints.stakes: The trial would continue without the witness who later challenges its procedure.

divergencePoints.label: Sentence First
divergencePoints.moment: The Queen demands sentence before verdict, and Alice protests.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Alice refuses to be silent, calls the court a pack of cards, and wakes as the pack flies at her.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Alice held her tongue when the Queen demanded sentence before verdict?
divergencePoints.stakes: The Knave's fate and Alice's confrontation with the court would remain unresolved.

visual.era: Victorian children's dress, waistcoats and livery, court wigs, pocket watches, brass doorplates, crockery, and formal gardens, transformed into a dream inhabited by animals and playing cards.
visual.palette: Summer greens and warm daylight on the bank; dark browns and lamplight in the hall; peppery grey in the kitchen; bright flower colours and red hearts in the garden.
motifs: A tiny golden key and glass table
A watch and white kid gloves
A grin suspended without a cat
visual.comicStyle: Victorian wood-engraving tradition: precise ink outlines, fine cross-hatching, expressive faces, and detailed natural textures. Use clear sequential panels, dramatic changes of scale, and crowded comic tableaux, with quieter open panels for the bank and the tearful shore.

glossary.note: The pink-eyed, waistcoated rabbit Alice follows.
The Rabbit's housemaid, for whom he mistakes Alice.
The name engraved on the Rabbit's brass doorplate.
Alice's cat, whose hunting frightens Wonderland animals.
A race with irregular starts and stops in which everybody wins.
Sweets Alice distributes as prizes after the race.
The Duchess's grinning, vanishing cat.
The Hatter's companion at the perpetual tea-party.
The sleepy tea-party guest who tells the treacle-well story.
The card queen who repeatedly orders beheadings.
The card accused of stealing the Queen's tarts.
The tearful creature who says he was once a real Turtle.
The creature who escorts Alice to the Mock Turtle and trial.
A sea dance involving lobster partners and a plunge into the water.
The label on Alice's first shrinking bottle.
The words marked in currants on Alice's first cake.
The King's asserted rule excluding persons more than a mile high from court.

a-christmas-carol.title: A Christmas Carol
a-christmas-carol.author: Charles Dickens
a-christmas-carol.premise: On Christmas Eve, Ebenezer Scrooge dismisses charity, family and the holiday itself while his clerk shivers over his work. That night his dead partner returns in chains, promising three spirits who will show him his own life and the lives around him.
a-christmas-carol.hook: A miser is given one haunted night to discover what his life has cost.
a-christmas-carol.logline: Warned by his condemned partner, Scrooge must face the past, present and possible future of his selfish life before his chance to change is lost.

world.setting: London counting-houses, crowded streets and modest homes at Christmas, with spectral journeys to Scrooge's childhood, other parts of Britain and the sea.
rules: Business runs on ledgers, bills, cash and credit; clerks copy letters by hand and depend on their employers for wages and working conditions.
Coaches, carts, cabs and walking carry people through the city; gas lamps, candles and coal fires light and warm its rooms.
Poverty is managed through institutions including prisons and Union workhouses; private charity seeks food, drink and warmth for those in need.
Spirits can pass through walls and transport Scrooge across great distances and times; their visits take place within a single Christmas Eve night.
Past scenes are shadows that do not perceive Scrooge. During the present tour he and the Spirit are invisible, and his voice is inaudible to the company at Fred's.
Marley says spirits who neglected their fellow humans in life wander after death, fettered by chains they forged themselves and unable to help those they see.
The future shown to Scrooge follows from existing courses of conduct; the book presents its feared outcomes as alterable through a changed life.
Christmas is marked by churchgoing, family meals, games, gifts and greetings; some people take their dinners to bakers' ovens.
world.tone: Gothic dread and social indignation yield repeatedly to exuberant comedy, tenderness and Christmas warmth.
themes: Memory and the possibility of change
sensitivities: The narrative uses period language about disability and portrays Tiny Tim's condition through sentiment and moral example.
Descriptions of poverty sometimes present poor people's bodies and neighbourhoods as grotesque or threatening.

voice.narration: An intrusive, companionable narrator tells the story chiefly in past-tense third person, staying close to Scrooge while addressing the reader directly, offering opinions and entering other households with confident sympathy.
style: Abrupt declarations and fragments alternate with long, rolling sentences joined by semicolons, colons and repeated conjunctions.
Exclamations, questions, capitals and dashes make the narration sound spoken; the narrator interrupts to argue a joke or insist on a detail.
Objects and weather acquire temper and purpose: fog brews, a bell shivers and food seems eager to be eaten.
Comic catalogues accumulate precise goods, gestures and people before turning toward generosity, loneliness or grief.
The grotesque and the homely stand together, with spiritual terror grounded in bed-curtains, gruel, chains and coal.
Victorian British diction and spellings include 'labour', 'colour', 'shew' where used, and contractions such as 'em and an't.
voice.dialogue: Speech is enclosed in double quotation marks, with expressive tags and interruptions. Scrooge's clipped repetitions and growls give way to breathless exclamations; Fred argues expansively, Bob speaks deferentially, and the spirits range from gentle correction to solemn rebuke.
samplePassages: Oh! But he was a tight-fisted hand at the grind-stone, Scrooge! a squeezing, wrenching, grasping, scraping, clutching, covetous, old sinner! Hard and sharp as flint, from which no steel had ever struck out generous fire; secret, and self-contained, and solitary as an oyster. The cold within him froze his old features, nipped his pointed nose, shrivelled his cheek, stiffened his gait; made his eyes red, his thin lips blue; and spoke out shrewdly in his grating voice. A frosty rime was on his head, and on his eyebrows, and his wiry chin.

There never was such a goose. Bob said he didn't believe there ever was such a goose cooked. Its tenderness and flavour, size and cheapness, were the themes of universal admiration. Eked out by apple-sauce and mashed potatoes, it was a sufficient dinner for the whole family; indeed, as Mrs. Cratchit said with great delight (surveying one small atom of a bone upon the dish), they hadn't ate it all at last! Yet every one had had enough, and the youngest Cratchits in particular, were steeped in sage and onion to the eyebrows!

cast.name: Scrooge
cast.role: A solitary London businessman whose supernatural visitors confront him with his life.
cast.age: Old man; also seen as a boy and young man in past shadows
cast.appearance: Lean, stiff-gaited old man with a pointed nose, shrivelled cheeks, red eyes and thin blue lips. Frosty white hair, eyebrows and wiry chin frame his face. He wears a dark business coat, waistcoat and cravat; at home he has a dressing-gown, slippers and nightcap.
cast.personality: Initially hard, suspicious and coldly witty; underneath are strong feelings, a sharp mind and a capacity for delighted play.
cast.motivation: He pursues money and security, then seeks to make amends and use his remaining time generously.
cast.fears: Poverty and worldly reproach; later, a lonely death and the irreversible loss of Tiny Tim.
cast.speech: At first he snaps 'Bah! Humbug!' and dismisses people with repeated 'Good afternoon.' Fear brings jokes and faltering pleas; repentance releases warm greetings, thanks and breathless cries of delight.
cast.arc: The spirits awaken his memories and pity; he vows to change, reconciles with Fred and becomes a generous employer and friend.

relationships.nature: Dead business partner who procures his chance of rescue.
Underpaid clerk; Scrooge later raises his salary and helps his family.
Nephew whose invitations he rejects before joining his Christmas dinner.
Former fiancée who releases him when gain becomes his ruling passion.
His clerk's sick child, whom he comes to cherish as a second father.

cast.name: Jacob Marley
cast.role: Scrooge's dead partner, who returns to warn him and arrange the spirits' visits.
cast.age: Dead seven years; formerly an older businessman
cast.appearance: A transparent male ghost with a livid face, fixed death-cold eyes, hair and pigtail bristling as if in hot air, and spectacles on his forehead. He wears a waistcoat, coat, tights and tasselled boots, with a kerchief binding his head and jaw. A long chain of cash-boxes, keys, padlocks, ledgers, deeds and steel purses encircles him.
cast.personality: Remorseful, urgent and severe, yet concerned enough for Scrooge to procure him hope.
cast.motivation: He warns Scrooge against the fate he earned by neglecting mankind for business.
cast.fears: Unending remorse and the knowledge that missed opportunities cannot be recovered.
cast.speech: He speaks in emphatic declarations and cries of grief, correcting Scrooge sharply: 'Mankind was my business.' His speech rises into biblical and moral appeals.
cast.arc: His single visit turns an old partner's apparent business success into a warning about wasted human obligations.

relationships.nature: Former partner and sole mourner, whom he warns.

cast.name: Bob Cratchit
cast.role: Scrooge's poorly paid clerk and the affectionate father of a large family.
cast.appearance: A small man in threadbare, carefully darned and brushed clothes, with a long white comforter whose ends hang below his waist. He has no great-coat in the counting-house winter; he wears a modest dark coat and trousers and carries himself briskly.
cast.personality: Gentle, playful and appreciative, with deep tenderness for his family and tact even toward Scrooge.
cast.motivation: He supports his family on fifteen shillings a week and treasures their happiness and companionship.
cast.fears: Losing his employment and, more deeply, losing Tiny Tim.
cast.speech: He addresses Scrooge respectfully as 'sir', softening requests with 'if quite convenient.' At home he proposes blessings, praises his family and speaks feelingly, sometimes with a trembling voice.
cast.arc: He is first seen enduring Scrooge's meanness; a possible future shows him mourning Tim, while the changed Scrooge raises his salary and helps the family.

relationships.nature: Employer who threatens his place, then becomes his generous friend.
His wife and partner in raising their children.
His beloved youngest son, whom he carries on his shoulder.
Scrooge's nephew, who kindly offers help in the future vision.

cast.name: Scrooge's nephew
cast.role: Scrooge's cheerful nephew, who persists in offering family fellowship.
cast.appearance: A young man with a ruddy, handsome face and sparkling eyes. He wears a respectable dark coat, waistcoat and cravat; after walking in the frost his face glows and his breath steams. His easy posture often gives way to laughter.
cast.personality: Merry, persistent and compassionate, able to laugh at his uncle while feeling sorry for him.
cast.motivation: He wants friendship with Scrooge and believes Christmas opens people's hearts across social divisions.
cast.fears: He regrets his uncle's isolation and the pleasant company Scrooge denies himself.
cast.speech: He greets people heartily, laughs 'Ha, ha!' and answers Scrooge's objections with lively questions and generous, fluent arguments. He keeps his temper even when rebuffed.
cast.arc: He continues to invite and toast Scrooge despite rejection, then welcomes him wholeheartedly to dinner.

relationships.nature: Nephew who seeks his uncle's friendship.
Treats the clerk kindly and offers help after Tim's death in the future vision.

cast.name: Ghost of Christmas Past
cast.role: The first spirit, who shows Scrooge scenes from his own past.
cast.age: Child-sized, with the appearance of both a child and an old man
cast.appearance: A child-sized figure with long white hair, an unwrinkled blooming face, unusually long muscular bare arms and delicate bare legs and feet. A white tunic with summer flowers and a shining belt accompanies a holly branch. A clear jet of light rises from its head; it carries a great extinguisher-cap.
cast.personality: Gentle in manner but firm and searching, refusing to spare Scrooge painful memories.
cast.motivation: It comes for Scrooge's welfare and reclamation, exposing memories his passions have suppressed.
cast.fears: It resists Scrooge's attempt to put out the light it gives.
cast.speech: Its voice is soft, low and seemingly distant. It asks precise questions, gives brief corrections and calls the scenes 'shadows of the things that have been.'
cast.arc: It leads Scrooge from remembered childhood pleasures to the loss of Belle, then disappears beneath its cap as its light streams out.

relationships.nature: Guides him through his own past to awaken regret and sympathy.

cast.name: Belle
cast.role: Scrooge's former fiancée, who releases him when she sees his devotion to gain.
cast.age: Young woman in the parting scene; later a mother
cast.appearance: A fair young woman with a gentle face and tearful eyes, wearing a plain mourning-dress. In the later family scene she is a comely matron in a modest dress, seated by the winter fire.
cast.personality: Steady, perceptive and affectionate, though firm in the face of pain.
cast.motivation: She wants a marriage founded on shared affection rather than Scrooge's fear of poverty and pursuit of gain.
cast.fears: A marriage made miserable by his changed priorities and his likely regret at choosing a dowerless wife.
cast.speech: She speaks softly and with measured, closely reasoned sentences, asking Scrooge to examine his feelings before releasing him with a blessing.
cast.arc: She ends their engagement and is later seen in a lively, loving household with her husband and children.

relationships.nature: Former fiancée who releases him from their old engagement.

cast.name: Ghost of Christmas Present
cast.role: A genial spirit who shows Scrooge Christmas celebrations and the suffering hidden among them.
cast.age: Very young at first; ages rapidly and dies at midnight
cast.appearance: A great giant with a genial face, sparkling eyes and long dark-brown curls that turn grey. He wears a loose green robe edged in white fur, open at his broad breast, with bare feet and a holly wreath set with icicles. At his waist hangs a rusty, empty antique scabbard; he carries a glowing horn-shaped torch.
cast.personality: Open-handed and exuberant, with fierce moral seriousness beneath his merriment.
cast.motivation: He spreads Christmas fellowship and teaches Scrooge to see and care for people in need.
cast.fears: He warns of the doom threatened by human Ignorance and Want, especially Ignorance.
cast.speech: He calls Scrooge in heartily, asks pointed questions and turns Scrooge's own cruel words back on him. His warnings become solemn and accusatory.
cast.arc: He leads Scrooge through homes and distant workplaces, ages during the journey and reveals Ignorance and Want before vanishing.

relationships.nature: His pupil and companion on the Christmas journey.
Shows Scrooge the child and warns that he will die if the shadows remain unchanged.

cast.name: Mrs. Cratchit
cast.role: Bob's wife, who manages the family meal and fiercely defends her household.
cast.appearance: A modestly dressed woman in a twice-turned gown, made festive with inexpensive ribbons. She wears a plain apron for the meal, with her hair arranged neatly beneath a simple cap.
cast.personality: Busy, loving and proud of her family; outspoken about the injustice of Scrooge's treatment of Bob.
cast.motivation: She makes their limited resources serve a cheerful Christmas and cares for her husband and children.
cast.fears: Her Christmas pudding failing; in the future vision, she struggles to contain grief for Tim.
cast.speech: She uses brisk domestic exclamations and affectionate blessings, but calls Scrooge an 'odious, stingy, hard, unfeeling man' when Bob toasts him.
cast.arc: She presides over the family's festive meal; in the possible future she and the household mourn Tim together.

relationships.nature: His wife, protective of him and affectionate toward him.
His mother, who mourns him in the future vision.
Resents her husband's stingy employer.

cast.name: Tiny Tim
cast.role: Bob and Mrs. Cratchit's disabled son, whose threatened death moves Scrooge.
cast.appearance: A very small boy with a withered little hand and slight limbs supported by an iron frame. He uses a little crutch and sits on a low stool. His modest clothes are worn and scanty, like his family's.
cast.personality: Patient, mild and thoughtful, with a cheerful share in family celebrations.
cast.motivation: He shares his family's affection and hopes his presence in church will remind people of Christ's healing.
cast.fears: The manuscript does not state a particular fear of his.
cast.speech: He speaks simply and devoutly, blessing the company with 'God bless us every one!' and sings in a plaintive little voice.
cast.arc: The spirits show his endangered life and a possible death; after Scrooge changes, Tim lives and gains a second father in him.

relationships.nature: His loving father, who carries him to and from church.
His mother.
His father's employer, who becomes like a second father.

cast.name: Ghost of Christmas Yet To Come
cast.role: The silent final spirit, who shows Scrooge the consequences of an unchanged life.
cast.appearance: A tall, stately figure entirely shrouded in a deep black hooded garment. Its face and form are concealed; only one outstretched hand is visible, pointing from the folds.
cast.personality: Grave, silent and implacable, though its hand appears to tremble at Scrooge's plea.
cast.motivation: It guides Scrooge through future shadows toward recognition of his own death and a chance to change.
cast.fears: The manuscript gives no fear for the Phantom.
cast.speech: It does not speak. It communicates by pointing, an apparent inclination of its hood and the movements of its hand.
cast.arc: It leads Scrooge from anonymous talk of a death to his own grave, then shrinks into his bedpost as he begs for a changed fate.

relationships.nature: His terrifying guide through shadows of the future.

places.name: Scrooge and Marley's counting-house
places.description: Scrooge's place of business, where he watches Bob work and keeps the coal under his own control.
places.visual: A warehouse door bears both partners' names. Inside, Scrooge's office has a small fire and an open door onto the clerk's dismal little cell, the Tank, with its stool, writing materials and nearly coal-less fire.

places.name: Scrooge's chambers
places.description: Marley's former rooms in an old building up a dark yard, where Scrooge lives alone and receives the spirits.
places.visual: A black gateway opens onto a yard so dark its stones must be felt for. A large knocker marks the door; a broad staircase leads to sitting-room, bedroom and lumber-room. The old fireplace has Dutch Scripture tiles, a small grate and a saucepan of gruel.

places.name: Scrooge's old school
places.description: The decaying boarding-school where the young Scrooge is left alone at Christmas and later fetched home by Fan.
places.visual: A dull red-brick mansion with a cupola, weathercock and bell; broken windows, mossy walls and grass-grown coach-houses surround cold, bare rooms. The schoolroom has deal forms and desks and a feeble fire.

places.name: Fezziwig's warehouse
places.description: The workplace of Scrooge's apprenticeship, transformed into a Christmas ballroom by his generous employer.
places.visual: A high desk nearly reaches the ceiling. Shutters are put up, movable goods cleared away, the floor swept and watered, lamps trimmed and the fire piled high; a fiddler plays from the desk.

places.name: The Cratchits' house
places.description: Bob's four-roomed home in Camden Town, where a small income sustains a close and festive family.
places.visual: A modest hearth and table hold the family circle, with a stool for Tim. A saucepan of potatoes, a goose from the baker, a pudding from the copper and two tumblers with a handleless custard-cup make up the Christmas feast.

places.name: Fred's house
places.description: The cheerful home where Fred and his wife host Christmas dinner, music and games.
places.visual: A bright, dry room with a fire, lamplight and dessert on the table; a harp, piano, chairs, curtains and footstool furnish the gathering.

places.name: Old Joe's shop
places.description: A dealer's den in a disreputable quarter, where stolen belongings from the dead man's room are sold in the future vision.
places.visual: A low shop under a pent-house roof is heaped with rusty iron, rags, fat and bones. Behind a rag curtain, old Joe sits by a brick charcoal stove and smoky lamp, chalking prices on the wall.

places.name: The churchyard
places.description: The burial ground where the final spirit reveals the name on the neglected grave.
places.visual: An iron gate opens onto a churchyard hemmed in by houses, overgrown with grass and weeds and crowded with burials; a gravestone bears Scrooge's name.

timeline.title: Chapter 1: Marley's Ghost
timeline.summary: On Christmas Eve Scrooge rejects fellowship and charity, then receives a terrifying warning from the ghost of his partner Marley.
events: Scrooge rebuffs Fred's invitation and threatens Bob after the clerk applauds Fred's defence of Christmas.
He refuses the charity collectors, invoking prisons and workhouses and saying the poor should decrease the surplus population.
He grudgingly gives Bob Christmas Day off; Bob goes home while Scrooge dines alone and returns to his chambers.
Marley's face appears in the door knocker; later the bells ring and his chained ghost enters the locked room.
Marley reveals his remorse and warns that Scrooge bears a heavier chain; he announces three spirits as Scrooge's chance of escape.
Scrooge sees other chained ghosts unable to help the living, then goes to bed.

knowledge.learns: Marley says his chain was forged by his own conduct, Scrooge's is heavier, and three spirits will offer a chance to escape his fate.
He sees wandering spirits who wish to help the living but can no longer do so.
Scrooge permits him Christmas Day off but orders him to come earlier the following morning.

timeline.title: Chapter 2: The First of the Three Spirits
timeline.summary: The Ghost of Christmas Past leads Scrooge through lonely childhood, remembered kindness and the loss of Belle, until he tries to extinguish its light.
events: Scrooge wakes to find the clocks at twelve and waits anxiously until the first spirit draws his bed-curtain at one.
The spirit takes him to his old school, where he sees his lonely younger self and remembers the carol singer he frightened away.
He sees Fan fetch him home, then watches Fezziwig turn his warehouse into a Christmas ball and regrets his treatment of Bob.
He witnesses Belle release his younger self from their engagement because gain has displaced her.
He sees Belle's happy family and hears her husband describe Scrooge sitting alone while Marley lies near death.
Unable to bear more, he presses the extinguisher over the spirit, whose light still streams out; he finds himself in bed and sleeps.

knowledge.learns: He recognizes how his lonely childhood makes him wish he had given the carol singer something.
Remembering Fezziwig's power to make work happy or burdensome, he wishes he could speak kindly to Bob.
He sees Belle's later family life and hears that her husband regarded him as alone in the world.

timeline.title: Chapter 3: The Second of the Three Spirits
timeline.summary: The Ghost of Christmas Present shows Scrooge festive generosity among rich and poor, warns him about Tiny Tim, and reveals Ignorance and Want.
events: Scrooge finds the second spirit in his transformed, greenery-filled room and willingly takes hold of its robe.
They visit Christmas streets and a baker's; the spirit denies responsibility for people who restrict poor people's pleasures in its name.
At the Cratchits' dinner Scrooge sees Tim, hears the family's toast to him, and learns that Tim will die if the shadows remain unchanged.
They visit miners, lighthouse keepers and a ship, finding Christmas fellowship even in isolation.
At Fred's party Scrooge joins in games inaudibly, hears Fred defend and toast him, and begs to stay longer.
The aging spirit shows him the children Ignorance and Want, warns of Doom and repeats Scrooge's words about prisons and workhouses; at midnight it vanishes and the last phantom approaches.

knowledge.learns: The spirit says acts of bigotry and selfishness done in its family's name belong to their human authors.
Tiny Tim will die if the present shadows are not altered; he hears his own 'surplus population' words turned against him.
Fred pities him, intends to renew his invitation yearly and drinks his health despite his refusal.
The two children beneath the spirit's robe are Man's Ignorance and Want; the spirit warns especially against Ignorance.

timeline.mood: Generous and exuberant, darkening into alarm

timeline.title: Chapter 4: The Last of the Spirits
timeline.summary: The silent Phantom shows Scrooge an unmourned death and the Cratchits' grief, then points him to his own grave.
events: Scrooge follows the silent Phantom and hears businessmen speak indifferently of an unnamed man's death.
At old Joe's shop he watches three people sell possessions taken from the dead man's room, including his bed-curtains and burial shirt.
He sees the covered body but cannot bring himself to uncover its face; at his request, the spirit shows a debtor's family relieved by the death.
He asks to see tenderness associated with death and witnesses the Cratchits mourning Tiny Tim, including Bob's account of Fred's kindness.
He finds another man in his future office and follows the Phantom into a churchyard.
Reading his own name on the grave, he vows to honour Christmas and live by the lessons of all three spirits; the Phantom becomes his bedpost.

knowledge.learns: The dead man's servants and associates have stripped his room, and a debtor's family is relieved by his death.
In the future shown, Tiny Tim has died and the Cratchits mourn him; Fred has offered Bob help.
The grave bears his own name; he recognizes himself as the man on the bed and believes an altered life may change the shadows.

timeline.title: Chapter 5: The End of It
timeline.summary: Scrooge wakes on Christmas morning, acts on his new generosity, joins Fred's dinner and raises Bob's salary; Tiny Tim lives.
events: Scrooge wakes in his own bed, rejoices that his curtains remain and learns from a boy that it is Christmas Day.
He pays the boy and a poulterer to send the enormous prize turkey anonymously to Bob's family by cab.
He apologizes to a charity collector and promises a substantial donation, then goes to church and walks happily through the streets.
After passing Fred's door repeatedly, he knocks and is welcomed to Christmas dinner.
The next morning he pretends to scold Bob for lateness, then raises his salary, promises help for his family and orders more coal.
Scrooge keeps his promises and becomes a second father to Tiny Tim, who does not die.

knowledge.learns: A boy tells him it is Christmas Day; Scrooge realizes the spirits have accomplished their visits in one night.
Scrooge has come to accept his invitation to dinner.
Scrooge is raising his salary and intends to help his struggling family.

divergencePoints.label: Dinner with Fred
divergencePoints.moment: Fred asks his uncle to dine with him on Christmas Day, despite Scrooge's attacks on the holiday.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Scrooge refuses, repeating 'Good afternoon' until Fred leaves with a cheerful greeting.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Scrooge accepted Fred's invitation to Christmas dinner when Fred first offered it?
divergencePoints.stakes: A family bond might reopen before the haunting begins.

divergencePoints.label: A Warning Refused
divergencePoints.moment: Marley tells Scrooge that three spirits are his chance to escape the fate of a wandering, chained ghost.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Scrooge reluctantly hears the appointed visits and watches Marley depart.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Scrooge refused to listen to Marley's warning and drove the conversation to an end before Marley named the spirits?
divergencePoints.stakes: Scrooge's chance of understanding the visits would be at risk.

divergencePoints.label: Belle's Release
divergencePoints.moment: Belle tells the younger Scrooge that gain has displaced her and releases him from their engagement.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: She leaves him, and they part.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if young Scrooge asked Belle to stay and persuaded her to reconsider their engagement?
divergencePoints.stakes: Their shared future and his devotion to gain could take a different course.

divergencePoints.label: Put Out the Light
divergencePoints.moment: Scrooge wrestles with the Ghost of Christmas Past and presses its extinguisher-cap over its head.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: The spirit drops beneath the cap, but its light pours out from underneath; Scrooge falls asleep.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if the extinguisher truly put out the Ghost of Christmas Past's light when Scrooge pressed it down?
divergencePoints.stakes: The spirit's hold on Scrooge and the force of its lesson would be altered.

divergencePoints.label: The Unheard Toast
divergencePoints.moment: At Fred's party the guests drink Scrooge's health, and Scrooge wants to return their greeting.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: His voice is inaudible to the company, and the scene vanishes before he can finish.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Fred heard Scrooge return the Christmas toast from beside the Ghost of Christmas Present?
divergencePoints.stakes: The nephew's affection could meet an answer before Scrooge wakes.

divergencePoints.label: The Face Beneath the Sheet
divergencePoints.moment: The Phantom points to the covered head of the dead man, and Scrooge longs to lift the sheet.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Scrooge cannot bring himself to uncover the face and asks to see someone affected by the death.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Scrooge found the courage to lift the sheet and look at the dead man's face?
divergencePoints.stakes: He could discover the identity of the corpse before reaching the grave.

divergencePoints.label: At His Own Grave
divergencePoints.moment: Scrooge reads his own name on the neglected gravestone and begs the silent Phantom to say the future can change.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: He vows to honour Christmas and live by the lessons of all three spirits; the Phantom becomes his bedpost.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if, at his own grave, Scrooge refused to promise a changed life and demanded a different answer from the Phantom?
divergencePoints.stakes: His defining commitment to change, and the hope attached to it, would be in doubt.

divergencePoints.label: The Door He Passed
divergencePoints.moment: On Christmas afternoon Scrooge passes Fred's door a dozen times before gathering courage to knock.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: He knocks, asks to come to dinner and is welcomed into the family party.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Scrooge lost his nerve at Fred's door and walked away without knocking?
divergencePoints.stakes: Their reconciliation would remain uncertain despite Scrooge's change of heart.

divergencePoints.label: Eighteen Minutes Late
divergencePoints.moment: Bob arrives late at the counting-house, and Scrooge summons him while pretending to be angry.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Scrooge surprises Bob with a salary increase and promises to help his family.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Bob, fearing dismissal, spoke up for himself before Scrooge could reveal the salary increase?
divergencePoints.stakes: The first encounter between the changed master and his clerk could take an unexpected turn.

visual.era: Early Victorian London: dark business coats and cravats, shawls and bonnets, horses and cabs, counting-house desks, gas lamps, candles and coal fires.
visual.palette: Sooty brown fog, blue-black frost and grey stone give way to firelit red and gold, holly green and snowy morning light.
motifs: A little crutch by the hearth
The pointing hand and neglected grave
visual.comicStyle: Victorian engraved-book illustration in ink and wash, with lively cross-hatching, expressive faces and dense street detail. Use deep shadows for the apparitions, crowded rhythmic panels for feasts and games, and quiet held panels for grief and recognition.

glossary.note: The firm's name remains above the warehouse door after Marley's death.
The dismal little cell where Bob copies letters.
Institutions Scrooge cites when refusing charity.
Bob's long white scarf, worn against the cold.
The first spirit, who shows Scrooge his own past.
Scrooge's former employer, celebrated for his Christmas ball.
The young woman who releases Scrooge from their engagement.
The giant spirit of the current Christmas.
Bob Cratchit's little son, who uses a crutch.
The boy revealed beneath the second spirit's robe.
The girl revealed beneath the second spirit's robe.

glossary.term: Ghost of Christmas Yet To Come
glossary.note: The silent, black-shrouded final spirit.

locales.en: Ghost of Christmas Yet To Come

glossary.note: The dealer who buys goods taken from the dead man's room.
The hot Christmas drink Scrooge proposes sharing with Bob.

treasure-island.title: Treasure Island
treasure-island.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
treasure-island.premise: Jim Hawkins finds a dead seaman’s papers and joins an expedition to an island marked with Captain Flint’s buried treasure. The schooner’s crew includes men who know more about Flint than their employers suspect.
treasure-island.hook: A cabin-boy seeking buried gold discovers that the pirates are already aboard.
treasure-island.logline: When a treasure voyage becomes a mutiny, Jim Hawkins must help a handful of loyal companions survive Long John Silver and recover their ship.

world.setting: An English coastal inn, the docks of Bristol, the schooner Hispaniola, and a wooded Atlantic island with sheltered anchorages, marshes, rocky hills and a pirate stockade.
world.period: The eighteenth century, in the reign of King George
rules: Ships depend on wind, tide, seamanship and navigators; a becalmed schooner can be moved by boats but cannot simply sail away.
Muskets and pistols require powder, shot and dry priming; a wet pistol may fail, and reloading takes time.
Pirates elect captains, hold councils and use the black spot to announce a summons or deposition; their rules do not make them trustworthy.
A gentleman’s word of honour binds him socially, while servants and seamen are expected to obey their employers and officers.
Island marshes breed fever; exposure, wounds, thirst, hunger and drunkenness have serious consequences.
There is no demonstrated supernatural intervention: Ben Gunn supplies the voice mistaken for Flint’s ghost, although the pirates fear spirits.
Treasure consists of heavy gold bars and mixed coin requiring repeated journeys to move; the map also marks separate caches of silver and arms.
world.tone: Eager, companionable adventure darkens into suspense, violence and remorse, with humour persisting among peril and hardship.
themes: Greed and the cost of treasure
The seduction and aftermath of adventure
sensitivities: The narrative uses dated racial descriptions and assumptions, including Trelawney’s speculation about Silver’s wife; these reflect the period’s prejudice.
Piracy brings murder, threatened torture, addiction, disability and traumatic memories; the adventure does not erase their human cost.

voice.narration: Jim Hawkins recalls the adventure in first-person past tense, addressing the reader and occasionally anticipating later discoveries. Chapters 16–18 are narrated by Dr. Livesey, whose account overlaps Jim’s shore adventure and has a brisker professional confidence.
style: Concrete actions and nautical mechanics build suspense step by step; a sudden cry, movement or short sentence breaks longer descriptions.
Jim admits fear, vanity, curiosity and disobedience, then judges his younger self with hindsight rather than posing as fearless.
Landscape is precise and sensory: sand, resin, marsh vapour, surf, light and the motion of water colour the action.
Similes draw on animals, weather, household objects, games and ships; lively exaggeration sits beside careful observation.
Colons, semicolons, dashes, exclamations and parentheses accommodate digression, contrast and abrupt turns.
Spelling and vocabulary follow the supplied nineteenth-century text, with eighteenth-century maritime terms and rank.
voice.dialogue: Double quotation marks frame quick exchanges. Gentlemen speak in complete, often formal clauses; seamen use contractions, dropped consonants, nautical metaphors, oaths and repeated phrases. Silver shifts from ingratiating endearments to threats, while Smollett makes terse, practical points.
samplePassages: I remember him as if it were yesterday, as he came plodding to the inn door, his sea-chest following behind him in a hand-barrow--a tall, strong, heavy, nut-brown man, his tarry pigtail falling over the shoulder of his soiled blue coat, his hands ragged and scarred, with black, broken nails, and the sabre cut across one cheek, a dirty, livid white. I remember him looking round the cove and whistling to himself as he did so, and then breaking out in that old sea-song that he sang so often afterwards:

“Well, gentlemen,” continued the captain, “I don’t know who has this map; but I make it a point, it shall be kept secret even from me and Mr. Arrow. Otherwise I would ask you to let me resign.”

“I see,” said the doctor. “You wish us to keep this matter dark and to make a garrison of the stern part of the ship, manned with my friend’s own people, and provided with all the arms and powder on board. In other words, you fear a mutiny.”

The cold evening breeze, of which I have spoken, whistled through every chink of the rude building and sprinkled the floor with a continual rain of fine sand. There was sand in our eyes, sand in our teeth, sand in our suppers, sand dancing in the spring at the bottom of the kettle, for all the world like porridge beginning to boil. Our chimney was a square hole in the roof; it was but a little part of the smoke that found its way out, and the rest eddied about the house and kept us coughing and piping the eye.

cast.name: Jim Hawkins
cast.role: Innkeeper’s son, cabin-boy and principal narrator.
cast.age: A boy, old enough to work at the inn and go to sea.
cast.appearance: A slim, short English boy with a youthful face, brown hair and fair skin. He wears a plain eighteenth-century shirt, waistcoat, jacket, breeches, stockings, shoes and sea-cap; his mother’s soft silk handkerchief is among his possessions.
cast.personality: Curious, observant and brave despite vivid fears; impulsive, proud and capable of sharp self-reproach.
cast.motivation: He wants adventure and discovery, but also strives to protect his mother and the companions whose lives his discoveries put in danger.
cast.fears: Pirates, torture, drowning and harm to his friends; the island returns in nightmares.
cast.speech: Polite and direct with gentlemen, he calls them sir; excitement makes him speak boldly and at length. His retrospective narration admits what he did not understand at the time.
cast.arc: His curiosity uncovers the plot and helps recover the ship, but his unauthorized adventures endanger others. He keeps his parole to Silver and returns unwilling ever to revisit the island.

relationships.nature: Her son and helper at the Admiral Benbow.
Trusted protector and physician who values his discoveries.
First trusts him, then opposes him; their bargain saves each other’s lives.
His captain, whose discipline he initially resents.
Finds the maroon and carries his proposal to the loyal party.

cast.name: the captain
cast.role: Flint’s former first mate, whose sea-chest contains the treasure map.
cast.appearance: Tall, strong and heavy, with nut-brown skin, a dirty livid-white sabre cut across one cheek, a tarry pigtail, ragged scarred hands and black broken nails. His soiled blue coat is heavily patched; one cock of his hat hangs down. His arm bears tattoos, including a gallows.
cast.personality: Silent and watchful when sober, bullying and violent in drink, yet frightened of his former shipmates.
cast.motivation: He wants rum, concealment and exclusive possession of the papers Flint entrusted to him.
cast.fears: The one-legged seaman, Flint’s surviving crew, the black spot and the horrors brought on by lack of rum.
cast.speech: Rough sea-talk and oaths alternate with wheedling appeals to Jim as ‘matey’; he sings the dead man’s chest song and orders company silent.
cast.arc: His enemies find him at the inn; weakened by a stroke and drink, he dies immediately after receiving the black spot.

relationships.nature: Pays him to watch for a one-legged sailor and later confides in him.
The doctor defies his threats and treats his stroke.
Dreads the one-legged former quartermaster of Flint’s crew.
His former shipmate delivers the black spot.

cast.name: Jim’s mother
cast.role: Widowed keeper of the Admiral Benbow.
cast.age: An adult woman with a son old enough to work.
cast.appearance: A fair-skinned English woman of middle height and ordinary build, with brown hair pinned beneath a modest cap. She wears a practical long gown, apron and sturdy shoes suited to keeping an eighteenth-century coastal inn.
cast.personality: Determined, scrupulous about money owed, frightened yet willing to act.
cast.motivation: She wants the captain’s unpaid lodging recovered for herself and her fatherless son.
cast.fears: The approaching pirates and leaving Jim unprovided for.
cast.speech: Plain and forthright; she reproaches the hamlet’s ‘chicken-hearted’ men and insists on her lawful dues.
cast.arc: She returns to open the chest despite danger, takes only part of the debt, and later keeps the repaired inn with an apprentice.

relationships.nature: Her son accompanies and protects her during the raid.
Her lodger leaves a long unpaid account.

cast.name: Dr. Livesey
cast.role: Physician, magistrate and loyal leader; narrator of three chapters.
cast.age: An established adult physician and former soldier.
cast.appearance: A neat, bright English gentleman with bright black eyes and close-cropped black hair beneath a snow-white powdered wig. He wears a clean eighteenth-century coat, waistcoat, breeches and stockings, and carries medical instruments and a snuff-box.
cast.personality: Calm under threat, decisive, dryly humorous and professionally conscientious.
cast.motivation: He wants to protect his companions, do his medical duty and bring the expedition safely home.
cast.fears: Fever, the party’s dwindling provisions and the consequences of the crew’s treachery.
cast.speech: Clear, kind and brisk, with dry rebukes and medical confidence; he says he will ‘stake my wig’ and treats even mutineers with professional composure.
cast.arc: He challenges Billy, helps organize the voyage, discovers Ben’s secret and bargains away the stockade and obsolete map before rescuing Jim.

relationships.nature: Protects and rebukes him, then promises to rescue him.
Friend and expedition partner whose loose tongue he cautions.
Respects the captain’s judgment and works with him.
Treats his sick crew and promises to help him short of perjury.
Wins his confidence and learns where the treasure lies.

cast.name: Squire Trelawney
cast.role: Wealthy owner and enthusiastic outfitter of the treasure expedition.
cast.age: An adult gentleman with long experience of travel.
cast.appearance: Over six feet tall and broad, with a bluff face roughened, reddened and lined by travel, and very black expressive eyebrows. He dresses as a gentleman and, for the voyage, in stout blue cloth like a sea-officer.
cast.personality: Generous, impulsive, outspoken and excitable; brave and cool when shooting.
cast.motivation: He wants Flint’s treasure and the glory of a sea voyage, and cares for his servants and friends.
cast.fears: The harm his decisions have brought upon his companions.
cast.speech: Grand, exclamatory and lavish with praise or indignation: ‘trump,’ ‘prodigious’ and ‘monstrous’ suit his open manner.
cast.arc: His indiscretion helps expose the venture; he admits Smollett was right, fights loyally and reluctantly agrees not to prosecute Silver.

relationships.nature: His friend tempers his enthusiasm with caution.
Initially distrusts him, then acknowledges his command.
Engages him as cabin-boy and repairs his mother’s inn.
Hires and admires him before discovering his deception.
His devoted old gamekeeper accompanies the expedition.

cast.name: Long John Silver
cast.role: Ship’s cook, pirate leader and Jim’s shifting ally.
cast.appearance: Very tall and strong, with a broad, smooth, pale blond face and a large mouth; his left leg is missing close to the hip. He moves on a crutch, sometimes hung by a lanyard, and wears a blue coat, sailor’s hat and, ashore, a cutlass and pistols. A green parrot often perches on his shoulder.
cast.personality: Affable, resourceful and formidable; a persuasive actor who can become ruthless in an instant.
cast.motivation: He wants treasure and comfortable independence, but adapts quickly to save his neck when the venture fails.
cast.fears: The gallows, poverty and losing control of his crew.
cast.speech: Mixes sea terms, flattery, ‘you may lay to that’ and ‘by the powers’ with elaborate politeness to gentlemen. To his men he alternates jokes, arguments and explosive threats.
cast.arc: He wins the expedition’s trust, leads the mutiny, protects Jim as hostage and witness, changes sides as circumstances shift, and escapes with a sack of coin.

relationships.nature: Flatters and later protects him; each becomes the other’s hope of survival.
Bargains with him and seeks his help against the gallows.
Respects his seamanship but opposes his authority.
His confidant and fellow mutineer.
His former shipmate fears him and helps the loyal party.

cast.name: Captain Smollett
cast.role: Master of the Hispaniola and commander of the loyal party.
cast.appearance: A sharp-looking man over six feet tall, with a lean, upright build, weathered fair skin, short dark hair and a clean-shaven face. He wears a practical eighteenth-century captain’s coat, waistcoat, breeches and sturdy shoes.
cast.personality: Stern, candid, disciplined and courageous, with dry humour beneath his reserve.
cast.motivation: He wants to discharge his duty to the ship, owner and crew, and keep his people alive.
cast.fears: A badly prepared voyage, mutiny and the loss of his ship and men.
cast.speech: Short, dry and exact; he states numbered points, gives brisk orders and refuses to have conclusions put into his mouth.
cast.arc: His precautions help the loyal party survive; wounded in the stockade assault, he returns home and retires from the sea.

relationships.nature: His employer initially resents his frank precautions.
Works with the doctor to defend the party.
Values his help but distrusts his independent streak.
Rejects the mutineer’s terms and refuses to strike his colours.

cast.name: Ben Gunn
cast.role: Marooned former pirate who has already recovered Flint’s treasure.
cast.appearance: A white man with a deeply sun-burned face and blackened lips, fair eyes and pleasing features. His ragged patchwork of old canvas and sea-cloth is fastened with brass buttons, sticks and tarry loops; a sound leather belt with a brass buckle circles his waist.
cast.personality: Lonely, talkative, sly and eager for human company; quick-footed and anxious about old shipmates.
cast.motivation: He wants passage home, a thousand pounds, respectable treatment and the Christian food he has missed, especially cheese.
cast.fears: Silver and the pirates, being abandoned again, and a future as a liveried lodge-keeper.
cast.speech: Rambling, confidential and full of ‘says you’; he repeats his own name, pinches Jim for emphasis and invokes his pious mother.
cast.arc: After three years marooned he makes contact through Jim, allies with the doctor, helps rescue Jim and returns home, where he quickly spends his reward.

relationships.nature: Entrusts him with a proposal to the gentlemen.
Reveals the treasure’s removal and helps his rescue party.
Fears his old quartermaster and later enables his escape.

cast.name: Israel Hands
cast.role: Silver’s confidant, former gunner and Jim’s adversary aboard the schooner.
cast.appearance: A weathered, brandy-faced old sailor with grizzled hair and a frayed whisker ringlet. He has a sturdy seaman’s build and wears a worn jacket, shirt, breeches and sea shoes; a bloody thigh wound later restricts his movement.
cast.personality: Experienced and crafty, greedy for comforts and ready to kill when an opportunity appears.
cast.motivation: He wants the ship and the cabin’s comforts, and later seeks to regain control from Jim.
cast.fears: Being outmanoeuvred while wounded and helpless.
cast.speech: Coarse and practical, with sailor’s contractions, cynical maxims and a favourite toast, ‘Here’s luck!’
cast.arc: He joins Silver’s plot, fights O’Brien, helps Jim beach the ship and then attacks him; Jim shoots him in the rigging.

relationships.nature: A trusted fellow mutineer who urges an earlier rising.
Temporarily pilots for him, then tries to murder him.

cast.name: Pew
cast.role: Blind pirate who delivers Billy’s summons and directs the raid on the inn.
cast.age: An adult who appears hunched with age or weakness.
cast.appearance: A hunched blind man in a huge tattered sea-cloak with a hood, and a great green shade over his eyes and nose. He taps the road with a stick and moves with startling speed despite his bent outline.
cast.personality: Cruel, commanding and fiercely determined, with a beggar’s practiced false humility.
cast.motivation: He wants Flint’s papers and a share of the wealth that could free him from begging.
cast.fears: Remaining a poor beggar and losing his chance at the treasure.
cast.speech: Begins in a soft, sing-song appeal to charitable strangers; once he has a grip on Jim, his voice becomes cold, threatening and peremptory.
cast.arc: He delivers the black spot, leads the search for Flint’s papers and is abandoned by his men and trampled by a horse.

relationships.nature: His former shipmate and target for the black spot.
Forces him to lead him to Billy and later hunts him.

cast.name: Tom Redruth
cast.role: Trelawney’s gamekeeper and loyal servant.
cast.age: An old man, the oldest of the loyal party.
cast.appearance: A tall, broad old English gamekeeper over six feet high, with weathered fair skin, grey hair and a lined face. He wears a plain country coat, waistcoat, breeches, stockings and sturdy shoes.
cast.personality: Grumbling and reluctant to leave home, but dogged, obedient and dependable in danger.
cast.motivation: He serves the squire faithfully, even on a voyage he does not welcome.
cast.fears: Leaving his familiar life for the voyage.
cast.speech: Brief and respectful to the squire, with country phrasing; he grumbles more freely when speaking to Jim.
cast.arc: He guards Jim, follows the party into the stockade and dies after being shot, asking for a prayer.

relationships.nature: His longtime employer, whom he serves to the end.
Guards him before and during the journey to Bristol.

cast.name: Abraham Gray
cast.role: Carpenter’s mate who leaves the mutineers to follow his captain.
cast.appearance: A working seaman of sturdy build with weathered skin and short brown hair, dressed in a plain shirt, waistcoat, breeches and sailor’s shoes. A knife cut on his cheek is bandaged after he escapes the mutineers.
cast.personality: Steady, courageous and practical once he commits himself.
cast.motivation: He chooses his captain’s service and thereafter works to defend the loyal party.
cast.fears: The immediate danger posed by the mutineers and their guns.
cast.speech: Respectful and concise with officers, using plain seamanship and occasional sea oaths among companions.
cast.arc: He breaks away from the mutineers, fights for the loyal party, saves Jim from Anderson and later becomes a mate and part owner of a ship.

relationships.nature: Answers his captain’s summons and serves him faithfully.
Fights beside him and kills Anderson as he threatens him.
Joins the doctor’s party to rescue Jim.

places.name: Admiral Benbow
places.description: The Hawkins family’s lonely coastal inn, where Billy lodges and his former shipmates come seeking his papers.
places.visual: A small inn above Black Hill Cove, with a hanging Admiral Benbow sign, parlour fire, bar, upstairs rooms and a road past the door; cliffs, beach and a little bridge lie nearby.

places.name: the hall
places.description: Trelawney’s country house, where the packet is opened and Jim waits before the voyage.
places.visual: A leafless avenue leads between old gardens to pale buildings; the great library has bookcases topped with busts and a bright fire.

places.name: the Spy-glass
places.description: Silver’s Bristol public-house, where Jim meets him and recognizes Black Dog.
places.visual: A little dockside tavern with a large brass telescope sign, red window curtains, a clean sanded floor and two open doors clearing tobacco smoke from its low room.

places.name: Hispaniola
places.description: Trelawney’s two-hundred-ton schooner, the prize both parties need to leave the island.
places.visual: A sailing schooner with white canvas, a long brass nine amidships, galley and forecastle forward, stern cabins and a white-and-gilt cabin with stern windows.

places.name: Captain Kidd’s Anchorage
places.description: The island’s southern haven behind Skeleton Island, where the schooner anchors and the mutiny begins.
places.visual: A landlocked basin ringed with woods and distant rocky hills; two swampy streams enter it, and low shores smell of sodden leaves and rotting trunks.

places.name: the stockade
places.description: Flint’s old defensible enclosure, first held by the loyal party and later ceded to Silver.
places.visual: A six-foot palisade without a gate surrounds a sandy knoll and a loopholed pine log-house. A spring wells beneath its porch into a bottomless iron ship’s kettle; the roof has a square smoke-hole.

places.name: North Inlet
places.description: A sheltered northern estuary where Jim beaches the recovered schooner.
places.visual: A long, narrow, wooded inlet with flat sand and a decaying three-masted wreck draped in seaweed and flowering bushes.

places.name: the tall pine
places.description: Flint’s marked treasure cache on the plateau below the Spy-glass, already emptied by Ben Gunn.
places.visual: A giant red-trunked pine rises above nutmeg and azalea; beneath it is a grass-grown excavation with broken pick shaft and boards branded WALRUS.

places.name: Ben Gunn’s cave
places.description: Ben’s refuge on the two-pointed hill and the hiding place of the recovered treasure.
places.visual: A black cave mouth above a gentle beach slope opens into an airy sandy chamber with a spring, fern-hung pool, fire and heaps of coins and gold bars.

timeline.title: Chapter 1: The Old Sea-dog at the Admiral Benbow
timeline.summary: Jim recalls Billy’s arrival at the inn, his reign of fear and his defeat in a confrontation with Dr. Livesey.
events: The scarred seaman arrives with his chest and pays in gold.
He pays Jim to watch for a one-legged sailor and terrorizes the inn’s company.
Livesey refuses his demand for silence and threatens him with the assizes.
Billy puts away his knife and stays quiet after the doctor leaves.

knowledge.learns: Billy fears a one-legged seafaring man and wants warning of his arrival.
The dangerous lodger is in his district and threatens him with a knife.

timeline.title: Chapter 2: Black Dog Appears and Disappears
timeline.summary: Black Dog confronts Billy, and a fight is followed by Billy’s stroke and the doctor’s warning.
events: Black Dog questions Jim and waits behind the parlour door.
Billy recognizes him; their private discussion ends in a cutlass fight.
Black Dog flees wounded and Billy collapses.
Livesey bleeds Billy and warns that continued rum drinking will kill him.

knowledge.learns: The visitor is Black Dog, an old shipmate of the captain; the captain’s arm bears the name Billy Bones.
Billy has suffered a stroke rather than a fighting wound.

timeline.title: Chapter 3: The Black Spot
timeline.summary: Billy confides in Jim, Jim’s father dies, and Pew delivers a summons that immediately precedes Billy’s death.
events: Jim gives the weakened Billy one glass of rum.
Billy says Flint’s crew seek his chest and tells Jim when to warn Livesey.
Jim’s father dies; Billy resumes drinking during the days around the funeral.
Pew forces Jim to lead him to Billy and passes Billy the black spot.
Billy reads its deadline, tries to rise and dies of apoplexy.

knowledge.learns: Billy was Flint’s first mate, received something from him at Savannah, and calls the black spot a summons.
The black spot gives him until ten o’clock.

timeline.title: Chapter 4: The Sea-chest
timeline.summary: Jim and his mother brave the inn to recover their debt and escape with part of the money and the oilskin packet.
events: Jim tells his mother what he knows; the hamlet refuses to defend the inn.
Mother insists on returning for her lawful money, and Jim accompanies her.
They find the black spot, Billy’s key and the contents of his chest.
Pew tries the bolted door while Mother counts the mixed coins.
A whistle sends them fleeing with some money and the packet; Jim hides his fainting mother beneath the bridge.

knowledge.learns: The black spot says Billy had until ten that night; the chest contains gold and an oilcloth packet.
Billy’s chest holds enough money to pay at least part of his debt.

timeline.title: Chapter 5: The Last of the Blind Man
timeline.summary: Pew’s raid fails to find the packet, and revenue officers arrive as his men abandon him.
events: Pew’s men search Billy and his chest while Jim watches from hiding.
Pew demands Flint’s writing and orders a search for the innkeepers.
A warning whistle and approaching riders scatter the pirates.
Pew is trampled to death; Dance’s officers find the lugger escaping.
Jim asks to place the packet with Livesey and rides with Dance.

knowledge.learns: The pirates want Flint’s writing rather than merely Billy’s money; the whistle warns them of danger.

timeline.title: Chapter 6: The Captain’s Papers
timeline.summary: At the hall, the packet yields Billy’s account-book and Flint’s treasure map, inspiring an expedition.
events: Dance and Jim report the raid to Livesey and Trelawney.
Jim hands over the packet and eats while Dance is dismissed.
The doctor opens Billy’s account-book and the sealed island map.
Trelawney proposes fitting out a ship and taking Jim and Livesey.
Livesey insists on secrecy and travelling with protection.

knowledge.learns: The packet contains an island map marked with three red crosses and directions to Flint’s caches.
The recovered papers provide a practical clue to Flint’s treasure.
The papers include a chart and a record interpreted as Billy’s shares of plunder.

timeline.title: Chapter 7: I Go to Bristol
timeline.summary: Trelawney’s letter announces the ship and crew; Jim says goodbye to his mother and travels to Bristol.
events: Jim waits at the hall under Redruth’s supervision and dreams over the map.
Trelawney writes that Silver has helped recruit the crew and the Hispaniola is ready.
Jim visits the repaired inn and meets the apprentice replacing him.
He leaves his mother and travels by mail with Redruth.
In Bristol, Trelawney tells Jim they sail tomorrow.

knowledge.learns: The squire has talked about treasure and hired a one-legged cook named Silver.
Leaving home means another boy will take his place beside his mother.

timeline.title: Chapter 8: At the Sign of the Spy-glass
timeline.summary: Jim meets Silver, recognizes Black Dog in his tavern and is persuaded of Silver’s innocence.
events: Jim takes Trelawney’s note to Silver’s tavern.
Black Dog flees when Jim recognizes him; Silver sends men after him.
Silver questions Morgan and performs outrage at the visitor’s escape.
He charms Jim on their walk and reports the affair to the gentlemen.
Livesey and Trelawney praise Silver.

knowledge.learns: Black Dog has been at Silver’s tavern, but comes to believe Silver is innocent.
Jim knows Black Dog and Pew and can identify Black Dog.

timeline.title: Chapter 9: Powder and Arms
timeline.summary: Smollett voices his doubts and secures precautions before the voyage.
events: Jim and the gentlemen board the schooner.
Smollett objects to the cruise, the crew and Arrow’s familiarity with the men.
He asks to move arms and loyal berths aft and keep the map secret.
Trelawney agrees reluctantly; the powder and berths are shifted.
Silver reports aboard, and Smollett sends Jim to work.

knowledge.learns: The owners will accept his precautions despite Trelawney’s resentment.
The crew know the island’s coordinates and details of the treasure voyage.

timeline.title: Chapter 10: The Voyage
timeline.summary: The Hispaniola sails; Arrow disappears, Silver wins Jim’s affection, and Jim hides in the apple barrel.
events: The crew sing as the schooner weighs anchor.
Arrow repeatedly appears drunk and disappears overboard on a dark night.
Silver tends his spotless galley, parrot and friendship with Jim.
The ship approaches the island after a generally successful passage.
Jim climbs into the apple barrel and hears Silver begin a dangerous conversation.

knowledge.learns: Silver’s opening words reveal a plot threatening the honest men, though Jim has not yet heard its full details.

timeline.title: Chapter 11: What I Heard in the Apple-Barrel
timeline.summary: Jim overhears Silver recruit Dick and discuss the timing and murderous purpose of the mutiny.
events: Silver tells Dick of his pirate service and savings.
Dick agrees to join the plot.
Hands presses for action; Silver insists they wait for the treasure and navigation.
Silver votes to kill the loyal party and claims Trelawney for himself.
Dick fetches rum instead of an apple, and the lookout cries land.

knowledge.learns: Silver was Flint’s quartermaster and plans murder after the treasure is aboard; some hands remain faithful.
Dick will join the mutineers.

timeline.title: Chapter 12: Council of War
timeline.summary: Jim secretly warns the officers, who decide to wait and identify their allies.
events: The island is sighted and Silver identifies the anchorage from an unmarked chart copy.
Jim privately asks Livesey to arrange a meeting.
The captain sends the men grog and calls Jim to the cabin.
Jim recounts Silver’s conversation; Trelawney admits Smollett was right.
The officers decide to continue and watch for a chance to strike.

knowledge.learns: Silver leads a plot to seize the treasure and kill the loyal party.
The conspiracy includes Hands and is larger and better concealed than he had suspected.
His admired cook is the mutineers’ leader.

timeline.title: Chapter 13: How I Began My Shore Adventure
timeline.summary: The crew’s discontent becomes dangerous, and Jim secretly goes ashore with the mutineers.
events: The becalmed ship is warped into the island anchorage.
Livesey notices the stagnant smell and predicts fever.
Smollett offers shore leave to ease the immediate crisis.
Thirteen men embark, leaving six aboard.
Jim slips into a boat and escapes into the thicket ahead of Silver.

knowledge.learns: The crew’s discipline is breaking down and Silver is openly managing the shore party.
Jim has joined the boats going ashore.

timeline.title: Chapter 14: The First Blow
timeline.summary: Jim explores the island and witnesses Silver murder the loyal sailor Tom.
events: Jim passes marsh, sandy ground and a rattlesnake.
He follows voices and hides near Silver and Tom.
A distant scream announces Alan’s death; Tom rejects Silver’s cause.
Silver throws his crutch at Tom and stabs him twice.
Jim flees in terror toward the two-peaked hill.

knowledge.learns: Silver will murder an unarmed loyal sailor; Alan has apparently been killed as well.
Tom refuses to join the mutiny.

timeline.title: Chapter 15: The Man of the Island
timeline.summary: Jim meets marooned Ben Gunn and learns enough to hope for an ally.
events: Jim confronts the strange figure pursuing him among the trees.
Ben identifies himself and asks for cheese and news of the ship.
Jim tells him about Silver and the mutiny.
Ben describes Flint’s burial party and his own marooning, and proposes terms.
A cannon sounds; the two run toward the anchorage and see a flag.

knowledge.learns: Ben has lived alone for three years, claims to be rich and has a homemade boat under a white rock.
Flint is dead, but Silver leads mutineers on the newly arrived ship.

timeline.title: Chapter 16: Narrative Continued by the Doctor: How the Ship Was Abandoned
timeline.summary: Livesey finds a defensible stockade and the loyal party transfers supplies from the ship.
events: Hunter reports Jim has gone ashore; Livesey and Hunter investigate the stockade.
Livesey finds its spring and hears a death cry he fears is Jim’s.
The loyal party loads the jolly-boat while Redruth guards the passage.
Livesey establishes Hunter and Joyce in the stockade and returns for another load.
Smollett summons Gray, who fights free of the mutineers and joins the boat.

knowledge.learns: The stockade encloses a spring, making it a defensible alternative to the waterless cabin.
Smollett will take him with the loyal party if he joins immediately.

timeline.title: Chapter 17: Narrative Continued by the Doctor: The Jolly-boat’s Last Trip
timeline.summary: The overloaded boat faces the ebb and the schooner’s gun, then sinks near shore with much of the supplies.
