events: The five men struggle to keep the overloaded boat afloat against the ebb.
They see the mutineers preparing the long nine.
Trelawney shoots at Hands but hits another man.
The gun fires as the captain backs water; the boat sinks in the shallows.
The party wades ashore with only two serviceable guns, leaving stores behind.

knowledge.learns: The mutineers possess the long nine and its ammunition; Gray identifies Hands as Flint’s former gunner.

timeline.title: Chapter 18: Narrative Continued by the Doctor: End of the First Day’s Fighting
timeline.summary: The party reaches the stockade, but Redruth is killed and the mutineers recover the lost stores.
events: The loyal party repels Anderson’s men near the stockade.
A shot from the woods mortally wounds Redruth.
The captain raises British colours and covers the dead man with a flag.
Cannonballs strike around the fort; Smollett refuses to lower the colours.
Gray and Hunter find the pirates carrying away the lost stores.
Jim arrives at the stockade.

knowledge.learns: A rescue consort cannot be expected until after the end of August, while provisions are very short.
Jim has survived and reached the stockade.

timeline.title: Chapter 19: Narrative Resumed by Jim Hawkins: The Garrison in the Stockade
timeline.summary: Jim rejoins the loyal party and tells them about Ben Gunn as they bury Redruth and assess their chances.
events: Ben identifies the British flag and tells Jim how a gentleman may approach him.
Cannon fire separates them; Jim watches the pirate flag and locates the white rock.
Jim reaches the stockade and tells his story.
Smollett assigns watches and work; Redruth is buried.
The leaders decide to reduce the pirates’ numbers while relying also on rum and fever.

knowledge.learns: Ben Gunn wants a gentleman to meet him alone with a white object; he has a particular craving for cheese.
The loyal party has lost Redruth and cannot expect its food to last until relief arrives.

timeline.title: Chapter 20: Silver’s Embassy
timeline.summary: Silver offers terms for the chart, but Smollett rejects him and prepares for an attack.
events: Silver approaches under a flag of truce.
He alludes to a pirate attacked during the night.
He offers the loyal party passage or provisions in exchange for the chart.
Smollett offers only surrender and trial, and threatens to shoot Silver next time.
Denied help to rise, Silver crawls to his crutch and leaves vowing an assault.

knowledge.learns: A pirate was attacked in the night and suspects Ben Gunn was responsible.
Smollett will not exchange the chart for Silver’s proposed terms.

timeline.title: Chapter 21: The Attack
timeline.summary: The pirates assault the stockade and are repelled at heavy cost to both sides.
events: Smollett scolds the defenders for leaving their posts and arranges the defence.
Joyce fires, and the pirates answer from the woods.
Attackers scale the palisade and press the log-house loopholes.
The defenders rush out with cutlasses; Gray kills Anderson as he threatens Jim.
The surviving pirates retreat; Joyce is dead, Hunter stunned and Smollett wounded.

knowledge.learns: The assault has cost the loyal party Joyce and left Hunter and the captain badly hurt.

timeline.title: Chapter 22: How I Began My Sea Adventure
timeline.summary: After the battle, Jim slips away to find Ben’s boat and plans to cut the schooner adrift.
events: Livesey treats the wounded; Hunter lingers unconscious and later dies.
The doctor leaves with the chart, apparently to visit Ben Gunn.
Jim takes biscuit and pistols and slips out while the others tend Smollett.
He finds the coracle beneath a goatskin tent by the white rock.
At night he carries it to the water, intending to cut the schooner’s cable.

knowledge.learns: Ben’s boat is a tiny, portable goatskin coracle; Silver leaves two men aboard the schooner.

timeline.title: Chapter 23: The Ebb-tide Runs
timeline.summary: Jim cuts the schooner loose and is carried with her toward the open sea.
events: The difficult coracle drifts to the schooner’s taut hawser.
Jim waits for wind to slacken the rope and cuts most strands.
He hears Hands and the other watchman quarrelling drunkenly.
He severs the last strands and glimpses the men wrestling in the cabin.
The ebb carries schooner and coracle through the narrows; Jim falls asleep expecting death.

knowledge.learns: Hands and the other watchman are drunk and fighting rather than guarding the ship.

timeline.title: Chapter 24: The Cruise of the Coracle
timeline.summary: Jim survives the swell, spots the unsteered schooner and boards her as she bears down on him.
events: Jim wakes off the island’s dangerous southwestern cliffs.
He avoids the surf and sea lions and learns to balance the coracle among the waves.
Thirst torments him as he drifts past the wooded coast.
He sees the schooner sailing erratically and paddles after her.
She turns toward him; he leaps onto the jib-boom as she destroys the coracle.

knowledge.learns: The schooner is apparently unsteered and may be recaptured.

timeline.title: Chapter 25: I Strike the Jolly Roger
timeline.summary: Jim takes possession of the schooner and bargains with wounded Hands for help sailing her.
events: Jim boards and finds O’Brien dead and Hands badly wounded.
He searches the wrecked cabin, eats and drinks, and brings Hands brandy.
Jim declares himself captain and throws the pirate flag overboard.
Hands agrees to pilot the ship in return for food, drink and a dressing.
They sail toward North Inlet while Hands watches Jim slyly.

knowledge.learns: Hands and O’Brien fought; Hands survives and knows how to navigate the schooner.
Jim intends to beach the schooner in North Inlet.

timeline.title: Chapter 26: Israel Hands
timeline.summary: Hands pilots the ship into North Inlet, then attacks Jim, who shoots him from the rigging.
events: Hands sends Jim for wine, but Jim secretly watches him retrieve a bloody dirk.
They discuss death and Hands pilots the schooner into the inlet.
Hands attacks; Jim’s wet pistol fails and they dodge around the mast.
The ship grounds and tips, and Jim climbs the shrouds and reloads.
Hands climbs after him, throws the dirk into his shoulder and is shot as Jim’s pistols discharge.

knowledge.learns: Hands can move and has hidden a dirk, making their bargain a prelude to attack.
Jim has reloaded his pistols while beyond his reach in the rigging.

timeline.title: Chapter 27: “Pieces of Eight”
timeline.summary: Jim leaves the recovered schooner and returns to the stockade, only to walk into Silver’s camp.
events: Hands sinks dead; Jim frees his lightly pinned shoulder from the mast.
Jim throws O’Brien’s body overboard and secures what sail he can.
He wades ashore and makes his way back through the woods.
He mistakes the stockade’s sleeping occupants for his friends.
Silver’s parrot cries out and Jim is captured.

knowledge.learns: The pirates occupy the stockade he thought still held his friends.
Jim has returned to the stockade and is in pirate hands.

timeline.title: Chapter 28: In the Enemy’s Camp
timeline.summary: Jim defies the pirates, and Silver protects him while seeking a witness against the gallows.
events: Silver says Livesey bargained away the stockade and that Jim’s friends have left.
Jim reveals he overheard the plot and took the schooner.
Morgan threatens Jim, but Silver defies the crew and protects him.
The pirates withdraw for a council.
Silver privately bargains with Jim: protection in return for help at his trial, and reveals that Livesey gave him the chart.

knowledge.learns: His friends were alive when they left, and Silver has the original chart.
Jim overheard the plot and removed the schooner; he believes Jim has hidden it safely.

timeline.title: Chapter 29: The Black Spot Again
timeline.summary: Silver defeats an attempt to depose him by answering the crew’s charges and producing the chart.
events: The crew return with a black spot cut from Dick’s Bible.
George Merry reads the charges against Silver and demands his deposition.
Silver answers each charge, calling Jim a valuable hostage.
He produces Flint’s chart, and the men crowd around it.
The crew restore Silver as captain; he gives Jim the black spot.

knowledge.learns: The crew had previously challenged Silver’s authority on landing and now fear they are near the gallows.
His possession of the chart can restore the crew’s confidence in him.

timeline.title: Chapter 30: On Parole
timeline.summary: Livesey visits the pirates, and Jim refuses escape because he has given Silver his word.
events: Livesey treats the pirates’ wounds and fever.
Silver obtains Jim’s parole and lets him speak to the doctor across the palisade.
Livesey urges Jim to escape, but Jim refuses to break his word.
Jim tells him the schooner is beached in North Inlet.
Livesey warns Silver about the treasure, promises help short of perjury and goes to seek assistance.

knowledge.learns: Jim recovered the schooner and left her on the southern beach of North Inlet.
Livesey intends to seek help and warns that danger awaits at the treasure.
Livesey will try to save him without perjury and advises him to keep Jim close.

timeline.title: Chapter 31: The Treasure-hunt--Flint’s Pointer
timeline.summary: Silver leads the pirates and tethered Jim toward the treasure, where a skeleton points the way.
events: Silver thanks Jim for keeping his parole and restores the crew’s confidence.
The pirates take both gigs across the anchorage with tools and provisions.
They climb toward the plateau, with Jim tied to Silver.
They find a skeleton laid straight with its arms above its head.
A compass bearing reveals that the bones point toward Skeleton Island.

knowledge.learns: The skeleton has been laid as a directional pointer and appears to be Allardyce.
The skeleton’s bearing matches the direction written on the treasure map.

timeline.title: Chapter 32: The Treasure-hunt--The Voice Among the Trees
timeline.summary: A mysterious voice terrifies the pirates, who press on to discover an empty treasure pit.
events: The party rests on the plateau and discusses Flint.
A voice sings the pirates’ song and calls for Darby M’Graw and rum.
Silver and the older hands recognize the voice as Ben Gunn’s.
The party checks successive tall trees and closes on the correct pine.
They find a grass-grown excavation with broken tools and empty packing-case boards.

knowledge.learns: Ben Gunn appears to be on the island, and the marked treasure cache has already been emptied.
The treasure has been removed before the pirates’ arrival at the marked site.

timeline.title: Chapter 33: The Fall of a Chieftain
timeline.summary: Livesey’s party rescues Jim at the empty cache, and Ben’s removal of the treasure is explained.
events: Silver arms Jim and places the pit between them and the angry pirates.
Livesey, Gray and Ben fire from concealment; Silver shoots the wounded Merry.
The three remaining pirates flee inland.
Livesey explains Ben found and moved the treasure and why he gave Silver the chart.
The rescuers recover and anchor the drifting schooner, then reunite at Ben’s cave among the gold.

knowledge.learns: Ben moved the treasure to his cave before the voyage arrived; Livesey’s bargain secured a safe move there.
Ben had found the treasure and the doctor knew the chart was obsolete.
The schooner has floated free but remains recoverable in North Inlet.

timeline.title: Chapter 34: And Last
timeline.summary: The survivors load the treasure, leave three pirates on the island, and return home after Silver escapes.
events: The party carries treasure to the beach and loads it over several days.
They leave supplies for the three surviving mutineers and sail despite their pleas.
In Spanish America, Ben helps Silver escape with a sack of coin.
The remaining company recruits hands and returns to Bristol.
Jim recounts the survivors’ fortunes and his enduring nightmares of the island.

knowledge.learns: Ben connived at Silver’s escape and Silver took a sack worth perhaps three or four hundred guineas.
Silver has escaped the ship with money.

divergencePoints.label: Billy Beats the Clock
divergencePoints.moment: Billy reads the black spot’s deadline and rises to act before ten.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: He suffers a fatal apoplectic stroke and falls dead on the parlour floor.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Billy survived the black spot and had six hours to get away with his chest?
divergencePoints.stakes: Billy’s papers, Jim’s safety and the pirates’ pursuit would all remain in play.

divergencePoints.label: The Whole Money-Bag
divergencePoints.moment: Jim urges his mother to take the whole bag when Pew has tried the bolted door.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: She refuses to take more than her due, then leaves with only what she has counted when a whistle sounds.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Jim’s mother took the whole money-bag as soon as Pew came to the door?
divergencePoints.stakes: A quicker escape could change what the pirates find and whether Jim takes the packet.

divergencePoints.label: An Apple for Silver
divergencePoints.moment: Silver sends Dick to fetch an apple while Jim is concealed in the barrel.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Hands calls for rum instead, and Dick leaves the barrel undisturbed.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Dick fetched Silver’s apple and found Jim hiding in the barrel?
divergencePoints.stakes: Jim’s life and the loyal party’s only warning of the plot are at risk.

divergencePoints.label: Tom Walks Away
divergencePoints.moment: Tom rejects the mutiny and turns his back on Silver beside the marsh.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Silver knocks him down with his crutch and stabs him twice.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Silver let Tom walk away after Tom refused to join the mutiny?
divergencePoints.stakes: A loyal sailor might survive with dangerous knowledge of Silver’s plans.

divergencePoints.label: Gray’s Thirty Seconds
divergencePoints.moment: Smollett calls Gray out of the forecastle and gives him thirty seconds to join the departing boat.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Gray fights free of the mutineers, receives a cut on his cheek and joins his captain.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Gray failed to break away before Smollett’s thirty seconds ran out?
divergencePoints.stakes: The loyal party would lose an able fighter, and Gray would remain among the mutineers.

divergencePoints.label: A Bargain at the Stockade
divergencePoints.moment: Silver offers provisions or passage in exchange for the treasure chart.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Smollett rejects the offer and demands unconditional surrender for trial.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Smollett accepted Silver’s proposed bargain for the chart?
divergencePoints.stakes: The defenders’ lives would depend on a pirate’s promises and the fate of the treasure.

divergencePoints.label: The Hawser Holds
divergencePoints.moment: Jim waits in the coracle for the schooner’s hawser to slacken enough to cut its last strands.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: A breeze slackens the rope, and Jim cuts the schooner adrift.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if the breeze never slackened the hawser and Jim had to abandon the cut?
divergencePoints.stakes: The pirates could retain their ship while Jim remains alone in a dangerous coracle.

divergencePoints.label: Silver’s Last Card
divergencePoints.moment: Morgan draws his knife after Jim boasts of thwarting the pirates and offers to speak for them at trial.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Silver stops Morgan and defends Jim, then privately makes a bargain with him.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Silver let Morgan seize Jim instead of standing between the boy and the crew?
divergencePoints.stakes: Jim’s life and Silver’s chance of a witness against the gallows hang together.

divergencePoints.label: Over the Palisade
divergencePoints.moment: Livesey urges Jim to climb over the stockade and escape while Silver waits out of earshot.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Jim refuses because he has given Silver his word not to escape.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Jim took the doctor’s offer and jumped the palisade despite his promise to Silver?
divergencePoints.stakes: Jim could escape immediately, but Silver would face his suspicious crew without his hostage.

divergencePoints.label: No Shore Boat for Silver
divergencePoints.moment: In the Spanish American port, Ben Gunn connives at Silver’s escape from the schooner.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Silver leaves in a shore boat with a sack of coins taken through a bulkhead.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Ben Gunn refused to help Silver escape at the Spanish American port?
divergencePoints.stakes: Silver’s freedom, his stolen money and the survivors’ homeward passage remain unsettled.

visual.era: Eighteenth-century English coastal dress and powdered wigs; wooden sailing schooners, hand-worked rigging, flintlock weapons, coaching roads and pirate stockades.
visual.palette: Frost-grey cove and candle yellow give way to Bristol tar-browns, blue sea, bleached sand, poisonous marsh greens and dark pine shadows; moonlight and firelight punctuate night scenes.
motifs: A crutch and one missing leg
visual.comicStyle: Use a nineteenth-century adventure-engraving tradition: fine ink contours, cross-hatched shadows and restrained watercolour washes. Alternate broad establishing panels of ship or island with close, crowded faces and sharp, sudden action; preserve the practical layout of rigging, palisade and terrain.

glossary.note: The Hawkins family’s coastal inn.
The cove beside the inn.
The schooner fitted out by Trelawney.
The island’s tallest hill; also the name of Silver’s Bristol tavern.
The islet sheltering the southern anchorage.
The sheltered southern harbour.
The northern estuary where Jim beaches the schooner.
The dead pirate; Silver also gives this name to his parrot.
A pirate’s paper summons or notice of deposition.
Ben Gunn’s small, portable goatskin boat.
The black flag flown by the mutineers.
A pirate’s flattering name for a pirate.
Flint’s former ship, named on boards at the empty cache.
Spanish coins and the parrot’s repeated cry.

the-picture-of-dorian-gray.title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
the-picture-of-dorian-gray.author: Oscar Wilde
the-picture-of-dorian-gray.premise: A painter’s portrait awakens Dorian Gray to his own beauty just as Lord Henry Wotton persuades him that youth is life’s greatest possession. Dorian’s wish to remain young while the picture ages becomes entangled with his pursuit of sensation and the harm he does to others.
the-picture-of-dorian-gray.hook: A beautiful young man keeps his face while his portrait records the life behind it.
the-picture-of-dorian-gray.logline: As his hidden portrait bears the marks of age and wrongdoing, Dorian Gray pursues pleasure while struggling to conceal the corruption it reveals.

world.setting: Fashionable London drawing-rooms, studios and clubs stand within reach of shabby theatres and riverside opium dens; Dorian also entertains at Selby Royal, his Nottinghamshire country house.
world.period: Late nineteenth-century England, chiefly London society
rules: Dorian’s portrait changes as his life and character change, while his own face retains its youthful beauty; the cause and precise mechanism remain unexplained.
The portrait’s altered surface still bears Basil’s brushwork and signature. Its changes can be seen by someone other than Dorian.
Dorian’s youth does not make him safe from ordinary violence: James Vane can threaten him with a revolver, and a knife can kill him.
Rank, wealth and respectable appearances protect reputations, while scandal can exclude people from houses, clubs and society.
Servants answer bells, carry notes and prepare carriages; hansoms, broughams, trains and telegrams connect the characters.
Marriage across class boundaries invites social objection, and a young man under age has guardians with a say in his affairs.
Murder risks arrest and hanging; an inquest examines a suspicious death, though its public verdict may differ from private belief.
Opium offers Dorian temporary oblivion, not an escape from memory or danger.
world.tone: Sensuous, witty and often languid, with satire giving way to dread, remorse and sudden violence.
sensitivities: The narration and characters use antisemitic caricature, notably in descriptions of the theatre manager.
Racist and colonial language depicts non-European people as exotic or inferior, especially in accounts of Dorian’s collections.
Lord Henry’s sweeping claims about women and class are provocative prejudices, not reliable accounts of their subjects.
Suicide, coercive blackmail, drug dependence and violence are central to the story.

voice.narration: A third-person past-tense narrator moves close to Dorian, Basil and Lord Henry, entering their thoughts while also making urbane generalizations and occasionally addressing shared human experience.
style: Lush descriptions accumulate colour, scent, texture and sound before a pointed observation or interruption changes the scene.
Long, balanced sentences and repeated clauses alternate with abrupt questions, exclamations and short verdicts.
Flowers, jewels, music, mirrors, theatre and classical myth supply recurring comparisons for faces, feelings and rooms.
Aphorisms turn familiar moral claims inside out; the narrator can echo a character’s reasoning without making it trustworthy.
Interiority moves through questions, reversals and imagined explanations, often leaving a motive or mystery unsettled.
British spelling and period French phrases sit naturally beside references to painting, poetry, music and antiquity.
voice.dialogue: Speech uses quotation marks and frequent descriptive tags, with interruptions, dashes, exclamations and pauses. Society exchanges are polished contests of paradox; intimate conversations become repetitive, pleading or brutally direct.
samplePassages: The studio was filled with the rich odour of roses, and when the light summer wind stirred amidst the trees of the garden, there came through the open door the heavy scent of the lilac, or the more delicate perfume of the pink-flowering thorn. From the corner of the divan of Persian saddle-bags on which he was lying, smoking, as was his custom, innumerable cigarettes, Lord Henry Wotton could just catch the gleam of the honey-sweet and honey-coloured blossoms of a laburnum, whose tremulous branches seemed hardly able to bear the burden of a beauty so flamelike as theirs

“Mother, Mother,” she cried, “why does he love me so much? I know why I love him. I love him because he is like what love himself should be. But what does he see in me? I am not worthy of him. And yet—why, I cannot tell—though I feel so much beneath him, I don’t feel humble. I feel proud, terribly proud. Mother, did you love my father as I love Prince Charming?”

He got up and locked both doors. At least he would be alone when he looked upon the mask of his shame. Then he drew the screen aside and saw himself face to face. It was perfectly true. The portrait had altered. As he often remembered afterwards, and always with no small wonder, he found himself at first gazing at the portrait with a feeling of almost scientific interest. That such a change should have taken place was incredible to him. And yet it was a fact.

cast.name: Dorian Gray
cast.role: Beautiful, wealthy young man whose portrait bears the visible marks of his life.
cast.age: Under twenty-one at the portrait sitting; thirty-eight by the later events
cast.appearance: A gracefully built, youthful-looking man with fair skin, finely curved scarlet lips, frank blue eyes and crisp gold curls. His beauty and apparent youth persist for years. He dresses with exquisite care in fashionable coats, evening clothes, rings and a carefully chosen necktie.
cast.personality: Initially affectionate, impulsive and impressionable; later charming, curious, secretive and capable of calculated cruelty.
cast.motivation: He wants beauty and youth to last, seeks new sensations, and later longs to escape his past and recover innocence.
cast.fears: Age, ugliness, exposure of the portrait, punishment and the approach of death.
cast.speech: He begins with eager questions and boyish exclamations, adopts Harry’s polished paradoxes, and becomes petulant or commanding when thwarted. Fear breaks his composure into urgent questions and pleas.
cast.arc: His wish seems fulfilled; after rejecting Sibyl he hides the changing portrait, pursues pleasure, murders Basil and tries to destroy the evidence of his conscience.

relationships.nature: Painter and devoted friend whose portrait becomes Dorian’s secret; Dorian murders him.
Fascinating friend whose theories shape Dorian’s pursuit of sensation.
Actress he loves and becomes engaged to, then cruelly rejects.
Sibyl’s brother, who hunts him to avenge her death.
Estranged former intimate whom he blackmails into disposing of Basil’s body.

cast.name: Lord Henry Wotton
cast.role: Dorian’s aristocratic friend and influential apostle of pleasure.
cast.age: A young man at the opening; about ten years older than Dorian
cast.appearance: Tall and graceful, with an olive-coloured, worn face, dark crescent-shaped eyebrows, brown agate eyes and a pointed brown beard. His pale, fine hands move expressively. He wears fashionable dark tailoring, gloves and a buttonhole, and often carries cigarettes and an ebony cane.
cast.personality: Brilliant, languid, curious and cynical, with flashes of tenderness beneath his polished detachment.
cast.motivation: He enjoys studying people, exercising influence and turning experience into stimulating conversation.
cast.fears: He explicitly fears death and dislikes vulgarity, boredom and the prospect of growing old.
cast.speech: His low musical voice delivers elegant paradoxes, reversals and teasing generalizations. He calls friends by their familiar names and treats even grave subjects as material for wit.
cast.arc: He makes Dorian a fascinating study and remains his friend, never accepting that Dorian could have murdered Basil.

relationships.nature: Friend and object of his intellectual influence and curiosity.
Old Oxford friend who distrusts his influence on Dorian.
Dorian’s fiancée, whose death he recasts as an artistic tragedy.

cast.name: Basil Hallward
cast.role: Painter of Dorian’s portrait and his devoted, increasingly alarmed friend.
cast.age: A young man at the opening; older than Dorian
cast.appearance: A solidly built man with a rugged, strong face, coal-black hair and a thoughtful expression. He wears a dark nineteenth-century suit or painter’s working clothes and sometimes tosses his head back in a distinctive gesture.
cast.personality: Earnest, loyal and conscientious, with a guarded intensity about his art and affections.
cast.motivation: He wants to protect Dorian, preserve their friendship and make art inspired by Dorian’s beauty.
cast.fears: Exposure of his idolatry, Dorian’s corruption and the loss of his friendship.
cast.speech: He speaks gravely and plainly, often addressing Harry or Dorian by name. Emotion draws out repetitions, protests and direct appeals; he challenges Harry’s paradoxes.
cast.arc: He hides his devotion, confesses it, then confronts Dorian over rumours and sees the portrait before Dorian kills him.

relationships.nature: His artistic inspiration and beloved friend, who eventually murders him.
Oxford friend whose influence on Dorian he fears.
He comes to support her engagement to Dorian and mourns her death.

cast.name: Sibyl Vane
cast.role: A young Shakespearean actress and Dorian’s fiancée.
cast.appearance: Small and graceful, with a flowerlike pale face, a small Greek-shaped head, dark-brown hair in plaited coils, violet eyes and rose-petal lips. She wears modest everyday dresses and, onstage, the costumes of Shakespeare’s heroines.
cast.personality: Imaginative, affectionate and trusting, with an intense capacity for delight and despair.
cast.motivation: She loves Dorian as her Prince Charming and wants a real life with him beyond the theatre.
cast.fears: She cannot bear the thought of Dorian leaving her and fears the loss of his love.
cast.speech: Her low, musical voice rises into rapturous repetitions and theatrical images. With Jim she is playful and fanciful; with Dorian she speaks in ardent declarations and, when rejected, desperate pleas.
cast.arc: Love makes her see acting as hollow; after a failed performance Dorian rejects her, and she dies from swallowing a theatrical substance.

relationships.nature: Her Prince Charming and fiancé, who abandons her.
Her protective younger brother.
Her mother, who depends on her acting income and hopes for a rich marriage.

cast.name: James Vane
cast.role: Sibyl’s sailor brother, who vows to kill the man who wrongs her.
cast.age: Sixteen when he leaves for Australia; about thirty-four when he returns
cast.appearance: Short and thick-set, with rough brown hair, large hands and feet and a heavy, stern face. He wears coarse, ill-fitting clothes; as a sailor he has tattoos on both arms and later wears a coarse shirt and blue trousers.
cast.personality: Protective, blunt and suspicious, but tender towards Sibyl.
cast.motivation: He wants to protect his sister and mother, make money, and after Sibyl’s death avenge her.
cast.fears: Sibyl being deceived or harmed by a gentleman while he is away.
cast.speech: He speaks slowly and directly, with terse questions, warnings and forceful promises. His roughness softens when he says goodbye to Sibyl.
cast.arc: Unable to see Dorian clearly before sailing, he hunts the man known as Prince Charming, briefly mistakes his youthful face for proof of innocence, and is accidentally shot at Selby.

relationships.nature: Beloved sister whose death he vows to avenge.
Mother whose protection of Sibyl he distrusts.
The man he seeks to kill for ruining Sibyl.

cast.name: Mrs. Vane
cast.role: Sibyl and James’s mother, a faded actress dependent on the theatre.
cast.appearance: A faded, tired-looking woman with a thin face, dry thin lips and hands whitened with bismuth powder. She wears worn theatrical clothing and false jewels, and often arranges herself with elaborate gestures.
cast.personality: Anxious, vain and theatrical, yet capable of feeling shame and affection for her children.
cast.motivation: She wants financial security and hopes Sibyl’s wealthy admirer will offer a respectable marriage.
cast.fears: Poverty, exposure of her past and her son’s judgment.
cast.speech: She uses stately stage gestures and repeated phrases, speaks querulously about money and propriety, and turns private distress into a scene.
cast.arc: She urges prudence and considers Dorian’s apparent wealth, admits to James that she never married his father, and later gives evidence at Sibyl’s inquest.

relationships.nature: Daughter whose acting supports them and whose romance she regards with mixed concern and ambition.
Son whose direct questions unsettle her.

cast.name: Alan Campbell
cast.role: Chemist and estranged former intimate whom Dorian coerces into destroying Basil’s body.
cast.appearance: A pale, lean-looking young man with coal-black hair, dark eyebrows and a steady gaze. He wears sober fashionable clothes and an Astrakhan coat, keeping his hands in its pockets when he first confronts Dorian.
cast.personality: Intelligent, reserved and resolute, with a deep aversion to Dorian after their estrangement.
cast.motivation: He wants to keep clear of Dorian and protect himself from the disgrace threatened in Dorian’s letter.
cast.fears: The exposure threatened by Dorian’s blackmail and involvement in his crime.
cast.speech: He speaks slowly, coldly and with deliberate, repeated refusals; under pressure his sentences become short and mechanical.
cast.arc: He refuses to help conceal the murder until Dorian blackmails him; he destroys the body and later shoots himself.

relationships.nature: Former close friend who forces him to dispose of Basil’s body.
The murdered man whose body he is compelled to destroy.

places.name: Basil Hallward’s studio
places.description: The painter’s London studio, where Dorian sits for the portrait and meets Lord Henry.
places.visual: A huge window with long tussore-silk curtains, an upright easel and a divan of Persian saddle-bags; an open door leads to a rose- and lilac-scented garden.

places.name: Dorian’s London house
places.description: His fashionable house near Grosvenor Square, a setting for hospitality and concealment.
places.visual: An oak-panelled entrance hall with a gilt Venetian lantern leads to a richly furnished library, a great hearth, a secret press and an octagonal bedroom hung with Renaissance tapestries.

places.name: The old schoolroom
places.description: Dorian’s locked childhood room at the top of the house, where he hides the portrait.
places.visual: Dust, worn carpet and mildew surround a painted Italian cassone, a nearly empty bookcase and faded Flemish tapestry; the portrait hangs behind a purple-and-gold curtain.

places.name: Royal Theatre, Holborn
places.description: The shabby theatre where Dorian discovers Sibyl and later rejects her.
places.visual: Flaming gas-jets and gaudy bills outside; within are dingy stalls, a crowded pit and gallery, tawdry Cupids, a vulgar drop-scene and a dusty greenroom.

places.name: The Vanes’ lodgings
places.description: The modest Euston Road home shared by Sibyl, James and their mother.
places.visual: A dingy sitting-room with one armchair, a stained tablecloth and worn theatrical clothing; omnibuses and cabs rumble outside.

places.name: Lord Henry’s library
places.description: His Mayfair room, where Dorian describes his love for Sibyl.
places.visual: Olive-stained oak panelling, cream raised plaster, a brickdust carpet and fringed Persian rugs; blue china jars and tulips stand by a Louis Quatorze clock.

places.name: The riverside opium den
places.description: A shabby house near the quay where Dorian seeks oblivion and James hears his nickname.
places.visual: Wedged between factories, it has a tattered green curtain, flaring gas-jets reflected in fly-blown mirrors, muddy sawdust, a painted bar and a dark room of ragged mattresses.

places.name: Selby Royal
places.description: Dorian’s luxurious Nottinghamshire country house and the scene of James’s death.
places.visual: A glass conservatory with palms and tiled floor opens towards terraces and gardens; beyond lie an avenue, pine-wood, alder thicket and the stables of the Home Farm.

timeline.title: Chapter 1
timeline.summary: Basil explains his devotion to Dorian and his refusal to exhibit the portrait; Lord Henry is determined to meet the sitter.
events: Lord Henry praises the portrait, but Basil refuses to exhibit it.
In the garden Basil describes meeting Dorian and the new artistic vision he inspires.
Basil says the portrait might expose his private idolatry.
Parker announces Dorian, and Basil asks Harry not to influence him.

knowledge.learns: Basil’s sitter is Dorian Gray, whose personality has transformed his art and whom he fears to expose in the portrait.
Harry knows Dorian’s name from Lady Agatha and is about to meet him.

timeline.title: Chapter 2
timeline.summary: Dorian meets Lord Henry, wishes the finished portrait could age in his place, and chooses Harry’s company.
events: Dorian persuades Basil to let Lord Henry remain during the sitting.
Harry speaks of temptation and youth, unsettling and fascinating Dorian.
Basil finishes the portrait; Dorian wishes it would age while he remained young.
Dorian stops Basil from slashing the canvas with a palette-knife.
Dorian goes to the theatre with Harry despite Basil’s plea to stay.

knowledge.learns: The portrait and Harry’s warning make him conscious of his beauty and its eventual loss.
Dorian is deeply disturbed by the portrait and resists its destruction.

timeline.title: Chapter 3
timeline.summary: Lord Henry learns Dorian’s family history and tightens his hold on him at Lady Agatha’s luncheon.
events: Lord Fermor tells Harry of Dorian’s beautiful mother and the suspected arranged killing of her husband.
Harry decides to dominate Dorian’s personality.
At Lady Agatha’s luncheon Harry entertains the guests with paradoxes while Dorian watches.
Dorian chooses to accompany Harry to the park instead of visiting Basil.

knowledge.learns: Dorian’s mother married a poor soldier who died in a duel under suspicious circumstances; she died within a year.
He decides he would rather follow Harry than keep his appointment with Basil.

timeline.title: Chapter 4
timeline.summary: Dorian tells Harry about discovering and loving Sibyl Vane; later he telegraphs news of their engagement.
events: Waiting for Harry, Dorian meets Lady Henry in the Mayfair library.
He describes finding Sibyl at a shabby theatre and being enchanted by her Shakespearean roles.
He plans to free her from her contract and present her in a West End theatre.
Harry and Dorian arrange to see her as Juliet with Basil.
That night Harry receives Dorian’s telegram announcing the engagement.

knowledge.learns: Dorian loves the actress Sibyl Vane and, by telegram that night, is engaged to her.
He recognizes Harry’s influence on his appetite for experience and expects to tell him everything.

timeline.title: Chapter 5
timeline.summary: Sibyl celebrates her love while James, leaving for Australia, fears for her and vows revenge on her unknown admirer.
events: Sibyl tells her mother of her happiness; Mrs. Vane worries about debts and considers the admirer’s wealth.
James asks his mother to protect Sibyl and takes his sister for a walk.
Dorian passes in a carriage, but another vehicle prevents James from seeing him.
James vows to kill Prince Charming if he wrongs Sibyl.
Mrs. Vane admits she was not married to their father; James repeats his threat and departs.

knowledge.learns: His mother was not married to his father, and Sibyl calls her unnamed admirer Prince Charming.
James threatens to find and kill Sibyl’s admirer if he wrongs her.

timeline.title: Chapter 6
timeline.summary: At dinner before the theatre, Dorian describes his engagement and defends love against Harry’s theories.
events: Harry tells Basil that Dorian is engaged to an actress.
Dorian arrives and recounts kissing Sibyl after her performance as Rosalind.
He says their engagement is secret and explains that she spoke of being unworthy to be his wife.
Basil and Harry dispute pleasure and morality with Dorian.
They leave for the theatre, Basil following alone and feeling his loss.

knowledge.learns: Dorian is secretly engaged to Sibyl and intends an irrevocable marriage.
Dorian and Sibyl became engaged without a formal proposal after exchanging a kiss.

timeline.title: Chapter 7
timeline.summary: Sibyl acts badly because real love has displaced the stage for her; Dorian rejects her and discovers a cruel change in the portrait.
events: Basil blesses the proposed marriage before Sibyl appears as Juliet.
Her performance fails, and Harry and Basil leave after the second act.
In the greenroom Sibyl says love has made theatrical passion unreal to her.
Dorian rejects her despite her pleas and wanders London until dawn.
At home he sees cruelty in the portrait’s mouth and resolves to make amends to Sibyl.

knowledge.learns: Sibyl believes love has destroyed her ability to act; he sees the portrait’s altered expression and suspects his wish has come true.
Dorian values her acting so highly that he says he no longer loves her.

timeline.title: Chapter 8
timeline.summary: Dorian confirms the portrait has changed, learns Sibyl is dead, and embraces the prospect of youth without visible shame.
events: Dorian uncovers the portrait and confirms the cruel expression remains.
He writes Sibyl a passionate letter asking forgiveness.
Lord Henry arrives and tells him she was found dead after swallowing a theatrical substance.
Harry frames her death as a beautiful tragedy and persuades Dorian towards detachment.
Dorian chooses to let the portrait bear his shame and goes to the opera.

knowledge.learns: Sibyl is dead; Harry believes she deliberately poisoned herself. Dorian confirms that the portrait has changed.
Dorian had not read his letter and did not know of Sibyl’s death; he does not learn the portrait’s secret.

timeline.title: Chapter 9
timeline.summary: Basil is shocked by Dorian’s response to Sibyl’s death and confesses his former artistic idolatry without seeing the portrait.
events: Basil visits to console Dorian and learns he went to the opera.
Dorian tells Basil he believes Sibyl killed herself and demands that he help him forget.
Basil tries to see the screened portrait and mentions his plan to exhibit it in Paris.
Dorian forbids him to look and demands his reason for originally concealing it.
Basil confesses his worship; Dorian keeps the portrait’s true change secret.

knowledge.learns: Dorian believes Sibyl’s death was suicide and refuses to let him see or exhibit the portrait.
Basil had feared the portrait revealed his intense devotion, not the supernatural change Dorian hides.

timeline.title: Chapter 10
timeline.summary: Dorian hides the portrait in his old schoolroom and becomes absorbed in a yellow book sent by Harry.
events: Dorian obtains the schoolroom key from Mrs. Leaf and covers the portrait with a purple-and-gold textile.
He sends Victor away and has Mr. Hubbard and an assistant carry the covered picture upstairs.
He locks the portrait in the dusty room of his childhood.
A newspaper reports the inquest’s verdict of death by misadventure.
Dorian reads Harry’s yellow book until he is late for their dinner.

knowledge.learns: The inquest has returned a verdict of death by misadventure; the yellow book fascinates him.

timeline.title: Chapter 11
timeline.summary: Over years Dorian cultivates sensation and luxury while the portrait ages and rumours of his conduct spread.
events: Dorian acquires nine differently bound copies of the yellow book.
He compares his unchanged face with the increasingly corrupt and aged portrait.
He pursues religion, perfumes, music, jewels, textiles and historical fantasies.
He visits disreputable places and fears discovery of the locked picture.
Scandals gather around him, though his beauty and wealth continue to protect him.

knowledge.learns: Across the years his own appearance remains youthful while the portrait shows both age and degradation.

timeline.title: Chapter 12
timeline.summary: On the eve of Dorian’s thirty-eighth birthday, Basil confronts him with damaging rumours and Dorian offers to show him his soul.
events: Basil stops Dorian in the fog before leaving for Paris.
In Dorian’s library Basil recounts rumours about ruined friends and women.
Dorian deflects blame and attacks society’s hypocrisy.
Basil says he would need to see Dorian’s soul to know the truth.
Dorian takes a lamp and invites Basil upstairs to see his secret.

knowledge.learns: Basil has heard detailed accusations about the harm associated with Dorian’s friendships.
Dorian refuses a plain denial and promises to show him a private record upstairs.

timeline.title: Chapter 13
timeline.summary: Dorian shows Basil the corrupted portrait, kills him, and begins to construct an alibi.
events: Dorian uncovers the portrait and Basil recognizes his signature and altered work.
Basil urges Dorian to pray and repent.
Dorian seizes a knife from the chest and repeatedly stabs Basil.
He hides Basil’s coat and bag, then leaves and rings his own bell to create an apparent return home.
He finds Alan Campbell’s address in the Blue Book.

knowledge.learns: His portrait has become a hideous image that Dorian claims is his soul.
Basil recognizes the picture and believes repentance might still be possible.

timeline.title: Chapter 14
timeline.summary: Dorian blackmails Alan Campbell into destroying Basil’s body and sees a bloodlike stain on the portrait’s hand.
events: Dorian sends for Alan and waits in mounting terror.
Alan refuses to help even after Dorian admits the death was murder.
Dorian writes a threat and shows him an already addressed letter; Alan yields.
Alan’s chemicals arrive, and Dorian sends the servant away.
Dorian covers the portrait after seeing red dew on its hand; Alan works upstairs and the body disappears.

knowledge.learns: Dorian has murdered a man upstairs and will send a damaging letter unless Alan destroys the body.
The portrait has developed a wet-looking red stain on one hand after the murder.

timeline.title: Chapter 15
timeline.summary: Dorian conceals his nerves at dinner, burns Basil’s belongings, and sets out seeking oblivion.
events: At Lady Narborough’s dinner Dorian struggles to eat while maintaining his polished manner.
Harry questions him about the previous night, and Dorian gives a confused account.
Dorian leaves early and burns Basil’s coat and bag in his library fire.
He examines a hidden box containing green paste, then puts it away.
In common dress and a muffler he hires a hansom towards the river.

knowledge.learns: Dorian is unusually nervous and gives an inconsistent account of his movements, though Harry does not know why.

timeline.title: Chapter 16
timeline.summary: At an opium den Dorian encounters Adrian Singleton; James Vane tracks him by his nickname but lets him go.
events: Dorian rides through rain and fog to a riverside den seeking forgetfulness.
He meets Adrian Singleton and decides to seek another den.
A woman calls Dorian Prince Charming as he leaves; a sailor follows.
James Vane threatens him with a revolver for Sibyl’s death.
Dorian points to his youthful face under a lamp, and James releases him.
The woman tells James Dorian has looked young for eighteen years; James pursues him too late.

knowledge.learns: The man called Prince Charming appears too young, but a woman swears he has remained youthful for eighteen years.
Sibyl’s brother James has sought him for years and intends to kill him.

timeline.title: Chapter 17
timeline.summary: At Selby Royal, society banter is broken when Dorian sees James Vane at the conservatory window.
events: Dorian takes tea with the Duchess of Monmouth and other house guests.
Harry and the duchess exchange rapid paradoxes about beauty, England and love.
Dorian goes to fetch orchids for the duchess.
He sees James’s face at the window and faints.
After recovering, he insists on coming down to dinner rather than being alone.

knowledge.learns: He sees James Vane watching him at Selby and believes his pursuer has found him.

timeline.title: Chapter 18
timeline.summary: Dorian fears pursuit, then discovers that the stranger accidentally shot during a hunt was James Vane.
events: Dorian remains indoors in terror, then persuades himself the face at the window was imaginary.
On the third day he joins the shooting-party and asks Geoffrey not to shoot a hare.
Geoffrey fires and fatally wounds a man hidden in the thicket.
Dorian calls the death a bad omen and plans to return to town.
The keeper says the dead stranger was a tattooed sailor carrying a revolver.
Dorian rides to the Home Farm and recognizes James’s body.

knowledge.learns: The man killed in the thicket was James Vane, so his immediate pursuer is dead.
A man has been accidentally shot during the hunt; Dorian is badly shaken.

timeline.title: Chapter 19
timeline.summary: Dorian tells Harry he has spared Hetty and intends to reform; Harry dismisses his hints about Basil’s murder.
events: Dorian tells Harry he left the village girl Hetty rather than take her away.
Harry questions the value and consequences of this renunciation.
Harry reports discussion of Basil’s disappearance, his own divorce and Alan Campbell’s suicide.
Dorian asks what Harry would think if he had murdered Basil; Harry refuses to believe him capable of it.
Dorian speaks of the soul and asks Harry never to lend the poisonous book again.

knowledge.learns: Dorian says he left Hetty and wants to change; Harry treats his suggestion that he killed Basil as a pose.
Alan Campbell has killed himself, and the police disagree about Basil’s journey to Paris.

timeline.title: Chapter 20
timeline.summary: Dorian seeks evidence of reform in the portrait, sees hypocrisy instead, and stabs the canvas; servants find him dead and aged.
events: Dorian returns home longing for the purity of his boyhood and smashes his mirror.
He considers confession but dwells chiefly on escaping his past.
He uncovers the portrait and finds a look of cunning and hypocrisy and more bloodlike staining.
Rejecting confession, he stabs the picture with the knife that killed Basil.
Servants enter by the balcony and find the restored portrait and an old, disfigured dead man identifiable by his rings.

knowledge.learns: The portrait shows no visible cleansing after his treatment of Hetty; he recognizes vanity, hypocrisy and curiosity in his supposed good deed.

divergencePoints.label: The Wish Unspoken
divergencePoints.moment: Confronted with his finished portrait and Harry’s warning about age, Dorian wishes that the picture could grow old in his place.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: He declares that he would give everything, even his soul, to remain young while the portrait ages.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Dorian held back his wish and told Basil instead how frightened he was of growing old?
divergencePoints.stakes: His bond with Basil and the fate of his beauty hang on the response.

divergencePoints.label: Basil’s Palette-Knife
divergencePoints.moment: Basil takes up a palette-knife, intending to destroy the portrait that has caused such distress.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Dorian tears the knife from Basil’s hand and saves the canvas.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Dorian reached Basil a moment too late to stop him cutting the portrait?
divergencePoints.stakes: The masterpiece and Dorian’s attachment to his painted image are at risk.

divergencePoints.label: After Juliet’s Failure
divergencePoints.moment: In the greenroom Sibyl explains that real love has made acting seem hollow and begs Dorian not to leave her.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Dorian tells her she has killed his love and leaves her sobbing on the floor.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Dorian stayed with Sibyl after her failed performance and listened to what love has changed for her?
divergencePoints.stakes: Their engagement and Sibyl’s life may turn on his response.

divergencePoints.label: Behind the Screen
divergencePoints.moment: Basil approaches the screened portrait and asks to see his work before exhibiting it.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Dorian threatens to end their friendship, and Basil agrees not to look.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Basil pulled the screen aside before Dorian could stop him?
divergencePoints.stakes: Dorian’s secret and Basil’s chance to intervene would be exposed years earlier.

divergencePoints.label: A Prayer Upstairs
divergencePoints.moment: Basil urges Dorian to kneel and pray after seeing the corrupted portrait; a knife lies on the painted chest.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Dorian’s hatred surges, and he seizes the knife and murders Basil.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Dorian knelt with Basil instead of reaching for the knife?
divergencePoints.stakes: Basil’s life and the possibility of Dorian’s repentance are at stake.

divergencePoints.label: Alan’s Refusal
divergencePoints.moment: Dorian threatens Alan with an already addressed letter unless he destroys the body upstairs.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Alan yields to the blackmail, obtains his chemicals and removes the body.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Alan refused even after reading Dorian’s threat and walked out of the house?
divergencePoints.stakes: Alan risks exposure while Dorian risks discovery of the murder.

divergencePoints.label: Under the Gas-Lamp
divergencePoints.moment: James holds Dorian at gunpoint, and Dorian asks him to judge his age by his face in the light.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: James thinks Dorian too young to be Sibyl’s lover and releases him.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if James refused to trust Dorian’s youthful face under the lamp?
divergencePoints.stakes: Dorian’s life and James’s long-sought revenge hang on a moment’s judgment.

divergencePoints.label: Let the Hare Live
divergencePoints.moment: Dorian asks Geoffrey not to shoot the hare running towards the alder thicket.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Geoffrey fires anyway and accidentally kills James Vane, who is hidden in the thicket.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Geoffrey listened to Dorian and lowered his gun before the hare reached the alders?
divergencePoints.stakes: James’s life and Dorian’s safety remain in direct conflict.

divergencePoints.label: The Last Confession
divergencePoints.moment: Dorian studies the portrait’s bloodstained hands and considers whether he must confess Basil’s murder.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: He rejects confession and stabs the picture, after which he is found dead and aged.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Dorian left the knife untouched and went downstairs to confess Basil’s murder?
divergencePoints.stakes: Public disgrace and punishment would replace the secrecy on which his life depends.

visual.era: Late Victorian London and country-house society: dark tailored suits, evening dress, gaslight, horse-drawn cabs, trains and richly furnished interiors.
visual.palette: Rose, lilac, gold and peacock blue in luxurious rooms; fog-grey, muddy ochre and gas-yellow by the river; cold winter greens at Selby.
motifs: The portrait behind purple and gold
visual.comicStyle: Use a late Victorian illustrated-book manner: precise ink contours and cross-hatching with restrained watercolour washes. Give rooms decorative borders and lingering panels of fabrics and flowers; tighten panels around faces, hands and objects as dread interrupts the polished surface.

glossary.note: The portrait’s sitter and its owner.
Dorian’s witty aristocratic friend.
The painter of Dorian’s portrait.
The young actress engaged to Dorian.
Sibyl’s sailor brother.
Sibyl’s name for Dorian, later heard by James.
The chemist blackmailed by Dorian.
Dorian’s Nottinghamshire country house.
The theatre where Sibyl acts.
A horse-drawn cab used for journeys in London.
An enclosed horse-drawn carriage.
The painted Italian chest in the old schoolroom.
The village girl Dorian says he spared.

strange-case-of-dr-jekyll-and-mr-hyde.title: The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
strange-case-of-dr-jekyll-and-mr-hyde.author: Robert Louis Stevenson
strange-case-of-dr-jekyll-and-mr-hyde.premise: A London lawyer grows alarmed by his old friend Dr. Jekyll's attachment to the repellent Edward Hyde, who has a key to the doctor's laboratory and stands to inherit his fortune. A brutal crime and Jekyll's increasing seclusion deepen a mystery guarded by friendship, professional honour and shame.
strange-case-of-dr-jekyll-and-mr-hyde.hook: A respectable doctor's back door opens onto a life his closest friends cannot imagine.
strange-case-of-dr-jekyll-and-mr-hyde.logline: As Hyde's violence threatens Dr. Jekyll's reputation and life, Utterson tries to protect his friend without knowing the secret that binds the two men.

world.setting: London, chiefly the respectable houses around Jekyll's square and Cavendish Square, a prosperous shopping by-street, Hyde's dismal Soho lodging, and the courts and rooms connecting them.
world.period: Victorian London, in an unspecified year of the 1800s
rules: Jekyll and Hyde are two bodily forms of one person, with memory in common; Jekyll is morally mixed, while he describes Hyde as wholly evil.
Jekyll's drug changes his body as well as his character. The same preparation restores him, but its action becomes uncertain and changes into Hyde begin without a dose.
The effective draught depends on an old salt supply; Jekyll believes an unknown impurity made it work, and fresh supplies fail to restore him.
Hyde is smaller and younger than Jekyll; clothes made for the doctor hang grotesquely loose on him. Witnesses sense deformity without identifying a specific malformation.
Respectable gentlemen guard reputations and confidences; a scandal or criminal association can ruin a name, while servants defer to their employers.
Letters travel by post or messenger; cabs and walking carry people through streets lit by gas lamps. Police investigate murder and circulate descriptions.

A will can transfer Jekyll's property on death or, under its unusual terms, prolonged disappearance; Utterson treats his clients' papers and a dead friend's sealed instructions as binding confidences.
world.tone: Sober, intimate and increasingly dreadful, with everyday comforts made uncanny by secrecy and sudden violence.
themes: The division and entanglement of good and evil
sensitivities: The narrative associates perceived ugliness, small stature and unspecified deformity with moral evil; those associations reflect its period rather than a reliable judgment of real bodies.
Hyde's violence against a child, a woman and Carew is described through intense horror; Carew's beating is especially graphic.
Class prejudice colours descriptions of Soho, its residents and servants, including references to women's nationalities.

voice.narration: A past-tense third-person narrator follows Utterson closely through the mystery, reporting his conjectures without granting him the hidden truth. The final two chapters change to Lanyon's and Jekyll's first-person written testimony, each with his own judgment and limits.
style: Long, balanced sentences accumulate clauses and qualifications, then yield to a short exclamation or sentence of dread.
Formal moral and legal diction mingles with vivid bodily sensations: cold blood, sickened flesh, trembling and a weight on the mind.
Fog, lamplight, doors and firelight make familiar London streets and rooms alternately welcoming and sinister.
The narrator describes outward gestures and rooms precisely, then moves into a character's doubts, often marking a supposition as such.
Colons, semicolons and dashes support elaborate turns of thought; pointed repetitions make fear and insistence audible.
British forms and period vocabulary include 'storey', 'neighbourhood', 'chemist', 'cab' and 'hansom'.
Jekyll's confession shifts between analytical argument, religious imagery and impassioned self-accusation, sometimes calling Hyde 'he'.
voice.dialogue: Double quotation marks frame spoken exchanges; quoted speech within a story uses single marks. Gentlemen address one another by surname and use courteous circumlocution, while fear breaks through in repetitions, abrupt questions and appeals to God. Servants say 'sir' but speak plainly and insistently when pressed.
samplePassages: Two doors from one corner, on the left hand going east the line was broken by the entry of a court; and just at that point a certain sinister block of building thrust forward its gable on the street. It was two storeys high; showed no window, nothing but a door on the lower storey and a blind forehead of discoloured wall on the upper; and bore in every feature, the marks of prolonged and sordid negligence. The door, which was equipped with neither bell nor knocker, was blistered and distained.

The besiegers, appalled by their own riot and the stillness that had succeeded, stood back a little and peered in. There lay the cabinet before their eyes in the quiet lamplight, a good fire glowing and chattering on the hearth, the kettle singing its thin strain, a drawer or two open, papers neatly set forth on the business table, and nearer the fire, the things laid out for tea; the quietest room, you would have said, and, but for the glazed presses full of chemicals, the most commonplace that night in London.

The most racking pangs succeeded: a grinding in the bones, deadly nausea, and a horror of the spirit that cannot be exceeded at the hour of birth or death. Then these agonies began swiftly to subside, and I came to myself as if out of a great sickness. There was something strange in my sensations, something indescribably new and, from its very novelty, incredibly sweet. I felt younger, lighter, happier in body; within I was conscious of a heady recklessness, a current of disordered sensual images running like a millrace in my fancy, a solution of the bonds of obligation, an unknown but not an innocent freedom of the soul.

cast.name: Mr. Utterson
cast.role: Lawyer, Jekyll's old friend and the chief investigator of the mystery.
cast.appearance: Lean and long, with a rugged, unsmiling face and sober, dusty appearance. He wears a dark Victorian suit, collar and tie, with a greatcoat and hat outdoors; his posture is reserved and upright. His hair is short and dark with some grey, his complexion pale and his eyes grey.
cast.personality: Austere, loyal and undemonstrative; his tolerance appears in practical help and in the discretion he grants troubled friends.
cast.motivation: He wants to protect Jekyll from disgrace and danger while honouring his duties as lawyer, trustee and friend.
cast.fears: He fears Hyde may ruin or murder Jekyll, and that a friend's hidden disgrace may come to light.
cast.speech: His speech is spare, courteous and probing, with 'Tut-tut' and carefully framed questions. With friends he can be dryly playful; under pressure he becomes firm and direct.
cast.arc: A reluctant investigator who prizes privacy, he moves from suspicion of blackmail to forcing the cabinet door, then reads the testimony that exposes the truth.

relationships.nature: Old friend and client whose safety and reputation he tries to protect.
Distrusted beneficiary of Jekyll's will whom he suspects of threatening the doctor.
Old school and college friend and fellow friend of Jekyll.
Distant kinsman and regular Sunday walking companion.
Jekyll's trusted servant, with whom he forces the cabinet.

cast.name: Mr. Enfield
cast.role: Man about town whose account of Hyde first alarms Utterson.
cast.appearance: A young, well-dressed Victorian gentleman of medium height and build, with a clean-shaven face, short brown hair, fair skin and brown eyes. He carries a cane and wears a dark coat, waistcoat, trousers and hat, standing erect on his walks.
cast.personality: Sociable, observant and decisive in an emergency, but ordinarily reluctant to ask questions that may expose a scandal.
cast.motivation: He wants the trampled child's family compensated and values discretion and his regular walks with Utterson.
cast.fears: He recoils from Hyde and dislikes the unpredictable harm caused by prying into private affairs.
cast.speech: He tells a fluent, colloquial story full of vivid comparisons and asides: 'Well, sir' and 'my gentleman'. He becomes terse and solemn when truly shocked.
cast.arc: His story sets the investigation in motion; later he discovers the door leads to Jekyll's and witnesses the doctor's terrifying change of expression.

relationships.nature: Distant cousin and devoted companion on Sunday walks.
Caught him after he trampled a child and extracted compensation.
Meets him at the cabinet window through Utterson.

cast.name: Mr. Hyde
cast.role: Jekyll's younger, violent second form and Carew's murderer.
cast.appearance: Small, dwarfish and pale, with a disturbing face, displeasing smile and an impression of deformity that observers cannot locate. His hand is lean, corded, knuckly and darkly hairy. He moves lightly and swiftly; he usually dresses plainly, though Jekyll's rich sober clothes hang vastly too large on him. His dark hair is short and his eyes dark.
cast.personality: Self-centred, cruel and quick to rage, yet capable of cool calculation, fear and desperate self-preservation.
cast.motivation: He pursues unrestrained pleasure and power, then struggles to escape capture and keep himself alive.
cast.fears: He fears the gallows, death and Jekyll's power to end their shared life by suicide.
cast.speech: His voice is husky, whispering and somewhat broken. He can be sneeringly polite, but snaps, snarls and repeats urgent questions; before Lanyon he turns taunting and grandly theatrical.
cast.arc: A secret means of indulgence, he grows more powerful and violent, becomes a hunted murderer and finally kills himself when the cabinet is forced.

relationships.nature: His other form; they share memories and a life but come to hate each other.
Jekyll's lawyer, whom he meets at the laboratory door.
The passer-by who catches him after he tramples a child.
Jekyll's old colleague, before whom he changes back into Jekyll.
Jekyll's butler, who knows his appearance and suspects him of murder.

cast.name: Dr. Lanyon
cast.role: Established physician and Jekyll's estranged scientific colleague.
cast.age: An ageing physician, an old schoolmate of Jekyll and Utterson
cast.appearance: A hearty, healthy-looking, dapper gentleman with a red face and a shock of prematurely white hair. He is of medium height and solid build, with fair skin and blue-grey eyes, wearing a dark physician's coat, waistcoat and formal collar; he carries himself briskly.
cast.personality: Genial, decided and proud of his scientific standards, with genuine affection beneath a somewhat theatrical manner.
cast.motivation: He wants to uphold sound medicine and answer an old friend's desperate appeal, despite suspecting Jekyll is insane.
cast.fears: The transformation and Jekyll's revelations leave him terrified, sleepless and unable to bear further mention of him.
cast.speech: He speaks heartily and decisively, chuckles with friends and calls Jekyll's theories 'unscientific balderdash'. His written account is precise and professional until horror breaks through.
cast.arc: He helps retrieve Jekyll's chemicals, chooses to witness Hyde's transformation and dies after the shock, leaving a sealed narrative.

relationships.nature: Old school and college friend entrusted with his sealed account.
Former close friend whose scientific views estranged him.
The repellent visitor he sees transform into Jekyll.
Jekyll's butler assists him in opening the cabinet.

cast.name: Poole
cast.role: Jekyll's long-serving butler who summons Utterson when the cabinet becomes terrifying.
cast.appearance: An elderly, well-dressed butler of medium height and spare build, with a lined, clean-shaven face, short grey hair, fair skin and grey eyes. He wears a dark formal servant's coat and waistcoat with a white collar; he stands deferentially upright and carries a red pocket-handkerchief.
cast.personality: Respectful and loyal, but observant, resolute and capable of blunt insistence when he believes his master is in danger.
cast.motivation: He wants to find and protect the master he has served for twenty years and to end the fearful uncertainty in the house.
cast.fears: He believes Jekyll has been murdered and dreads the unknown figure shut in the cabinet.
cast.speech: He repeatedly addresses Utterson as 'sir', gives concrete evidence and uses homely emphases such as 'main angry' and 'my bible-word'. Terror makes him whisper or speak harshly.
cast.arc: Initially reassuring Utterson that Hyde has his master's authority, he comes to suspect foul play and helps break into the cabinet.

relationships.nature: His master of twenty years, whom he knows by voice, height and tread.
The trusted lawyer he calls for help and follows into the cabinet.
A man his master ordered the household to obey, later suspected of murder.
He receives the physician under Jekyll's written instructions.

cast.name: Dr. Jekyll
cast.role: Respected physician and experimenter whose divided life produces Hyde.
cast.age: Fifty when Utterson discusses the will with him
cast.appearance: A large, tall, well-made man with a smooth, handsome face, a slightly sly cast and large, firm, white hands. He wears a sober Victorian gentleman's suit and waistcoat. His hair is short and greying, his skin fair and his eyes grey; in his final illness he becomes visibly wasted and weak.
cast.personality: Affectionate and generous, but proud, secretive and susceptible to pleasure; his remorse coexists with a habit of excusing himself.
cast.motivation: He wants both public respect and freedom for concealed pleasures, then seeks to control Hyde and make amends for his harm.
cast.fears: He fears disgrace, permanent loss of his own identity and Hyde's violence; later he dreads sleep and the failure of his drug.
cast.speech: With friends he is warm and expansive, using repeated assurances and appeals to trust. Pressed about Hyde, he becomes pale, evasive and emphatic; his confession argues, qualifies and condemns itself.
cast.arc: He creates Hyde to separate his impulses, renounces him after murder, and struggles against involuntary change until the effective salt runs out.

relationships.nature: His own other form, first an instrument of freedom and finally a hated rival.
Beloved friend and lawyer whom he trusts but refuses to enlighten until his final papers.
Old friend estranged by scientific differences; his witness to the transformation.
His loyal butler, whom he sends in search of the old salt.
Utterson's cousin, briefly introduced at the cabinet window.

places.name: The by-street and laboratory door
places.description: A prosperous shopping street conceals the neglected back entrance to Jekyll's laboratory; Hyde uses its key.
places.visual: Freshly painted shop shutters and polished brass flank a court and a two-storey, windowless gable. Its blistered, stained door has neither bell nor knocker; children play on the steps and tramps strike matches on its panels.

places.name: Dr. Jekyll's house
places.description: Jekyll's comfortable front house stands in an old square, connected across a former garden to the laboratory.
places.visual: A wealthy front door with a fanlight opens onto a large, low hall paved with flags, warmed by an open fire and furnished with costly oak cabinets. A yard separates the house from the laboratory.

places.name: The laboratory and cabinet
places.description: A former surgeon's dissecting theatre, converted to chemical work, leads upstairs to Jekyll's private cabinet.
places.visual: A gaunt, windowless theatre holds chemical apparatus, crates and packing straw beneath a foggy cupola. Stairs rise to a red-baize door; beyond are glazed presses, a cheval-glass, a business table, a hearth and three dusty, iron-barred windows.

places.name: Hyde's house in Soho
places.description: Hyde's separate lodging lets him pursue his secret life away from Jekyll's respectable square.
places.visual: A dingy, muddy street has a gin palace, a low French eating house, ragged children and cheap shops. Inside, two rooms contain deep carpets, silver, elegant linen, wine and a good picture.

places.name: Dr. Lanyon's house
places.description: The physician's house in Cavendish Square is where Hyde brings Jekyll's desperate errand to its conclusion.
places.visual: A respectable London house with a pillared portico, dining-room and brightly lit consulting room. A drawer of powders, a phial and a notebook lies behind a consulting-room table.

places.name: Utterson's house and office
places.description: The lawyer's bachelor home shelters his fireside consultations and the safe containing confidential papers.
places.visual: A firelit room with a reading desk and old wine gives way to a private business room with a safe and candle; a great dark bed stands behind curtains.

timeline.title: Chapter 1: Story of the Door
timeline.summary: On a Sunday walk, Enfield tells Utterson how Hyde trampled a child and paid compensation with a respectable man's cheque. Utterson recognizes the unnamed connection, and the cousins agree not to discuss it again.
events: Utterson and Enfield pass a neglected door in a prosperous London by-street.
Enfield recounts catching a small man who calmly trampled a girl and bringing him back to her family.
Threatened with scandal, the man pays £10 in gold and a cheque for the balance of £100; the cheque proves genuine.
Enfield calls the place Black Mail House and explains his rule against asking intrusive questions.
Utterson asks the man's name and learns it is Hyde; Enfield confirms Hyde still has the door key.
Utterson admits he knows the cheque's drawer, and the cousins agree to let the matter rest.

knowledge.learns: Enfield's child-trampler is Hyde, who used and still possesses a key to the neglected door.
Utterson already knows the identity of the respectable man who signed the cheque.

timeline.title: Chapter 2: Search for Mr. Hyde
timeline.summary: Utterson studies Jekyll's will, consults Lanyon and seeks out Hyde. After meeting the repellent beneficiary, he learns that Jekyll's servants are ordered to obey him and fears for his friend.
events: Utterson rereads Jekyll's will, which leaves Hyde everything on death or an unexplained absence exceeding three months.
Lanyon says scientific differences have estranged him from Jekyll and that he has never heard of Hyde.
Haunted by imagined scenes of Hyde's cruelty, Utterson watches the laboratory door until Hyde appears.
Hyde shows his face, gives Utterson a Soho address and angrily denies that Jekyll described him.
At Jekyll's front house, Poole says the doctor is out and the household has orders to obey Hyde.
Utterson imagines an old disgrace binding Jekyll to Hyde and fears Hyde may want to hasten his inheritance.

knowledge.learns: Lanyon has never heard of Hyde and regards Jekyll's scientific ideas as unscientific.
Hyde has a Soho address, a key to the laboratory and authority over Jekyll's servants.
Utterson knows him by sight and is Jekyll's lawyer and old friend.

timeline.title: Chapter 3: Dr. Jekyll Was Quite at Ease
timeline.summary: After a dinner, Utterson urges Jekyll to confide in him about Hyde. Jekyll refuses, claims he can be rid of Hyde whenever he chooses and secures a promise that Utterson will protect Hyde's rights.
events: A fortnight later Utterson stays behind after one of Jekyll's dinners.
Jekyll dismisses Lanyon as a pedant and turns pale when Utterson mentions Hyde.
Utterson offers confidential help, but Jekyll calls the affair private and says he can be rid of Hyde at will.
Jekyll asks Utterson to bear with Hyde and secure his rights if Jekyll is taken away.
Despite admitting he cannot like Hyde, Utterson promises.

knowledge.learns: Utterson has heard something abominable about Hyde and remains willing to help Jekyll in confidence.
Jekyll claims he can end his connection with Hyde at will and asks that Hyde's rights be protected.

timeline.title: Chapter 4: The Carew Murder Case
timeline.summary: A maid witnesses Hyde beat Sir Danvers Carew to death. Utterson identifies the victim and the broken weapon, then leads Inspector Newcomen to Hyde's ransacked Soho rooms.
events: Nearly a year later, a maid sees Hyde attack an elderly gentleman with a cane in a moonlit lane.
The maid faints; on waking at two she summons police, who find a letter addressed to Utterson on the victim.
Utterson identifies the body as Sir Danvers Carew and recognizes the broken cane as one he gave Jekyll.
Utterson takes Inspector Newcomen by cab through fog to Hyde's Soho address.
Hyde's housekeeper admits the visitors; they find ransacked rooms, a burned cheque book and the other half of the cane.
The inspector finds money in Hyde's bank account and plans to watch for him, though witnesses cannot give a consistent description.

knowledge.learns: Hyde has been identified as Carew's killer, and the murder weapon was a cane Utterson gave Jekyll.
Hyde returned briefly to his Soho rooms after a long absence and left evidence there.

timeline.title: Chapter 5: Incident of the Letter
timeline.summary: Jekyll gives Utterson a letter supposedly from Hyde and swears he is finished with him. Poole's account and Guest's handwriting comparison leave the lawyer suspecting Jekyll forged it.
events: Poole leads Utterson through the former dissecting theatre to Jekyll's cabinet.
Jekyll swears he will never see Hyde again and gives Utterson a letter in which Hyde claims a safe means of escape.
Jekyll says the letter was handed in and admits Hyde dictated the will's disappearance clause.
Poole tells Utterson no letter was delivered that day except posted circulars.
Over wine, Utterson shows the letter to his clerk Guest, who compares it with a new note from Jekyll.
Guest finds the hands nearly identical but differently sloped; Utterson locks up the note and suspects forgery.

knowledge.learns: Jekyll claims to have broken with Hyde and says Hyde proposed the will's disappearance clause.
Poole received no hand-delivered letter, and Guest finds a close resemblance between Hyde's and Jekyll's writing.
He comes to suspect that Jekyll forged a letter for the murderer.

timeline.title: Chapter 6: Incident of Dr. Lanyon
timeline.summary: Hyde remains missing while Jekyll enjoys a period of renewed friendship and good works. Abruptly Jekyll shuts himself away, Lanyon sickens and dies, and Utterson honours the seal on Lanyon's account.
events: Police uncover Hyde's disreputable past but cannot find him; Jekyll returns to society, charity and religion.
After dining with Jekyll and Lanyon on 8 January, Utterson is refused admission to Jekyll's house on subsequent visits.
Utterson finds Lanyon gravely changed; Lanyon says he has suffered a fatal shock and refuses to discuss Jekyll.
In a letter, Jekyll confirms an incurable breach with Lanyon and asks Utterson to respect his seclusion.
Lanyon dies, and Utterson opens an outer envelope addressed to him but leaves the inner narrative sealed as instructed.
Poole reports Jekyll's continued confinement to the cabinet, and Utterson gradually visits less often.

knowledge.learns: Lanyon regards Jekyll as dead to him and attributes his own decline to an unnamed shock.
Jekyll believes his estrangement from Lanyon is incurable and says he has brought an unnamed punishment and danger on himself.
Lanyon's inner account must remain sealed until Jekyll's death or disappearance.

timeline.mood: Brief renewal, then dread and bereavement

timeline.title: Chapter 7: Incident at the Window
timeline.summary: On their Sunday walk, Utterson and Enfield see Jekyll at his cabinet window. He refuses a walk, then abruptly shuts the window with a look of terror that leaves both men shaken.
events: Enfield tells Utterson he has discovered that the neglected door is a back entrance to Jekyll's house.
The cousins enter the court and find Jekyll sitting at the half-open middle window.
Jekyll says he is very low and refuses Utterson's invitation to walk, though he welcomes their company from below.
His smile abruptly gives way to terror and despair, and he thrusts down the window.
The two men leave in silence; Utterson says, 'God forgive us.'

knowledge.learns: Enfield has discovered the connection between the by-street door and Jekyll's house.
Utterson has met Hyde and shares his repulsion.
Jekyll says he cannot venture out and witnesses a sudden, terrifying change in his expression.
He witnesses Jekyll's sudden expression of terror and the abrupt closing of the window.

timeline.title: Chapter 8: The Last Night
timeline.summary: Poole brings Utterson to Jekyll's frightened household. They force the cabinet and find Hyde dead, Jekyll missing and papers directing Utterson to read Lanyon's narrative and Jekyll's confession.
events: On a wild March evening, Poole tells Utterson he fears foul play and takes him to the house.
Poole makes Utterson hear the changed voice behind the cabinet door and describes urgent, unsuccessful searches for a chemical.
Poole says he saw a masked, dwarf-sized figure; he and Utterson come to believe Hyde has murdered Jekyll.
They station Bradshaw and the boy at the back door, then force the cabinet after the voice begs for mercy.
