An eclipse darkens the shore; he sees a black, tentacled creature moving on a sandbank.
Sick and afraid of fainting, he climbs back onto the machine.

knowledge.learns: He has travelled forward rather than home and observes life persisting on the shore more than thirty million years hence.

timeline.title: Chapter 15: The Time Traveller’s Return
timeline.summary: The Traveller journeys backward to his own laboratory and joins the guests at dinner.
events: The dials run backward as the sun, landscape and familiar buildings return.
He sees Mrs. Watchett cross the laboratory in reverse.
He stops and notices that the machine has shifted across the laboratory.
He checks the newspaper date and clock, smells meat and enters the dining-room.

knowledge.learns: The machine’s displacement corresponds to its movement from the future lawn to the Sphinx pedestal; the date is still his departure day.

timeline.title: Chapter 16: After the Story
timeline.summary: The guests question the story; the next day the Traveller departs again, leaving the narrator waiting for a return that has not come.
events: The Traveller offers his account as truth, fiction or prophecy; the guests react sceptically.
He refuses to give away Weena’s flowers and checks the damaged machine when his own memory falters.
The narrator returns the next day and finds the Traveller preparing a camera and knapsack.
The Traveller promises proof at lunch and enters the laboratory.
The narrator hears a thud and finds the machine gone; three years later the Traveller has not returned.

knowledge.learns: He sees the damaged machine and witnesses signs of its second departure; the Traveller remains missing three years later.
Seeing the damaged machine reassures him that his account was true.
He cannot identify the flowers’ natural order.

timeline.title: Epilogue
timeline.summary: The narrator imagines possible destinations for the vanished Traveller and finds comfort in Weena’s preserved flowers.
events: The narrator wonders whether the Traveller went into prehistoric time or a nearer future.
He recalls the Traveller’s pessimism about civilisation and contrasts it with his own hope.
He regards the two shrivelled flowers as evidence that gratitude and tenderness survived.

divergencePoints.label: The Model Stays
divergencePoints.moment: The Psychologist presses the model’s lever while the guests watch the brightly lit table.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: The model becomes indistinct and vanishes, leaving the guests debating where it went.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if the model stayed visible after the Psychologist pressed the lever?
divergencePoints.stakes: The demonstration and the guests’ confidence in the invention would change.

divergencePoints.label: Guard the Machine
divergencePoints.moment: The flower-garlanded Traveller follows the Eloi toward their hall, leaving the machine on the lawn.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: He leaves it unattended after removing its levers.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if the Traveller refused to leave the machine alone and stayed beside it?
divergencePoints.stakes: His access to home and his first relations with the Eloi are at stake.

divergencePoints.label: The Empty Lawn
divergencePoints.moment: The Traveller sees the lawn by moonlight and realises that his machine is gone.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: He rushes down in panic, searches and later infers that it is inside the pedestal.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if he noticed whoever had taken the machine before they could hide it?
divergencePoints.stakes: A chance to recover the machine would expose him to its unknown takers.

divergencePoints.label: The River Rescue
divergencePoints.moment: Weena drifts downstream while the other Eloi make no attempt to save her.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: The Traveller wades in below her, brings her ashore and later receives her grateful friendship.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if another Eloi plunged in to save Weena before the Traveller reached her?
divergencePoints.stakes: Weena’s survival and the bond that sustains the Traveller could take a different course.

divergencePoints.label: Weena at the Well
divergencePoints.moment: Weena cries out and pulls at the Traveller as he starts down the shaft.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: He shakes her off and descends into the Morlocks’ underground world.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Weena persuaded him to leave the well unexplored that morning?
divergencePoints.stakes: He would avoid the immediate danger but lose his best clue to the Morlocks.

divergencePoints.label: Fire at the Forest Edge
divergencePoints.moment: The Traveller sets down his collected fuel at the dark wood and decides to light it.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: The fire spreads behind him and eventually sweeps through the forest.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if he carried the firewood onward without lighting the pile at the forest edge?
divergencePoints.stakes: Weena, the pursuing Morlocks and the forest would face a different danger in the dark.

divergencePoints.label: The Open Bronze Doors
divergencePoints.moment: The Traveller sees his machine inside the open pedestal and recognises the possibility of a trap.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: He enters, throws away his bar and is shut in with the Morlocks, but escapes on the machine.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if he kept his iron bar and refused to enter the open pedestal?
divergencePoints.stakes: His only known way home lies inside a chamber controlled by his enemies.

divergencePoints.label: A Witness for the Journey
divergencePoints.moment: The Traveller asks the narrator to wait for lunch while he takes his camera and knapsack to the laboratory.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: The narrator waits outside; the Traveller departs and has not returned three years later.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if the narrator followed him into the laboratory before he started the machine?
divergencePoints.stakes: The Traveller’s second departure and the promised evidence would have an immediate witness.

visual.era: Late Victorian evening dress, gaslit and electrically lit interiors, brass instruments and a workshop; the future retains monumental ruins and simple draped garments.
visual.palette: Warm amber firelight and polished brass give way to lush greens, white stone and purple flowers, then black shafts, red forest fire and a dying scarlet sun.
motifs: Flowers tucked into a coat pocket
The red sun above a silent sea
visual.comicStyle: Use ink and watercolour in a late Victorian illustrated scientific romance: precise architectural and mechanical linework, fine cross-hatching in the underground scenes, and broad luminous washes for the future landscape. Alternate crowded conversational panels with wide, silent views of ruins and sky.

glossary.note: The Traveller’s vehicle for movement through time.
The inventor and principal storyteller.
The Eloi rescued by the Traveller.
The small, graceful people of the upper world.
The pale subterranean descendants of humanity.
The statue whose bronze pedestal hides the machine.
The ruined museum on the high ground.
The moonless nights that Weena fears.
The professional title used for the sceptical guest.
The guest who presses the model’s lever.

the-hound-of-the-baskervilles.title: The Hound of the Baskervilles
the-hound-of-the-baskervilles.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
the-hound-of-the-baskervilles.premise: After Sir Charles Baskerville is found dead near his moorland home, a doctor brings Sherlock Holmes a family legend and evidence of a gigantic hound. Sir Charles's Canadian heir arrives to claim the estate, carrying a fortune and a warning to keep away from the moor.
the-hound-of-the-baskervilles.hook: A stolen boot, a family curse, and a hound whose jaws appear to burn.
the-hound-of-the-baskervilles.logline: As Sir Henry Baskerville takes possession of his ancestral home, Holmes and Watson must discover who is stalking him and how a legendary hound can kill.

world.setting: Baker Street and hotel-lined London give way to Baskerville Hall and scattered settlements on Dartmoor, Devon: granite tors, prehistoric stone huts, lonely roads, and the treacherous Grimpen Mire.
world.period: Late Victorian England, with the main Dartmoor investigation in October
rules: The apparent hell-hound is a living, savage animal made luminous with a phosphorus preparation; it can be wounded and killed.
The hound follows scent, including that retained on a worn boot or clothing; its phosphorescent coating does not prevent it from scenting.
The Grimpen Mire swallows animals and people; a few concealed routes cross it, marked in places by planted wands, and fog can make them impossible to follow.
Trains, horse-drawn cabs and traps, telegrams, letters, and hired messengers connect London with Devon; travel and messages take time.
A baronet owns an entailed estate, commands servants, and is expected to support the neighbourhood; a fortune may be disposed of separately by will.
A married woman's movements and prospects are constrained by law and reputation; a private night visit to a bachelor's house risks scandal.
An arrest and conviction require evidence that can persuade a jury, not merely a detective's conviction about a suspect's guilt.
The family legend and sightings create real fear, but no supernatural agency is established as the cause of the modern crimes.
world.tone: A rational investigation moves through dread, loneliness, and sudden violence, relieved by affectionate banter and flashes of comedy.
themes: The moral cost of solving a crime
sensitivities: The text uses racialized language and discredited theories connecting skull shape, ancestry, character, and criminality.
Watson describes Selden in dehumanizing, animalistic terms and associates his appearance with moral depravity.
Beryl suffers coercive control, confinement, and physical abuse; Laura's vulnerability is shaped by marriage law and the threat of scandal.

voice.narration: Dr. Watson narrates in the first person, mostly in retrospect and the past tense, admiring Holmes while recording his own mistakes, loyalties, and fear. Letters and dated diary entries give the moorland inquiry the immediacy of his incomplete knowledge.
style: Combine lucid accounts of physical clues with long, rhythmically balanced sentences that build atmosphere and suspense.
Render the moor as a vast living presence through colour, weather, sound, and comparisons to seas, monsters, and grasping hands.
Let Watson state a hypothesis, test it against particulars, and admit when a later discovery overturns it.
Use emphatic dashes, exclamations, and short questions at moments of surprise; end scenes on a decisive revelation or sound.
Contrast Holmes's precise professional reasoning with Watson's emotional, sometimes Gothic impressions.
Use British period spelling and terms such as moor, trap, wicket-gate, and baronet.
voice.dialogue: Dialogue uses quotation marks and frequent brief exchanges, interrupted by gestures and observations. Holmes moves from courteous questions to rapid deductions and dry jokes; Watson asks for explanations; Sir Henry speaks directly with Western and American turns of phrase. Speakers address one another by title or surname until familiarity warrants more.
samplePassages: He had never said as much before, and I must admit that his words gave me keen pleasure, for I had often been piqued by his indifference to my admiration and to the attempts which I had made to give publicity to his methods. I was proud, too, to think that I had so far mastered his system as to apply it in a way which earned his approval. He now took the stick from my hands and examined it for a few minutes with his naked eyes. Then with an expression of interest he laid down his cigarette, and carrying the cane to the window, he looked over it again with a convex lens.

A long, low moan, indescribably sad, swept over the moor. It filled the whole air, and yet it was impossible to say whence it came. From a dull murmur it swelled into a deep roar, and then sank back into a melancholy, throbbing murmur once again. Stapleton looked at me with a curious expression in his face.

“Queer place, the moor!” said he.

“But what is it?”

“The peasants say it is the Hound of the Baskervilles calling for its prey. I’ve heard it once or twice before, but never quite so loud.”

cast.name: Dr. Watson
cast.role: Narrator, physician, Holmes's companion and Sir Henry's appointed protector.
cast.appearance: A solidly built, medium-height English gentleman with a moustache, short brown hair, and a weathered face. He wears a dark Victorian suit and hat in town, and a practical coat and boots on the moor; a revolver may be in his pocket.
cast.personality: Loyal, observant, courageous, and susceptible to the moor's terrors; sensitive to Holmes's praise and to the duties of friendship.
cast.motivation: He wants to protect Sir Henry, supply Holmes with useful facts, and prove worthy of his friend's confidence.
cast.fears: He dreads harm to Sir Henry through his own negligence and fears the unknown watcher on the moor.
cast.speech: Courteous and earnest, he asks direct questions, ventures theories, and readily admits bewilderment. With Holmes he is affectionate, sometimes piqued, and frank about his own feelings.
cast.arc: Sent as Holmes's eyes and ears, he follows several misleading clues, finds Holmes's hiding place, and helps save Sir Henry from the hound.

relationships.nature: Friend, chronicler, and trusted investigative assistant.
Companion and protector who grows sincerely attached to him.
Initially studies the helpful naturalist before recognizing him as the enemy.

cast.name: Sherlock Holmes
cast.role: Consulting detective who investigates the threat to the Baskervilles.
cast.appearance: A tall, thin, athletic man with a keen, clean-shaven face and grey eyes. His posture can be austere or stooping with his head thrust forward; on the moor he wears a tweed suit and cloth cap, with immaculate linen.
cast.personality: Analytical, secretive, resourceful, and capable of warmth, vanity, irony, and intense excitement in a difficult case.
cast.motivation: He wants to protect Sir Henry and obtain evidence that will expose and convict the murderer.
cast.fears: He fears losing a client through his own miscalculation and letting a formidable criminal escape justice.
cast.speech: Incisive and controlled, he asks sequences of exact questions, distinguishes observation from inference, and calls Watson 'my dear fellow.' He teases friends and can be sharply impatient.
cast.arc: He moves from physical clues and guarded hypotheses to a secret vigil, then uses Sir Henry as bait and acknowledges the danger his plan caused.

relationships.nature: Close friend whose reports and courage he values, though he conceals his presence from him.
Client whom he protects and ultimately exposes to danger as bait.
A cunning opponent whom he seeks to catch with evidence.
Client whose observations first bring him the case.

cast.name: Dr. Mortimer
cast.role: Country medical practitioner, Sir Charles's friend and executor, who brings Holmes the problem.
cast.age: A young man, under thirty by Holmes's estimate
cast.appearance: Very tall and thin, with a bowed back, a long beak-like nose, and close-set keen grey eyes behind gold-rimmed glasses. His dingy frock-coat and frayed trousers are professionally cut but slovenly; his long fingers quiver and his head thrusts forward.
cast.personality: Benevolent, absent-minded, scientifically enthusiastic, and uncertain when evidence seems to support superstition.
cast.motivation: He wants sound advice about Sir Henry's safety while preserving the prosperity that an occupied Hall brings to the district.
cast.fears: He fears that the Baskerville curse may be real and that Sir Henry may meet his uncle's fate.
cast.speech: Polite and precise about his modest medical title, he digresses eagerly into skulls and comparative anatomy. His account of the hound becomes hushed and emotional.
cast.arc: He discloses the private evidence withheld at the inquest, assists the heir, and later accompanies the recovering Sir Henry on a long voyage.

relationships.nature: Consults him about the heir and the mysterious death.
Executor, adviser, physician, and travelling companion.
Neighbour and apparent scientific friend who learned from him of Sir Charles's weak heart.

cast.name: Sir Henry Baskerville
cast.role: Sir Charles's heir, newly returned from North America to take possession of Baskerville Hall.
cast.appearance: Small, sturdy, and alert, with weather-beaten skin, thick black eyebrows, a strong pugnacious face, and large hazel eyes. He wears a ruddy tweed suit and carries himself with quiet assurance.
cast.personality: Generous, courageous, impulsive, proud of his family, and quick-tempered when he thinks himself wronged.
cast.motivation: He wants to restore his family's house and estate, face the danger surrounding them, and marry the woman he knows as Miss Stapleton.
cast.fears: The hound's cry shakes his courage, and he fears being left alone amid the Hall's unexplained dangers.
cast.speech: Direct and warm, with Western and American expressions such as 'by thunder' and 'right away.' Anger broadens his dialect; with friends he speaks openly and gratefully.
cast.arc: He insists on claiming the Hall, falls in love with Beryl, becomes Holmes's unwitting bait, and survives the hound but needs a long recovery.

relationships.nature: Welcomes him as companion and protector and trusts his frankness.
Loves and proposes to her, believing her unmarried.
Trusts the detective and agrees to follow his directions blindly.
Employer who first suspects him and then shows him mercy.

cast.name: Stapleton
cast.role: Naturalist of Merripit House and concealed Baskerville heir who engineers the attacks.
cast.appearance: Small, slim, and lean-jawed, with a clean-shaven prim face, flaxen hair, and light grey eyes. He wears a grey suit and straw hat, often carrying a green butterfly-net and a tin specimen box; he moves with nimble, jerky speed.
cast.personality: Patient, calculating, outwardly courteous, and capable of sudden jealous fury and calculated cruelty.
cast.motivation: He wants the Baskerville estate and fortune and uses the family legend to remove the lives between him and the inheritance.
cast.fears: He fears exposure and losing control of the women whose knowledge could implicate him.
cast.speech: Smooth and educated, he offers help and speaks enthusiastically of natural history. He probes for information under polite conversation, retreats when challenged, and can turn peremptory or violent.
cast.arc: Having killed Sir Charles through the hound, he pursues Henry under a false identity; his plan fails and he is presumed swallowed by the mire.

relationships.nature: His wife, whom he passes off as his sister, controls, and abuses.
Promises marriage and manipulates her into arranging Sir Charles's fatal appointment.
Secretly plans to kill his cousin and take the succession.
Recognizes him as a dangerous opponent and tries to mislead him.

cast.name: Mrs. Stapleton
cast.role: Stapleton's wife, presented as his sister, who tries to warn Sir Henry.
cast.appearance: Tall, slim, and elegantly dressed, with a perfect figure, a dark complexion, a proud finely cut face, a sensitive mouth, and beautiful dark, eager eyes. Her dark hair is arranged in a period style.
cast.personality: Proud, passionate, and compassionate, but cautious under her husband's surveillance.
cast.motivation: She wants to keep Sir Henry safe while, for much of the story, avoiding betrayal of the husband whose love she hopes to retain.
cast.fears: She fears her husband's violence and the discovery of her warnings.
cast.speech: Her English has a curious lisp. In private she speaks urgently and emotionally; before Stapleton she changes the subject, gives evasive explanations, and checks herself.
cast.arc: She refuses to lure Sir Charles, repeatedly warns Henry, and turns decisively against Stapleton after learning of his betrayal and suffering confinement.

relationships.nature: Abused wife compelled to pose as his sister and assist his deception.
Warns the man who loves her while concealing her marriage.
Mistakes him for Henry and urgently warns him away from the moor.

cast.name: Barrymore
cast.role: Baskerville Hall's butler, whose secret signals conceal help for his wife's brother.
cast.appearance: Tall and handsome, with pale distinguished features, dark eyes, and a square full black beard. He wears the dark, formal clothes of a Victorian butler and holds himself with a subdued, trained manner.
cast.personality: Reserved and dutiful, protective of his wife, and capable of firm defiance when her secret is threatened.
cast.motivation: He wants to help his wife keep her brother alive and honour the kindness shown by the Baskervilles.
cast.fears: He fears Selden's capture, trouble for his wife, and the danger gathering around Sir Henry.
cast.speech: Respectful and formal with his employer, using 'sir'; under pressure he pleads, then speaks bluntly about foul play and black villainy.
cast.arc: His furtive conduct makes him a suspect; after his secret is exposed, he gains Henry's mercy and shares the clue of the burned letter.

relationships.nature: Husband who helps her feed and shelter her fugitive brother.
Butler whose trust he risks but whose kindness he repays with information.
Initially the object of his suspicions; later tells him about another man on the moor.

cast.name: Mrs. Barrymore
cast.role: Baskerville Hall's housekeeper and the escaped convict Selden's elder sister.
cast.appearance: A large, solid, heavy-featured woman with an impassive face and a stern-set mouth. She wears a plain dark housekeeper's dress and apron, with a shawl over her shoulders at night.
cast.personality: Respectable and apparently unemotional, but deeply loyal and capable of intense grief and courage.
cast.motivation: She wants to keep her younger brother from starving or being taken, remembering the child she once cared for.
cast.fears: She fears Selden's recapture or death and the disgrace her secret brings upon her husband.
cast.speech: Usually restrained, she speaks with urgent, heartfelt plainness when defending her brother and takes responsibility for her husband's actions.
cast.arc: Her hidden grief and food signals arouse suspicion; she reveals the truth to protect her husband and later mourns Selden.

relationships.nature: Wife whose husband shares the risk of helping her brother.
His housekeeper, who appeals to his compassion for her family.
Her tears and nighttime secret draw his attention.

cast.name: Mrs. Laura Lyons
cast.role: Frankland's estranged daughter, whose letter brings Sir Charles to the moor-gate.
cast.appearance: A very handsome brunette with rich hazel hair and eyes, freckled cheeks, and a pink flush. She wears a neat late Victorian dress and works at a Remington typewriter in her well-appointed rooms.
cast.personality: Proud, defensive, and resourceful, with a capacity for fierce indignation when deceived.
cast.motivation: She wants freedom from her husband and believes Stapleton will marry her if she can obtain a divorce.
cast.fears: She fears scandal, exposure of her appointment with Sir Charles, and being compelled to live with her husband.
cast.speech: Initially guarded and sharp under questioning, she denies and qualifies; when cornered or betrayed, she speaks in a rapid, passionate torrent.
cast.arc: She conceals Stapleton's role until Holmes proves he is married, then reveals his dictation of the letter and his pressure to remain silent.

relationships.nature: Trusts his promise of marriage until she learns he already has a wife.
Gives him the hidden facts after he shows her proof of Stapleton's marriage.
Admits writing the letter to him but withholds Stapleton's involvement.

places.name: Baker Street
places.description: Holmes and Watson's London sitting-room, where Mortimer presents the case and Holmes later reconstructs it.
places.visual: A breakfast table with a silver-plated coffee-pot, a hearth-rug, a settee, papers, a lamp, and a fire; tobacco smoke can fill the room.

places.name: Baskerville Hall
places.description: The ancestral estate, newly inherited by Sir Henry, with a gloomy old centre and more modern wings.
places.visual: Twin crenelated towers rise above ivy-covered black granite; boars' heads top the gate pillars. Inside are oak rafters, stained glass, ancestral portraits, a great fireplace, and a shadowy dining-room.

places.name: The yew alley
places.description: Sir Charles's nightly walk and the place where he waited for a woman and died.
places.visual: A gravel path runs between twelve-foot clipped yew hedges, with grass strips on each side, a white moor-gate halfway along, and a decaying summer-house at the far end.

places.name: Dartmoor
places.description: The broad, sparsely populated landscape around the Hall, crossed by tracks and dotted with prehistoric remains.
places.visual: Russet and olive slopes, jagged granite tors and boulders, roofless circles of ancient stone huts, scattered cottages, and changing banks of mist under wide skies.

places.name: The great Grimpen Mire
places.description: A dangerous bog concealing the island where Stapleton kennels his hound.
places.visual: Bright green rushes and cotton grass break up green-scummed pools and quivering black mud; small wands mark a zigzag route to an island with abandoned mine machinery and ruined cottages.

places.name: Merripit House
places.description: The Stapletons' isolated home, a former grazing farm repaired as a modern dwelling.
places.visual: A bleak house with serrated roof and chimneys stands in a stunted orchard behind a low wall. Its large rooms are elegantly furnished; an out-house and a butterfly collection are close at hand.

places.name: Holmes's stone hut
places.description: A prehistoric shelter Holmes uses when he needs to watch the moor unseen.
places.visual: A low circular stone ruin with a partly surviving roof, blankets on a stone slab, a crude grate, cooking utensils, empty tins, and a flat stone table.

places.name: Coombe Tracey
places.description: The town where Laura Lyons works, and a base for Holmes's secret investigation.
places.visual: A railway station and central, well-appointed rooms where a Remington typewriter stands ready for work.

timeline.title: Chapter 1: Mr. Sherlock Holmes
timeline.summary: Holmes and Watson reconstruct the owner of a forgotten walking-stick before the owner, James Mortimer, returns to consult Holmes.
events: Watson examines the inscribed stick and offers his deductions.
Holmes corrects him, inferring a young country practitioner and a dog from the stick.
The Medical Directory confirms Mortimer's hospital and country appointments.
Mortimer arrives with his spaniel and explains that the stick was a marriage present.
Mortimer admires Holmes's skull and asks his help with an extraordinary problem.

knowledge.learns: Most of his deductions from the stick were wrong; Mortimer left hospital on marrying.
The stick was presented on Mortimer's marriage, complicating his inference about the occasion.

timeline.title: Chapter 2: The Curse of the Baskervilles
timeline.summary: Mortimer reads the Baskerville legend and a newspaper account of Sir Charles's death, then reveals evidence he withheld at the inquest.
events: Mortimer produces the family manuscript dated 1742.
He reads how Hugo pursued an abducted woman and was found with a monstrous hound at his throat.
He reads the newspaper account of Sir Charles's death in the yew alley and the natural-death verdict.
He describes Sir Charles's fear and a large black creature seen before the death.
He reveals that he saw fresh gigantic hound footprints near the body.

knowledge.learns: Mortimer withheld the hound tracks and Sir Charles had been intensely afraid of the family legend.
The official account omitted gigantic hound footprints found near Sir Charles.

timeline.title: Chapter 3: The Problem
timeline.summary: Holmes questions Mortimer about the physical evidence and the arriving heir, then studies the moor and develops a theory of Sir Charles's last movements.
events: Mortimer describes the alley, locked gate, cigar ash, and distant hound prints.
He reports pre-death sightings of a luminous creature and asks what to do with Sir Henry.
Holmes tells Mortimer to meet the heir and bring him to Baker Street next morning.
Holmes studies an Ordnance map while Watson spends the day at his club.
Holmes concludes Sir Charles was waiting at the gate and then ran desperately away from the house.

knowledge.learns: Sir Henry is arriving from Canada; Mortimer knows of no sightings of the apparition after Sir Charles's death.
Holmes interprets the altered footprints as running and the cigar ash as evidence of waiting.

timeline.title: Chapter 4: Sir Henry Baskerville
timeline.summary: Sir Henry receives a warning, learns the family evidence, and insists on going to the Hall; Holmes spots but loses the man following him.
events: Henry shows Holmes an anonymous warning assembled from printed words and reports a missing new tan boot.
Holmes identifies the printed words as cut from a Times leader and examines the disguised address.
Mortimer tells Henry the story, and Henry declares that neither man nor devil will keep him from his home.
Holmes and Watson follow Henry and Mortimer and spot a black-bearded watcher in a cab.
The watcher escapes; Holmes notes cab number 2704 and sends Cartwright to search hotel waste-paper.

knowledge.learns: The private circumstances of his uncle's death and the danger associated with the hound.
Henry is being watched in London by a man in a cab; the warning's printed words came from the Times.

timeline.title: Chapter 5: Three Broken Threads
timeline.summary: A second boot disappears, Watson agrees to accompany Henry to Devon, and Holmes's London leads fail to identify the watcher.
events: Holmes checks the hotel register and questions the staff about recent guests.
Henry reports that an old black boot has vanished as well as the new brown one.
Mortimer explains the legacies and identifies the apparent next heir, James Desmond.
Holmes recommends Watson as Henry's companion, and Watson accepts.
The new brown boot reappears; telegrams and the cabman fail to identify the watcher, who called himself Sherlock Holmes.

knowledge.learns: Henry inherits a residue of £740,000; the cab passenger gave the driver Holmes's own name.
He is to accompany Henry and report carefully to Holmes.
He was followed in London and Barrymore has a black beard like the watcher's.

timeline.title: Chapter 6: Baskerville Hall
timeline.summary: Watson, Henry, and Mortimer travel to Devon, hear of an escaped murderer, and reach the sombre Hall.
events: Holmes instructs Watson to report facts, carry his revolver, and keep Henry from going alone.
The travellers see the moor from the train and take a wagonette from the station.
Perkins explains that Selden, the Notting Hill murderer, has escaped from Princetown.
The party reaches Baskerville Hall; Mortimer goes home and the Barrymores receive the guests.
Barrymore says he and his wife wish eventually to leave; that night Watson hears a woman sobbing.

knowledge.learns: Selden is loose on the moor and the Barrymores intend to leave after new arrangements are made.
The Hall's servants wish to leave because Sir Charles's death made the house painful to them.

timeline.title: Chapter 7: The Stapletons of Merripit House
timeline.summary: Watson discovers a flaw in the telegram test, meets Stapleton and his supposed sister, and receives her urgent warning.
events: Barrymore denies that his wife sobbed, but Watson sees her swollen, tear-reddened eyes.
At Grimpen, Watson learns the test telegram was handed to Mrs. Barrymore rather than her husband.
Stapleton meets Watson, takes him toward Merripit House, and shows him the deadly mire.
They hear a strange moan; Stapleton pursues a butterfly into the mire.
Beryl mistakes Watson for Henry and warns him to return to London before concealing the exchange from Stapleton.
After Watson visits Merripit House, Beryl intercepts him and gives an evasive explanation of her warning.

knowledge.learns: The telegram did not prove Barrymore was at the Hall; Beryl urgently wants Henry away but will give no definite reason.
The man she warned is Watson, not Sir Henry.
Watson is at the Hall and says Holmes cannot leave London at present.

timeline.title: Chapter 8: First Report of Dr. Watson
timeline.summary: Watson's report describes the neighbours and Henry's attraction to Beryl, then records Barrymore's mysterious nighttime vigil.
events: Watson reports that the district believes Selden has left the moor.
Stapleton shows Watson and Henry the legendary valley; Henry meets Beryl at Merripit House.
Mortimer shows the party the yew alley, and Watson describes the litigious Frankland.
Henry questions Barrymore about the telegram and later gives him old clothes.
At night Watson follows Barrymore to an empty room and sees him hold a candle against a window overlooking the moor.
Watson and Henry plan to investigate the nocturnal movements.

knowledge.learns: Barrymore claims his wife brought him the telegram; his candle vigil suggests a secret connected with the moor.
Watson's account leaves the telegram test unable to establish Barrymore's whereabouts independently.

timeline.title: Chapter 9: The Light upon the Moor [Second Report of Dr. Watson]
timeline.summary: Stapleton interrupts Henry's courtship; the Barrymores' signal is explained, and a pursuit of Selden ends with a glimpse of another man.
events: Watson and Henry decide to watch Barrymore at night.
Henry goes to meet Beryl; Watson follows and sees Stapleton furiously interrupt Henry's proposal.
Stapleton apologizes and secures Henry's promise to wait three months before pressing his suit.
After one fruitless vigil, Watson and Henry confront Barrymore at the window and see an answering light.
Mrs. Barrymore reveals that the lights arrange food for her fugitive brother Selden.
Henry and Watson pursue Selden, hear the hound's cry, and fail to catch him; Watson sees a tall stranger on a tor.

knowledge.learns: Beryl warns him of danger; Barrymore's signal helps Selden, Mrs. Barrymore's brother.
The Barrymores feed Selden, and another tall man is watching from the moor.
Henry and Watson have discovered the signal and Selden's identity.

timeline.title: Chapter 10: Extract from the Diary of Dr. Watson
timeline.summary: Henry agrees not to inform on Selden; Barrymore repays him with a clue to Sir Charles's appointment, and Watson identifies two new lines of inquiry.
events: Watson reflects on the hound and resolves to find the stranger on the tor.
Barrymore protests the chase and says arrangements are being made to send Selden to South America.
Henry agrees not to tell the police; Barrymore reveals a burned letter signed L. L. asking Sir Charles to meet at ten.
Mortimer tells Watson that Laura Lyons of Coombe Tracey has those initials.
Barrymore tells Watson that Selden saw another man living among the stone huts and supplied by a boy.

knowledge.learns: Sir Charles had an appointment at the gate with a woman signing herself L. L.
Laura Lyons is a possible L. L.; the unknown man has a boy bringing supplies to a stone hut.
Henry will not report Selden's presence to the police.

timeline.title: Chapter 11: The Man on the Tor
timeline.summary: Watson questions Laura Lyons, follows a clue from Frankland's telescope to a stone hut, and discovers that its occupant knows his movements.
events: Watson tells Henry about Laura Lyons and goes alone to Coombe Tracey.
Laura first denies the appointment, then admits writing the letter but says she never went.
She explains that she sought help with divorce expenses but received help elsewhere.
Frankland shows Watson a boy carrying a bundle toward the moor and refuses to help the police.
Watson finds the occupied stone hut and a note reporting his own visit to Coombe Tracey.
He waits armed for the tenant, whose familiar voice addresses him from outside.

knowledge.learns: Laura wrote the appointment letter but claims not to have gone; someone in the hut receives reports on his movements.
Watson knows the burned postscript and is investigating Sir Charles's death.

timeline.title: Chapter 12: Death on the Moor
timeline.summary: The stranger proves to be Holmes, who identifies the Stapletons' deception; a hound pursuit kills Selden in Henry's clothes.
events: Holmes reveals himself and explains his secret presence and use of Cartwright.
Watson recounts his interview with Laura; Holmes reveals that Beryl is Stapleton's wife.
Screams and a hound's cry send them racing across the moor to a fallen body in Henry's tweed.
They discover the dead man is Selden, wearing clothes Henry gave Barrymore.
Stapleton arrives, recognizes Holmes, and explains that he had invited Henry over.
Holmes and Watson return toward the Hall; Holmes plans for Henry to dine alone at Merripit House.

knowledge.learns: Holmes is the moorland watcher, Beryl is Stapleton's wife, and Selden died in Henry's clothes.
Laura sought divorce expenses and Selden had Henry's discarded clothes; he infers the hound followed their scent.
Holmes is on the moor and Selden, not Henry, is the dead man.

timeline.title: Chapter 13: Fixing the Nets
timeline.summary: Holmes recognizes Stapleton's likeness to Hugo, sets a trap using Henry, and persuades Laura to reveal Stapleton's role.
events: Watson tells the Barrymores of Selden's death; Henry agrees to obey Holmes's directions.
Holmes notices Hugo's portrait and shows Watson its resemblance to Stapleton.
Holmes orders Henry to dine at Merripit House and walk home by the straight path.
Holmes and Watson appear to leave for London; Cartwright is sent ahead to dispatch a misleading telegram.
Holmes shows Laura evidence of Stapleton's marriage, and she reveals that he dictated the letter and stopped her attending.
Lestrade arrives from London with an unsigned warrant.

knowledge.learns: Laura confirms Stapleton dictated the appointment letter, dissuaded her from going, and made her keep silent.
Stapleton is married to the woman presented as his sister and has deceived her.
Holmes infers from Hugo's portrait that Stapleton is a Baskerville with designs on the succession.
Holmes wants him to dine at Merripit and walk home alone along the specified path.

timeline.title: Chapter 14: The Hound of the Baskervilles
timeline.summary: Holmes's ambush saves Henry from the luminous hound; Beryl is freed, and the search of the mire suggests Stapleton has perished.
events: Holmes, Watson, and Lestrade hide near Merripit House as fog advances.
Watson sees Henry dining with Stapleton and watches Stapleton visit a locked out-house.
Henry walks home; the glowing hound emerges from the fog, and Holmes shoots it after it reaches him.
They find Beryl bound and bruised in the house; she directs them toward the mire.
Henry learns the truth about Beryl and falls ill with fever.
Next morning the party follows the marked route, recovers Henry's black boot, and finds the hound's island lair but no trace of Stapleton reaching it.

knowledge.learns: The hound's apparent fire is a phosphorus preparation; Stapleton kept it on the mire island.
Beryl is Stapleton's wife and the hound pursuing him was real.
Henry survived and the hound is dead.
Beryl can identify Stapleton's refuge; the recovered boot and absence of tracks suggest he died in the mire.

timeline.title: Chapter 15: A Retrospection
timeline.summary: At the end of November Holmes reconstructs Stapleton's history and methods for Watson and acknowledges the cost to Sir Henry.
events: Henry and Mortimer call in London before their restorative voyage.
Holmes identifies Stapleton as Rodger Baskerville's son and recounts his marriage and schoolmastering past.
He explains the hound's purchase, concealment, and use against Sir Charles after Laura's dictated letter.
He reconstructs Beryl's warning, the stolen boots, and Stapleton's surveillance in London.
He explains his own secret investigation, the use of Henry as bait, and Beryl's final revolt against her husband.
Holmes admits uncertainty about how Stapleton would have claimed the inheritance and proposes an evening at the opera.

knowledge.learns: Stapleton was Rodger Baskerville's son; Holmes had inferred a real hound from the boots and suspected a woman from the warning's scent.
From later conversations with Beryl and inquiries, he has established Stapleton's background and the women's parts in the plot.

divergencePoints.label: The Footprints Withheld
divergencePoints.moment: Mortimer reaches the private evidence he concealed from the inquest and tells Holmes about the tracks near Sir Charles.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: He reveals that the fresh, clear footprints were those of a gigantic hound.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Mortimer kept the hound footprints secret from Holmes as well as the coroner?
divergencePoints.stakes: Holmes's first understanding of the death and the danger to Henry would change.

divergencePoints.label: The Heir Turns Back
divergencePoints.moment: After hearing the legend and the circumstances of his uncle's death, Henry decides whether to go to Baskerville Hall.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: He declares that neither devil nor man will prevent him from going to his family's home.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Sir Henry heeded the warning and refused to go to Baskerville Hall?
divergencePoints.stakes: His inheritance, the district's hopes, and the attacker's access to him hang on the decision.

divergencePoints.label: The Cab Shadowed
divergencePoints.moment: Holmes spots the cab following Henry and Mortimer and moves to get a closer look at its passenger.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: The passenger sees Holmes and escapes in the cab before Holmes can follow.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Holmes quietly hired another cab and followed the bearded watcher instead of exposing himself?
divergencePoints.stakes: The watcher's identity and movements might be exposed before the journey to Devon.

divergencePoints.label: Beryl Speaks Plainly
divergencePoints.moment: Beryl intercepts Watson after her warning and hesitates when he presses her to explain Henry's danger.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: She attributes her warning to the family curse and refuses to give definite information.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Beryl told Watson what she knew about her husband and the hound on that lonely path?
divergencePoints.stakes: Henry could be warned, but Beryl would risk Stapleton's retaliation.

divergencePoints.label: A Shot at Selden
divergencePoints.moment: Selden flees across the moonlit moor while Watson has a chance of a long revolver shot.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Watson refuses to shoot an unarmed fleeing man, and Selden escapes.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Watson fired at the fleeing Selden and brought him down?
divergencePoints.stakes: A fugitive's freedom and the Barrymores' hopes would depend on the shot.

divergencePoints.label: The Butler's Bargain
divergencePoints.moment: Barrymore begs Henry not to tell the police that Selden remains on the moor.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Henry agrees to stay silent, and a grateful Barrymore reveals the burned L. L. letter.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Sir Henry refused Barrymore's plea and reported Selden to the police?
divergencePoints.stakes: Selden's escape, the Barrymores' trust, and the clue to Sir Charles's appointment are at risk.

divergencePoints.label: The Wrong Man Hunted
divergencePoints.moment: Holmes and Watson hear a man screaming as the hound pursues him across the dark moor.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: They reach the fallen man too late and discover that Selden has died wearing Henry's clothes.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Holmes and Watson reached Selden before he fell and saved him from the hound?
divergencePoints.stakes: Selden's life and the evidence available against Stapleton would change.

divergencePoints.label: Laura's Silence
divergencePoints.moment: Holmes shows Laura evidence that the man who promised to marry her already has a wife.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: She turns against Stapleton and reveals that he dictated the letter and stopped her attending.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Laura refused to believe Holmes's evidence and kept Stapleton's secret?
divergencePoints.stakes: A crucial account of Sir Charles's last appointment would remain concealed.

divergencePoints.label: The Hound Breaks Through
divergencePoints.moment: The luminous hound bursts from the fog and runs past the startled men toward Sir Henry.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: Holmes and Watson fire, pursue it, and Holmes kills it after it knocks Henry down but before it wounds him.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if the fog hid the hound from Holmes and Watson until it had reached Sir Henry?
divergencePoints.stakes: Henry's life and the success of Holmes's dangerous trap hang on a few moments.

divergencePoints.label: The Missing Wands
divergencePoints.moment: Beryl reveals that she and Stapleton planted wands to mark the route through the mire and wishes she had removed them that day.
divergencePoints.canonOutcome: The markers remain, and Stapleton flees into the fog-bound mire while pursuit must wait until morning.
divergencePoints.whatIf: What if Beryl had pulled out the guiding wands before Stapleton fled toward the mire?
divergencePoints.stakes: Stapleton's escape route and the search for his refuge would be altered.

visual.era: Late Victorian England: frock-coats, tweeds, long skirts, horse-drawn vehicles, railway carriages, telegraph offices, and a granite ancestral house with older Tudor and Cavalier details.
visual.palette: Smoke-grey London and warm firelight; russet, olive, granite grey, and cold moon-silver on the moor; startling blue-green phosphorescence in fog.
motifs: A black hound with luminous jaws
A candle answering another across darkness
Granite tors and roofless stone circles
The white gate between high yew hedges
An old black boot in green mire
visual.comicStyle: Use the ink line and engraved cross-hatching of a late Victorian illustrated magazine, with restrained watercolour washes. Give the moor broad, quiet panels and crowded interiors deep shadows; reserve sharp close-ups and broken, urgent panels for discoveries and pursuit.

The hamlet where Mortimer practises and the local telegraph is delivered.

The thick, bulbous-headed walking-stick Mortimer leaves at Baker Street.
Mortimer's medical qualification, which he carefully distinguishes from a doctorate.
The local word used in the legend for a deep dip or narrow valley.
The initials on the surviving fragment of Sir Charles's burned letter.
The name Stapleton used while running a Yorkshire school.
The gate from the yew alley onto the moor.
The messenger boy who assists Holmes in London and on the moor.
The escaped Notting Hill murderer and Mrs. Barrymore's brother.

persuasion.title: Persuasion
persuasion.author: Jane Austen
persuasion.premise: Anne Elliot, overlooked by her proud family, meets again the naval officer whose engagement she was persuaded to break eight years before. As her father lets their Somersetshire home and moves to Bath, Anne must observe Captain Wentworth's apparent courtship of another woman while concealing her own attachment.
persuasion.hook: Eight years after giving him up, Anne must watch the man she still loves choose a wife.
persuasion.logline: When Captain Wentworth returns wealthy and resentful, Anne Elliot must discover whether a love broken by persuasion can survive pride, misunderstanding, and the claims of others.

world.setting: Somersetshire country houses and villages, the Dorset seaside town of Lyme, and the streets, lodgings, shops, and assembly rooms of Bath.
world.period: England, 1814 to early 1815, during the peace following the Napoleonic wars
rules: There is no supernatural element; chance meetings, letters, observation, gossip, and mistaken inference carry the plot.
Rank governs introductions, precedence, and marriage prospects; a baronet's title and the Kellynch estate are expected to pass to the male heir.
A woman's fortune and family connections affect her prospects, while her freedom to travel, earn, and initiate courtship is constrained.
Naval officers can rise through service and gain prize money, but war brings separation, danger, injury, and death; peace leaves officers ashore.
Country visits are made on foot, horseback, or by carriage; longer journeys require horses, inns, and hours on the road.
Letters and cards arrange visits and carry news; information also travels through servants, nurses, newspapers, and social calls.
Doctors, apothecaries, surgeons, nursing, warm baths, and sea air are available, but recovery from a head injury remains uncertain.
Hospitality ranges from elaborate formal calls and precedence to the Harvilles' open invitation despite their small rooms and limited means.
world.tone: Tender and quietly painful, with sharp social comedy, irony, and a growing sense of recovered hope.
themes: Rank and the actual worth of people
Loss, recovery, and the passage of time
sensitivities: The narration mocks physical size and disability, notably Mrs Musgrove's grief and Sir Walter's contempt for weathered faces.
Class prejudice, inherited rank, and contempt for tradespeople shape the characters' judgments and language.
Women's limited legal and economic independence and the vulnerability of a poor widow are central conditions of the story.

voice.narration: Third-person past tense, mostly close to Anne's perceptions and private reasoning, with an omniscient narrator who occasionally enters other minds or addresses the reader with ironic authority.
style: Long, balanced sentences accumulate qualifications, parallel clauses, and semicolons; short exclamations interrupt them at moments of feeling.
Free indirect discourse lets Anne's hopes, doubts, and self-reproaches blend into the narrator's measured judgments.
Social absurdity is exposed by exact habits, ranks, furnishings, and a quietly devastating reversal rather than broad caricature alone.
Emotional crises are rendered through glances, pauses, blushes, movements, and the effort to remain composed in company.
The narrator ranges from teasing general observations to sincere feeling, sometimes allowing irony and compassion to stand together.
Use the manuscript's British spelling and period diction, including connexion, shewn, staid, and enquire.
voice.dialogue: Speech appears in quotation marks, often with semicolons, dashes, interruptions, and brief narrative comments. Polite conversation conceals feeling; characters reveal themselves through repeated complaints, solicitous questions, flattery, or frank naval idiom.
samplePassages: A few years before, Anne Elliot had been a very pretty girl, but her bloom had vanished early; and as even in its height, her father had found little to admire in her, (so totally different were her delicate features and mild dark eyes from his own), there could be nothing in them, now that she was faded and thin, to excite his esteem. He had never indulged much hope, he had now none, of ever reading her name in any other page of his favourite work.

“Oh! Frederick! But I cannot believe it of you.—All idle refinement!—Women may be as comfortable on board, as in the best house in England. I believe I have lived as much on board as most women, and I know nothing superior to the accommodations of a man-of-war. I declare I have not a comfort or an indulgence about me, even at Kellynch Hall,” (with a kind bow to Anne), “beyond what I always had in most of the ships I have lived in; and they have been five altogether.”

“Perhaps I shall. Yes, yes, if you please, no reference to examples in books. Men have had every advantage of us in telling their own story. Education has been theirs in so much higher a degree; the pen has been in their hands. I will not allow books to prove anything.”

“But how shall we prove anything?”

“We never shall. We never can expect to prove any thing upon such a point. It is a difference of opinion which does not admit of proof.

cast.name: Anne Elliot
cast.role: The neglected middle Elliot daughter and emotional centre of the story.
cast.age: Twenty-seven at the beginning; in her twenty-eighth year at the reunion.
cast.appearance: A small, slender woman with delicate, very regular pretty features and mild dark eyes. Her face is thin and faded at first; colour and animation return to her cheeks and eyes. Dark hair is dressed simply up; she wears modest high-waisted gowns, a pelisse and bonnet outdoors, and little ornament.
cast.personality: Observant, cultivated, patient, and tender, with quiet humour and practical composure under pressure.
cast.motivation: She wants to do her duty without sacrificing honest feeling, and still loves Wentworth despite expecting no return.
cast.fears: She dreads exposing her attachment, losing Wentworth to another woman, and causing pain through family folly.
cast.speech: Gentle and measured, often asking or suggesting rather than commanding; in emergencies she gives clear, rapid directions. With trusted company she can argue warmly and precisely.
cast.arc: Having broken an engagement under advice, she learns to trust her judgment, acts on her enduring love, and accepts Wentworth again while defending the duty she once felt to Lady Russell.

relationships.nature: Former fiancé; their attachment survives estrangement and is renewed.
Beloved godmother and maternal adviser who persuaded her to break the engagement.
Her vain father consistently overlooks her.
Her younger sister relies on her attention and nursing.
Her cousin courts her; she grows suspicious and learns of his duplicity.
An old school friend whose confidence exposes Mr Elliot.

cast.name: Captain Wentworth
cast.role: Anne's former fiancé, a successful naval captain seeking a wife.
cast.appearance: A fine, strongly made man with an open, glowing, manly face, bright proud eyes and a handsome expressive mouth. His hair is dark and neatly dressed; he wears a well-cut dark coat, pale breeches or trousers, waistcoat and neckcloth, with a hat and, at sea, naval uniform.
cast.personality: Warm, lively, confident, generous and proud; his resentment can make him unjust.
cast.motivation: He seeks marriage and happiness, while pride leads him to believe he has overcome his attachment to Anne.
cast.fears: He fears renewed rejection and being bound in honour to Louisa when his heart belongs elsewhere.
cast.speech: Animated and witty, with naval comparisons and teasing exaggeration; feeling makes him abrupt, earnest, or silent. Among officers he speaks with unguarded warmth.
cast.arc: He mistakes anger for indifference, flirts with the Musgrove sisters, recognises Anne's worth at Lyme, and overcomes jealousy to offer himself again.

relationships.nature: Former fiancée whom he has never ceased to love.
His frank, affectionate sister.
His attentions encourage her; he feels honour-bound if she expects him.
A close naval friend whose household welcomes him.
A valued former officer and friend whom he supported in grief.

cast.name: Sir Walter Elliot
cast.role: Anne's vain father, a baronet whose debts force him to let Kellynch Hall.
cast.appearance: A tall, still very handsome man with carefully arranged hair, fine features and an erect, self-conscious bearing. He dresses immaculately in fashionable coats, waistcoats and neckcloths, and attends closely to his reflection and grooming.
cast.personality: Conceited, extravagant, rank-conscious and preoccupied with beauty.
cast.motivation: He wants to preserve his consequence, comforts, appearance and intact estate despite debt.
cast.fears: He recoils from social degradation, visible ageing, and economies that diminish his dignity.
cast.speech: Polished but complacent, full of judgments on rank and appearance; he turns even practical questions into reflections on his own consequence.
cast.arc: He leaves Kellynch for Bath, enjoys fashionable connections, and accepts Wentworth once his fortune, profession and appearance satisfy him.

relationships.nature: His middle daughter, whom he habitually undervalues.
His favourite daughter and companion in vanity.
His heir presumptive, first estranged and then reconciled.
Elizabeth's companion, whose flattery gains his favour.
His late wife's friend and adviser in his financial difficulties.

cast.name: Elizabeth Elliot
cast.role: Sir Walter's eldest daughter and mistress of his household.
cast.appearance: A very handsome woman, still in full bloom, with an elegant figure and a strong likeness to her father. Her hair is carefully dressed; fashionable gowns, a fine pelisse and bonnet, and an assured upright carriage mark her position.
cast.personality: Self-possessed, proud, socially ambitious and cold toward Anne.
cast.motivation: She seeks an alliance worthy of her birth and the social consequence she feels is due to her.
cast.fears: She fears remaining unmarried and suffering visible loss of rank or style.
cast.speech: Decisive and ceremonious with fashionable company; dismissive of Anne, and comfortably confidential with Mrs Clay.
cast.arc: She leaves Kellynch, pursues Bath society and imagines Mr Elliot's attentions are hers, only to see him withdraw.

relationships.nature: Her father and closest ally in matters of status.
Her sister, whose convenience and advice she disregards.
Her favoured companion, whom she trusts despite warnings.
Her cousin and former hoped-for match.

cast.name: Lady Russell
cast.role: Anne's godmother, her mother's intimate friend and a wealthy widow.
cast.age: A woman of steady, mature age.
cast.appearance: A dignified, upright woman with a composed face and crow's feet at her temples. Her hair is neatly dressed beneath a cap or bonnet; she favours formal, carefully arranged gowns, a shawl and a respectable carriage.
cast.personality: Benevolent, conscientious and decorous, but prejudiced in favour of ancestry and polished manners.
cast.motivation: She wants Anne secure and happy, and the Elliot family honourably protected.
cast.fears: She fears imprudence, financial dependence and alliances that expose Anne or the family to hardship.
cast.speech: Courteous, serious and reasoned; her advice combines affection with appeals to principle, prudence and propriety.
cast.arc: She hopes Anne will marry Mr Elliot, then recognises her errors about him and Wentworth and welcomes Anne's happiness.

relationships.nature: Her beloved goddaughter and closest young friend.
She opposed his early engagement to Anne, then learns to value him.
Her old neighbour, whom she advises with regard for his dignity.
She misjudges his polished manner as evidence of principle.

cast.name: Mary Musgrove
cast.role: Anne's younger sister, married to Charles Musgrove and mother of two boys.
cast.age: A young married woman, born in 1791.
cast.appearance: A well-grown woman once called a fine girl, less handsome than her sisters, with a tendency to look coarse or flushed. She wears fashionable high-waisted gowns and bonnets; at home she may recline on a sofa among the Cottage's worn furnishings.
cast.personality: Affectionate when pleased but querulous, self-important, jealous and readily convinced she is neglected or ill.
cast.motivation: She wants attention, amusement, precedence and the recognition due to an Elliot.
cast.fears: She dreads being left alone, overlooked, ill-used or placed below her relations.
cast.speech: Exclamatory and repetitive: she insists that nobody attends to her, then changes her account as circumstances change.
cast.arc: Her complaints repeatedly redirect others' plans, including Anne's nursing at Lyme; she later takes credit and comfort from Anne's advantageous marriage.

relationships.nature: Her elder sister, whom she claims as companion and nurse.
Her good-humoured husband, with whom she often disagrees.
Her sister-in-law, whose bedside she insists on remaining at.
Her sister-in-law, whose proposed marriage to Hayter she despises.

cast.name: Charles Musgrove
cast.role: Mary's husband and heir to the Uppercross estate; he once proposed to Anne.
cast.appearance: A pleasant, well-built country gentleman with a healthy complexion and easy bearing. He wears practical shooting clothes and boots outdoors, and a plain coat and neckcloth for visits; a gun, dogs or riding gear often accompany him.
cast.personality: Good-natured and sociable, more sensible than Mary but chiefly energetic about sport.
cast.motivation: He wants his family comfortable and his days occupied with shooting and company.
cast.fears: He is alarmed by serious harm to his children or sisters, though he does not dwell on ordinary anxieties.
cast.speech: Direct, cheerful and informal, with sporting details and blunt teasing; he defends friends and family without much ceremony.
cast.arc: His affection and practical kindness support the family after Louisa's fall; his chance errand leaves Anne and Wentworth alone to reconcile.

relationships.nature: His wife, whose complaints he alternately indulges and resists.
His sister-in-law and former choice for a wife.
His sister, whose injury deeply distressses him.
His shooting companion and warmly admired friend.

cast.name: Louisa Musgrove
cast.role: Charles's high-spirited sister, admired by Wentworth before her fall at Lyme.
cast.age: One of the two Musgrove sisters aged nineteen and twenty.
cast.appearance: A rather pretty young woman with lively eyes, an animated face and a light, active figure. Her hair is fashionably dressed; she wears a fresh high-waisted gown and, outdoors, a pelisse and bonnet suitable for walking.
cast.personality: Merry, enthusiastic, affectionate and determined, with a taste for having her own way.
cast.motivation: She wants pleasure, companionship and the freedom to follow her feelings; she admires naval warmth and courage.
cast.fears: After her injury she becomes highly susceptible to noise and nervous agitation.
cast.speech: Eager and emphatic, full of quick praise and declarations; she speaks firmly when defending a decision.
cast.arc: Her insistence on a second jump ends in a severe head injury; during recovery she and Benwick become engaged.

relationships.nature: Her close and affectionate sister.
His attentions and praise encourage her; he catches her after her fall.
Her companion during recovery and eventual fiancé.
Her affectionate brother.

cast.name: Henrietta Musgrove
cast.role: Louisa's sister, courted by her cousin Charles Hayter and briefly attracted to Wentworth.
cast.age: One of the two Musgrove sisters aged nineteen and twenty.
cast.appearance: A rather pretty, fashionably dressed young woman, perhaps the prettier of the sisters, with a gentle expression and a neat, youthful figure. Her hair is dressed up beneath a bonnet; she wears a high-waisted gown and walking pelisse.
cast.personality: Pleasant and affectionate, but more easily influenced than Louisa.
cast.motivation: She wants a happy marriage with Charles Hayter and advancement in his clerical prospects.
cast.fears: She is overwhelmed by the apparent loss of Louisa after the fall.
cast.speech: Warm and sociable, with eager repetitions; she speaks earnestly about Dr Shirley's health and Hayter's prospects.
cast.arc: Diverted by Wentworth, she renews her attachment to Hayter and gains family consent to marry him.

relationships.nature: Her close sister, who encourages her visit to Hayter.
His arrival temporarily distracts her from her cousin.
A sympathetic companion at Uppercross and Lyme.

cast.name: Mrs Croft
cast.role: Wentworth's sister and the admiral's wife; a welcoming tenant of Kellynch.
cast.appearance: Neither tall nor fat, but square, upright and vigorous, with bright dark eyes, good teeth and an agreeable face. Her complexion is reddened and weather-beaten. She wears practical, neat gowns, a bonnet and shawl for walking or driving.
cast.personality: Open, capable, good-humoured and decisive, with a brisk independence.
cast.motivation: She values being with her husband and making a comfortable, useful home together.
cast.fears: Separation from her husband at sea has caused her real anxiety and imaginary complaints.
cast.speech: Frank and sensible, puncturing refinements with practical examples; affectionate and brisk with her husband and brother.
cast.arc: She establishes a happy home at Kellynch, befriends Anne, and later witnesses the renewal of Anne's bond with her brother.

relationships.nature: Her affectionate brother, whose views she can challenge.
Her husband and constant companion ashore and at sea.
A neighbour she treats with considerate warmth.

cast.name: Admiral Croft
cast.role: A retired naval officer who rents Kellynch Hall with his wife.
cast.appearance: A hale, hearty, well-looking man with a slightly weather-beaten face and an easy, substantial figure. He wears a plain dark coat, waistcoat and neckcloth, and often stands with his hands behind his back.
cast.personality: Frank, generous, simple-hearted and cheerful, with an absent-minded streak.
cast.motivation: He wants a comfortable home in Somerset and the company of his wife and naval friends.
cast.fears: He is troubled by others' distress and seeks treatment in Bath when thought gouty.
cast.speech: Bluff and conversational, full of digressions, hearty exclamations and naval comparisons; he readily offers practical help.
cast.arc: He becomes a considerate tenant and friend to Anne, and brings her reassuring news of Wentworth.

relationships.nature: His wife, partner in journeys and household decisions.
His brother-in-law, welcome at Kellynch as at home.
His landlord's daughter, whom he treats as a friend.
His landlord, whose vanity he regards with good humour.

cast.name: Mr Elliot
cast.role: Sir Walter's heir presumptive and Anne's polished, calculating cousin.
cast.appearance: An agreeable-looking man with a well-shaped face, sensible eyes and a noticeably under-hung jaw. He has a fashionable, well-groomed appearance and easy posture; at Lyme he wears mourning, including crape on his hat.
cast.personality: Discreet, observant and agreeable in company, but secretive and self-interested.
cast.motivation: He wants the baronetcy secured against a possible new heir and comes to desire Anne as his wife.
cast.fears: He fears Sir Walter's marriage to Mrs Clay and the loss of his expected title and estate.
cast.speech: Polished, attentive and controlled; he flatters subtly, adapts to his listener and withholds damaging information.
cast.arc: He reconciles with the Elliots to watch Mrs Clay, courts Anne, and after her engagement leaves Bath; Mrs Clay is later established under his protection.

relationships.nature: His cousin, whom he admires and hopes to marry.
His relative and predecessor in the expected baronetcy.
A rival schemer whom he seeks to keep from marrying Sir Walter.
His former friend's widow, whom he has refused to assist.
His cousin, who once expected to marry him.

cast.name: Mrs Clay
cast.role: Mr Shepherd's widowed daughter and Elizabeth's insinuating companion.
cast.age: A young widow, between thirty and forty.
cast.appearance: A well-looking woman with freckles, a projecting tooth and a clumsy wrist. Her hair is neatly dressed, and she wears becoming, carefully maintained gowns and a bonnet; her expression is often ready with a smile.
cast.personality: Clever, tactful, observant and adept at making herself useful and agreeable.
cast.motivation: She seeks security and advancement through the Elliot household, with designs on Sir Walter.
cast.fears: Exposure or interruption of her prospects threatens her position in the household.
cast.speech: Fluent and ingratiating, with ready compliments and apparently self-effacing concern for others.
cast.arc: She accompanies Elizabeth to Bath, remains close to Sir Walter despite suspicion, and eventually leaves under Mr Elliot's protection.

relationships.nature: Her friend and patroness, whom she flatters.
Her prospective target for an advantageous marriage.
Her opponent in the matter of Sir Walter's remarriage and later protector.
An observer alert to the danger of her intimacy with Sir Walter.

cast.name: Mrs Smith
cast.role: Anne's former school friend, now a poor and disabled widow in Bath.
cast.appearance: Formerly fine-looking and well-grown, she is now an infirm woman whose legs were damaged by rheumatic fever. Her hair is simply dressed; she wears a modest gown and shawl, and sits among knitting, thread-cases and small articles for sale.
cast.personality: Intelligent, resilient and cheerful, with a shrewd appreciation of human weakness.
cast.motivation: She wants companionship, means to help poorer neighbours, and recovery of her husband's West Indian property.
cast.fears: She fears poverty, neglected claims and the loss of Anne's friendship through marriage to Mr Elliot.
cast.speech: Candid, lively and ironic, drawing on Nurse Rooke's reports; when recalling injury she becomes grave and intensely direct.
cast.arc: She renews Anne's friendship, reveals Mr Elliot's past and present designs, and gains Wentworth's help with her property.

relationships.nature: Her former school protégée and devoted friend.
Her husband's former friend, whose refusal to act as executor injured her.
Anne's husband, who helps her pursue her property.

cast.name: Captain Harville
cast.role: Wentworth's wounded naval friend and Benwick's almost brother-in-law.
cast.appearance: A tall, dark man with strong features, a sensible benevolent countenance and a slight lameness. Ill health makes him look older than Wentworth. He wears a plain dark coat and often occupies his hands with tools or a fishing net.
cast.personality: Warm, unaffected, hospitable and ingenious, with deep feeling beneath a practical manner.
cast.motivation: He wants to care for his family and friends and make their limited lodgings comfortable.
cast.fears: He fears for those he loves and grieves his sister Fanny's death.
cast.speech: Frank, affectionate and vivid, using naval images; strong feeling can interrupt his easy conversation.
cast.arc: He shelters Louisa after her fall, mourns Benwick's changed attachment, and unknowingly helps prompt Wentworth's declaration.

relationships.nature: His close friend, who brought Benwick news of Fanny's death.
His guest and his late sister's former fiancé.
A valued friend with whom he debates constancy.
The injured guest whom his household nurses.

cast.name: Captain Benwick
cast.role: A young naval commander mourning Fanny Harville, later engaged to Louisa.
cast.age: A young man, the youngest of the three captains at Lyme.
cast.appearance: A small man with a pleasing face and melancholy air, younger-looking than Wentworth or Harville. He wears a dark, restrained coat and neckcloth and often carries or sits with a book.
cast.personality: Shy, sensitive, affectionate and serious, with a strong taste for poetry.
cast.motivation: He seeks comfort and sympathetic companionship after the death of his fiancée.
cast.fears: He is oppressed by grief and initially withdraws from unfamiliar company.
cast.speech: Quiet and hesitant with strangers; he becomes expressive when discussing poetry and passages of grief.
cast.arc: Anne draws him into conversation and recommends prose; during Louisa's recovery he forms a new attachment and becomes engaged to her.

relationships.nature: His host and the brother of his late fiancée.
His former captain and loyal friend.
A sympathetic reader who recommends books to him.
His companion during her recovery and future wife.

places.name: Kellynch Hall
places.description: The Elliot family seat, let furnished to the Crofts when Sir Walter's debts force retrenchment.
places.visual: A substantial country house amid park, lawns, groves, shrubberies and flower gardens; formal rooms hold pictures and many looking-glasses. The Crofts hang umbrellas by a shrubbery door.

places.name: Kellynch Lodge
places.description: Lady Russell's home near the Hall, a refuge and familiar base for Anne.
places.visual: A comfortable country lodge with modern, elegant apartments, carriage access and grounds close to the village and the Hall.

places.name: Uppercross
places.description: The Musgroves' busy village, three miles from Kellynch, where Anne stays with Mary.
places.visual: The old Great House has high walls, great gates and trees; its square parlour has a shining floor, small carpet, portraits, piano-forte, harp and scattered tables. The Cottage has a veranda, French windows and a faded sofa.

places.name: Winthrop
places.description: The Hayter family home, destination of the November walk and Henrietta's renewed attachment.
places.visual: An undistinguished low house enclosed by barns and farm buildings, seen from a hill beyond fields, hedges and stiles.

places.name: Lyme
places.description: A Dorset seaside town visited out of season, where the naval friends live and Louisa is injured.
places.visual: A steep street descends to the sea; a walk skirts a small bay to the old Cobb, its high and lower levels joined by steep steps. Cliffs, sands and a small house near the pier frame the shore.

places.name: The Harvilles' house
places.description: The hospitable naval household near the Cobb, where Louisa is nursed.
places.visual: Very small rooms fitted with handmade shelves and storm protections, curious objects from distant countries, children's toys, tools and a large fishing net.

places.name: Camden Place
places.description: Sir Walter's fashionable Bath residence, the centre of the Elliots' pursuit of consequence.
places.visual: A lofty town house with two adjoining drawing-rooms and folding doors, elegant furniture, mirrors, china and a mantel clock with silver sounds.

places.name: Westgate Buildings
places.description: The modest Bath lodgings where Anne renews her friendship with Mrs Smith.
places.visual: A noisy parlour and a dark bedroom behind it, near the hot baths; a small inlaid box of papers and handmade goods occupy the room.

places.name: The White Hart
places.description: The Bath inn where the Musgroves stay and Wentworth gives Anne his letter.
places.visual: A spacious, busy dining-room with windows, separate tables, writing materials, parcels and visitors continually arriving.

places.name: The Bath rooms
places.description: Public rooms for fashionable gatherings and the concert at which Anne recognises Wentworth's jealousy.
places.visual: An Octagon Room with fires leads to a crowded concert room of benches, orchestra, concert bills, slamming doors and elegantly dressed company.

timeline.title: Chapter 1
timeline.summary: The Elliot family history, Sir Walter's vanity, Elizabeth's disappointment and the debts threatening Kellynch are established.
events: Sir Walter consults the Baronetage and his own family entry.
The family history describes Lady Elliot's death and Anne's neglect.
Elizabeth's hopes of marrying the heir, Mr Elliot, are frustrated by his marriage and estrangement.
Sir Walter confesses the extent of his debts to Elizabeth.
Mr Shepherd and Lady Russell are called upon to advise.

knowledge.learns: She learns the full extent of her father's financial embarrassment.

timeline.title: Chapter 2
timeline.summary: A plan to economise at Kellynch fails, and the family decides to move to Bath and secretly let the Hall.
events: Lady Russell consults Anne and drafts a scheme to clear the debts.
Sir Walter rejects reductions in his household and proposes leaving Kellynch.
Mr Shepherd supports a change of residence and steers the choice toward Bath.
The family settles on letting the Hall only to an acceptable unsolicited tenant.
Lady Russell hopes the move will separate Elizabeth from Mrs Clay.

knowledge.learns: She learns that Bath, which she dislikes, is to be her home.
She sees an opportunity to interrupt Elizabeth's intimacy with Mrs Clay.

timeline.title: Chapter 3
timeline.summary: A naval tenant is proposed, and Anne hears that his wife is connected to the Wentworth family.
events: Shepherd advocates naval tenants while Sir Walter objects to sailors' rank and weathered looks.
Anne defends the navy's claim to domestic comforts.
Shepherd reports Admiral Croft's interest and describes his means and family.
Anne identifies Mrs Croft's brother as Mr Wentworth of Monkford.
Sir Walter authorises negotiations, and Anne walks alone in the grove thinking of another Wentworth.

knowledge.learns: She learns that Mrs Croft is a Wentworth and anticipates Captain Wentworth's possible return.
He learns that a prosperous admiral wishes to rent Kellynch.

timeline.title: Chapter 4
timeline.summary: The history of Anne and Wentworth's broken engagement explains her agitation at the Crofts' arrival.
events: In 1806 Anne and Frederick Wentworth fall in love and become engaged.
Sir Walter is cold, and Lady Russell urges Anne against the uncertain match.
Anne breaks the engagement, believing the sacrifice also benefits Wentworth.
Anne later refuses Charles Musgrove, while Wentworth prospers at sea.
In the present Anne considers the past and hopes the Crofts know nothing of the engagement.

knowledge.learns: At twenty-seven she believes she would have been happier keeping the engagement, though she does not blame Lady Russell or herself.

timeline.title: Chapter 5

Mary asks Anne to remain at Uppercross Cottage instead of going straight to Bath.

Sir Walter, Elizabeth and Mrs Clay leave for Bath.

timeline.title: Chapter 6
timeline.summary: Anne settles into Uppercross life and learns that Captain Wentworth is expected at Kellynch.
events: Anne finds the Musgroves absorbed in their own local concerns.
She listens to competing complaints between Mary and the Great House.
She plays country dances while the young people enjoy themselves.
The Crofts take possession at Michaelmas and return Mary's visit.
Louisa reports that her mother has connected Captain Wentworth with the late Dick Musgrove.

knowledge.learns: She learns that Frederick Wentworth is expected soon and that the Musgroves intend to seek his acquaintance.

timeline.title: Chapter 7
timeline.summary: Little Charles's injury delays Anne's reunion with Wentworth; when they meet, his coldness wounds her.

timeline.title: Chapter 8
timeline.summary: Anne and Wentworth meet repeatedly in company, where his naval stories and formal politeness intensify their estrangement.

He comforts Mrs Musgrove about her dead son despite private amusement.
He and Mrs Croft dispute the comfort of women aboard ships.
Anne plays for dancing while the young women admire Wentworth.
He offers Anne her seat at the instrument with studied politeness.

knowledge.learns: She hears how narrowly the Asp escaped a fatal gale and observes Wentworth's kindness to Mrs Musgrove.

timeline.title: Chapter 9
timeline.summary: Wentworth's attentions disturb Henrietta's cousin, while a small act of kindness deeply moves Anne.
